The return is continuing in 2025 with an increase of 44% in February 2025 than the previous month. rationaleUpdates.text:
Between April and early May 2025, the forced return of Afghan nationals from Pakistan intensified, aggravating humanitarian challenges in Afghanistan. In April alone, over 118,400 Afghans returned, including approximately 25,600 deportees. The majority of these returnees are undocumented individuals, constituting 72% of the April returns, followed by Afghan Citizen Card holders (22%) and Proof of Registration cardholders (6%). Women and girls constitute approximately 49% of the returnees. Many arrive with limited resources, facing immediate shortages in food, shelter, and livelihoods. A significant number report difficulties in securing basic necessities, with many unable to return to their original provinces or districts, compounding their vulnerability. The situation is particularly dire for women, children, and minority groups, who face heightened risks of persecution and exploitation upon return, particularly given the current sociopolitical situation in Afghanistan.
Despite many organisations providing support with basic urgent needs, the huge number of returnees are anticipated to face severe shortages of food, housing, and healthcare, along with protection risks, in the coming days. Considering the urgent needs of returnees, organisations such as IOM, UNHCR, and IFRC have launched emergency appeals, highlighting the need for further protection and integration concerns.

title: La Niña in Afghanistan worsens drought and leads to widespread agricultural losses, water scarcity, and acute food insecurity in 2026
rationale: In Afghanistan, La Niña conditions started in October 2025 and are likely to persist until the February–March 2026 period. La Niña typically brings below-normal snowfall and rainfall combined with above-average temperatures in the country, driving drought-like conditions that significantly degrade agricultural productivity and water availability. Central, northeastern, northwestern, and western regions face a heightened risk of both agricultural and hydrological drought, directly threatening food security and rural livelihoods for farming and pastoralist communities. The current agricultural deficit reflects cumulative climate stress. In the 2024–2025 period, Afghanistan faced its fourth consecutive season of below-average production, with documented crop failures across eastern and northern areas. Dry conditions are likely to affect 2025 second-season crops (rice, cotton, and maize), most of which are harvested at the end of October, while forecasted below-average winter precipitation between November 2025 and January 2026 is likely to affect winter wheat production in 2026. rationaleUpdates.text: As of March 2026, Afghanistan faces escalating climate-driven risks linked to ongoing La Niña conditions that began in October 2025. Below-average snowfall and rainfall, combined with above-normal temperatures, are reinforcing drought conditions nationwide. Central, northeastern, northwestern, and western regions are particularly affected, with rising agricultural and hydrological drought risks. This follows four consecutive years (2022–2025) of below-average production and crop failures in key regions. Second-season crops in 2025, including rice, maize, and cotton, have been impacted, while reduced winter precipitation threatens 2026 wheat production. Limited snowmelt and weakened river flows are expected to worsen water scarcity, constraining irrigation, pasture growth, and drinking water access. Pastoralist households face fodder shortages, reducing livestock productivity. Combined with earthquake impacts and large-scale population movements, these overlapping shocks are intensifying food insecurity, straining livelihoods, and overwhelming coping capacities ahead of the 2026 lean season. ([Fews Net 04/03/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/afghanistan/afghanistan-seasonal-monitor-favorable-soil-moisture-conditions-are-beneficial-spring-wheat-planting-march-3-2026), [AP News 30/03/2026](https://apnews.com/article/weather-floods-afghanistan-storm-landslide-e6be89ef89f32f5d8c68f3380bdebbe7), [FAO 21/01/2026](https://media.un.org/unifeed/en/asset/d352/d3526668), [Reuters 03/03/2026](https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/un-warns-200000-more-afghan-children-face-acute-malnutrition-2026-2026-03-03/)

In February 2026, drought risk remains high across the country. Despite some improvements in western areas, multiple sources confirm the persistence of below-average winter precipitation, low snowpack, and above-average temperatures, continuing to place significant strain on water availability, agricultural production, and food systems. The 2025 wet season began significantly below average from October–November across most areas, leading to widespread deficits. Late rains, combined with low soil moisture from earlier months, disrupted rain-fed winter wheat planting, particularly in the north and northeast, and reduced the overall planted area. Between October 2025 and January 2026, southern provinces, especially Helmand and Kandahar, experienced the highest precipitation deficits of 30–60% below average. This is constraining irrigation supplies and increasing soil moisture stress ahead of the spring 2026 agricultural season.
The WFP estimates that 17.4 million people will face acute food insecurity through March 2026, including nearly five million malnourished women and children. These outcomes are driven in part by drought-related impacts on crops and rural livelihoods, compounded by economic shocks and large-scale returnee inflows. ([FEWS NET 02/02/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/afghanistan/afghanistan-seasonal-monitor-january-precipitation-reduced-seasonal-deficits-benefiting-surface-and-groundwater-resources-february-2-2026), [IPC 16/12/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/afghanistan/afghanistan-ipc-acute-food-insecurity-analysis-september-2025-september-2026-issued-16-december-2025#:~:text=Some%20seasonal%20improvement%20is%20expected,levels%20of%20acute%20food%20insecurity.), [Crop Monitor 05/02/2026](https://www.cropmonitor.org/crop-monitor-for-early-warning), [WFP accessed 09/02/2025](https://www.wfp.org/countries/afghanistan), [FAO 06/01/2026](https://openknowledge.fao.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/46600ceb-a104-4223-88e9-0ccfae273327/content))

title: Continued attacks between Pakistan and Afghanistan increase protection risks, food security needs, and access constraints in Afghanistan’s border provinces
type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale: Humanitarian needs, particularly related to protection, food security, and access, are increasing and are at high risk of deteriorating further along the Durand Line between Afghanistan and Pakistan given the conflict escalation and air strikes between the two countries. Hostilities have spiked since 28 June 2026 along Aghanistan’s border provinces, including Kunar, Paktia, and Paktika, when a Pakistani attack killed 28 civilians and wounded 49. Pakistani authorities stated that the strikes targeted the Tehrik-e Taliban Pakistan (TTP), which they held responsible for a deadly militant attack in Karachi that killed three security personnel. Pakistan has consistently accused Afghanistan of harbouring armed groups responsible for attacks on Pakistani security forces and civilians, including the TTP, which Islamabad accuses of operating from Afghan soil. Afghanistan has denied these allegations and threatened retaliation against Pakistan for the air strikes. The latest attack comes as part of a series of tit-for-tat attacks between Afghanistan and Pakistan that started in February. After

Historically, such events have served as the primary political trigger for Pakistani retaliatory airstrikes and ground operations in Afghan border provinces like Paktia and Paktika. Th

triggers.description: Clashes between army forces in bordering areas and the closure of borders will limit movement, constrain access of humanitarian aid, interrupt livelihoods and trade between communities. In past border closures food security and livelihoods have been significantly impacted.

rationaleUpdates.text: Protection risks for communities in border areas increased in September as clashes and cross-border strikes between Pakistan and Afghanistan resumed after a temporary decline. Repeated Pakistani airstrikes and Afghan military operations have heightened the risk of civilian casualties, damage to homes, and displacement, particularly in eastern Afghanistan. Pakistan said its strikes on 21 September killed 28 fighters, while Afghan officials reported civilian casualties; the UN confirmed three civilian deaths. On 27 September, Afghan forces reported killing 28 fighters and capturing 32 in Nuristan province after they crossed from Pakistan. Further Pakistani strikes on 1 October targeted locations in Afghanistan, including Kunar and Helmand provinces. Pakistan reported 22 militants killed and weapons depots destroyed, while Taliban authorities reported 9–10 civilian deaths, including women and children, and damage to homes. The conflicting accounts highlight the risks to civilians in affected areas, where renewed hostilities could cause further casualties, displacement, and disrupted access to essential services. ([AJ 27/09/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/9/27/afghanistan-says-28-fighters-killed-as-islamabad-kabul-trade-accusations), [BBC 01/10/202](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cw4grg92lmr5o), [DW 03/10/2026](https://www.dw.com/en/pakistan-vs-afghanistan-from-allies-and-neighbors-to-war/a-79532115))

title: Escalating clashes between Interim Taliban Authority forces and armed opposition groups in Badakhshan deteriorates food security and increases protection risks
rationale: Persistent tension in Badakhshan, driven by disputes over mining resources, ethnic differences, contested territorial control, and grievances over Interim Taliban Authority (ITA) governance, risk creating recurrent instability and protection risks for communities. Armed opposition to the ITA has been building in the province over the course of 2026. ACLED recorded 22 anti-ITA armed-opposition events in Badakhshan between January–July 2026, up from just four between June–December 2025. While the recent surrender of Fateh-aligned fighters has eased the immediate risk of renewed clashes, the ITA's broader efforts to consolidate control over powerful opposition commanders and curb their influence are likely to generate resentment among these groups, increasing the risk of further infighting. ACLED forecasts at least 34 violent events nationwide in September 2026, of which 19 (roughly 56%) are projected to occur in Badakhshan alone, meaning a 17% rise in violence against civilians compared to the previous month's average. Repeated fighting over district centres could trigger short- and medium-term displacement as families flee active front lines, restricting mobility and disrupting livelihoods in turn. rationaleUpdates.text: Clashes between armed groups and Taliban forces continued in Badakhshan province in September. Between 29 August and 25 September, battles increased by 68% (eight events) and organised violence by 31% (11 events) compared with the previous year’s average. On 30 September, the Afghanistan Freedom Front reported Taliban attacks in Zebak district, following repeated clashes in recent weeks. On 29 September, the Taliban Defence Ministry declared its operation over in Kamdesh district, Nuristan province, claiming 41 people killed and 62 detained. Continued fighting could expose rural communities to casualties, movement restrictions, forced recruitment, and disruptions to education and livelihoods, although these impacts remain unverified. Humanitarian needs are compounded by food insecurity: an estimated 671,800 people (at least 40% of Badakhshan’s population) face Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse. Below-average harvests and above-national-average prices for rice, sugar, and cooking oil are likely to further constrain food access. Limited vaccination coverage and access barriers in remote areas also increase vulnerability to measles outbreaks. ([ACLED accessed 01/10/2026](https://acleddata.com/platform/trends), [AmuTv 27/09/2026](https://amu.tv/253227/), [Afintl 30/09/2026](https://www.afintl.com/en/202609302275), [FEWS NET 02/09/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/afghanistan/afghanistan-key-message-update-july-2026-january-2027-favorable-harvest-temporarily-improves-food-access-despite-lingering-drought-impacts), [KT 29/09/2026](https://thekabultribune.com/en/0011343), [Data for Afghanistan 29/09/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/afghanistan/data-afghanistan-afghanistan-food-prices-food-insecurity-report-august-2026))

title: Resource-related clashes and political tensions in Tindouf camps restrict humanitarian access and increase protection risks for Sahrawi refugees
rationale: The risk of increased instability and localised clashes in the Sahrawi refugee camps in Tindouf, Algeria, may rise over the coming months as humanitarian pressures, political uncertainty, and governance challenges compound a protracted displacement crisis. Several incidents between April–June 2026 suggest growing tensions within the camps. On 20 April, armed confrontations involving Polisario-linked elements and the Algerian National Army over humanitarian aid distribution highlighted tensions related to influence, compounded by the lack of resources. On 28 April, clashes between members of the Fakra and Oulad Moussa tribes in Smara camp escalated from a dispute over access to a water tap into armed confrontations involving live ammunition. The violence resulted in injuries and damage to tents, houses, and vehicles, raising concerns about the capacity of camp authorities to manage local disputes and prevent escalation. In this context, tensions are most likely to unfold through repeated, low-level disputes between tribes, families, or Polisario-affiliated actors in camps such as Smar
expectedImpact: Additional intercommunal violence and political tensions in the Tindouf camps would likely affect aid distribution, local governance, and social cohesion rather than trigger large-scale displacement. Humanitarian impacts would be concentrated around the camp-level systems through which assistance is delivered. rationaleUpdates.text: Political tensions within the Polisario Front intensified in August 2026. Ahead of the front's 17th General Congress, leader Ibrahim Ghali delivered increasingly hardline rhetoric at the youth and student conferences between 6–7 August, framing international pressure around UNSC Resolution 2797 as a ‘conspiracy’ and calling supporters to ‘close ranks’. This signals leadership actively managing internal dissent rather than consolidating authority, affirming leadership fragmentation. Separately, two sit-ins were held at the Tindouf camps from 16–17 August over social and humanitarian complaints directed at Polisario leadership, confirming that camp-level frustration is translating into organised protest. ([AJ 07/08/2026](https://www.aljazeera.net/amp/news/2026/8/7), [Hespress 17/08/2026](https://www.hespress.com/%D8%A7%D8%AD%D8%AA%D8%AC%D8%A7%D8%AC%D8%A7%D8%AA-%D9%85%D8%AA%D8%B2%D8%A7%D9%85%D9%86%D8%A9-%D8%AA%D9%87%D8%B2-%D8%AA%D9%86%D8%AF%D9%88%D9%81-%D9%88%D8%AA%D8%B6%D8%B9-%D9%82%D9%8A%D8%A7%D8%AF%D8%A9-1793456.html))

The risk has deteriorated. Since late July 2026, fires have destroyed vehicles of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Saguia el Hamra and Rio de Oro (Polisario) in both Smara and the Rabouni administrative headquarters, with local accounts alleging retaliatory acts linked to tribal tensions and disputes over leadership positions ahead of the 17th Polisario Congress – suggesting intra-camp tensions are moving from interpersonal disputes towards organised confrontations affecting governance infrastructure. This coincides with a WFP-confirmed funding shortage expected to halt food distributions by September, threatening food assistance for over 80% of the 133,672 Sahrawi refugees dependent on humanitarian aid across Algeria, likely to intensify competition over diminishing resources within camps. Internationally, mounting pressure around Polisario's legal status, including a US House bill gaining co-sponsors and 11 members of the European Parliament calling for a terrorist-designation assessment, and Spain's postponement of the Sahrawi citizenship bill add political uncertainty at a moment when camp governance is already under strain, increasing the likelihood of further instability ahead of the congress in late 2026. ([Yabiladi 22/07/2026](https://ar.yabiladi.com/articles/details/199090/%D8%AD%D8%B1%D8%A7%D8%A6%D9%82-%D8%AA%D9%86%D8%AF%D9%88%D9%81-%D8%AA%D8%B7%D8%A7%D9%84-%D9%85%D9%82%D8%B1-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A8%D9%88%D9%84%D9%8A%D8%B3%D8%A7%D8%B1%D9%8A%D9%88.html), [WFP 21/07/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/algeria/wfp-algeria-country-brief-july-2026-reporting-period-june-2026), [24saa 13/07/2026](https://24saa.com/%D8%A7%D9%86%D8%B6%D9%85%D8%A7%D9%85-%D9%86%D8%A7%D8%A6%D8%A8%D9%8A%D9%86-%D8%AC%D8%AF%D9%8A%D8%AF%D9%8A%D9%86-%D9%81%D9%8A-%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%83%D9%88%D9%86%D8%BA%D8%B1%D8%B3-%D9%8A%D8%B9%D8%B2%D8%B2/), [Alittihad 19/07/2026](https://alittihad.info/%D8%A8%D8%B1%D9%84%D9%85%D8%A7%D9%86%D9%8A%D9%88%D9%86-%D8%A3%D9%88%D8%B1%D9%88%D8%A8%D9%8A%D9%88%D9%86-%D9%8A%D8%AF%D8%B9%D9%88%D9%86-%D8%A5%D9%84%D9%89-%D8%B1%D8%A8%D8%B7-%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%85%D8%B3/), [Assahifa 13/07/2026](https://www.assahifa.com/%D8%A7%D9%86%D8%AA%D9%83%D8%A7%D8%B3%D8%A9-%D9%84%D9%80%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%84%D9%88%D8%A8%D9%8A-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%AF%D8%A7%D8%B9%D9%85-%D9%84%D9%84%D8%A8%D9%88%D9%84%D9%8A%D8%B3%D8%A7%D8%B1%D9%8A%D9%88/)).

title: Heavy rains in late August 2022 cause floods that affect previously affected areas, especially in the northeast, and new areas, especially in the southeast, aggravating the humanitarian situation.
type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale: Northeastern Bangladesh has been experiencing heavy pre-monsoon rains, followed by monsoon downpours, since late May 2022. The incessant rains and floodwater flowing downstream from India have inundated a significant portion of landmass. The floods have affected 15 out of 64 districts; the most inundated has been the northeast districts of Habiganj, Moulvibazar, Sunamganj, and Sylhet in Sylhet division and Netrokona in Mymensingh division. The floods have affected more than seven million people and left 3.4 million in need, with at least 1.5 million facing increased vulnerabilities. Heavy rains are expected in the northeast (along with the southeast) again. Bangladesh Meteorological Department has warned of short-term to medium-term floods in the last half of August. In July 2022, the government told that it was preparing for a flood in August. This might lead to flooding of previously affected areas (referring to the floods that occurred in May and June 2022) as well as flooding of new areas. Rohingya camps could be affected if the floods hit the southeast. The result of the floods

rationale: Since the election announcement in December 2025, at least 16 political assassinations have been reported, predominantly targeting opposition figures. Weakening institutional control has also allowed opportunistic criminal groups to exploit the unrest and further contribute to lethal incidents. The continued circulation of weapons looted during the July 2024 uprising – numbering over 3,600, with many still unrecovered – compounds the security situation. title: Prolonged fuel shortages in Bangladesh worsen food security and disrupt health, telecommunications, and other essential services
type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale: Geopolitical shocks, import dependency, and market distortions risk a prolonged or widespread fuel shortage across Bangladesh, worsening the humanitarian situation. The country imports about 95% of its petroleum – 63% from Iraq, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates via the Strait of Hormuz. The 2026 war between Israel–US and Iran has disrupted this corridor, constraining imports; continued disruptions would further limit fuel supply. Despite diversifying imports towards the US after a February 2026 trade deal, alternative routes are unable to replace Middle Eastern volumes at scale, leaving near-term shortfall risks. Bangladesh's capacity to absorb disruptions is eroding as economic conditions worsen. Inflation reached 9.13% in February 2026, and Bangladesh Petroleum Corporation import costs rose by 29% year-on-year. Pressure on foreign exchange reserves, including reduced remittance inflows from the Gulf countries affected by the war, may constrain fuel imports. Distribution practices – hoarding, panic-buying, and first-come-first-served allocation – further limit access. Thes

rationaleUpdates.text: The Haor region was hit by flash floods from pre-monsoon rainfall and upstream inflows during peak Boro harvest, damaging cropland in districts reliant on a single annual crop cycle. Farmers are facing crop losses, debt, and forced sales of wet paddy at reduced prices. Boro output is estimated to be down to 10% nationally. QatarEnergy, Bangladesh's largest LNG supplier, halved its 2026 scheduled deliveries, with Petrobangla citing Hormuz-related war disruptions and turning to costlier spot market purchases. 15.3 million people are estimated to face Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse food insecurity in May–August, rising to 18.1 million by September–December. ([Reuters 06/07/2026](https://www.reuters.com/business/energy/qatarenergy-halves-2026-scheduled-deliveries-lng-bangladesh-says-petrobangla-2026-07-06/), [IPC 30/06/2026](https://www.ipcinfo.org/fileadmin/user_upload/ipcinfo/docs/IPC_Bangladesh_Acute_Food_Insecurity_May_Dec2026_Report.pdf), [The Daily Star 01/05/2026](https://www.thedailystar.net/business/economy/news/what-it-means-rice-production-and-prices-4165046))

Available indicators suggest that the crisis has continued to deteriorate. The Government implemented two fuel price hikes, the first in April and again on 1 June, with diesel now at 115 Bangladeshi taka (USD 0.93) and petrol at 140 Bangladeshi taka (USD 1.14) per litre. Electricity tariffs were raised by 16.7%, compounding household expenditure pressures. Inflation reached a 16-month high of 9.42% in May 2026, driven by food (9.06%), housing (9.26%), and transport (9.86%), further eroding the purchasing power of low-income households. Hormuz disruptions now also threaten fertiliser supply chains, with 30–35% of global fertiliser trade transiting the route, raising acute concerns for crop yield impacts beyond the Boro season into the upcoming Aman season (rice cultivation seasons).
([The Daily Start 31/05/2026](https://www.thedailystar.net/news/environment/natural-resources/energy/news/fuel-prices-rise-again-petrol-octane-tk-5-litre-4187466),[TBS 04/06/2026]( https://www.tbsnews.net/bangladesh/energy/retail-power-tariff-hiked-tk152-amid-subsidy-cuts-1453181), [Trading Economics accessed 14/06/2026]( https://tradingeconomics.com/bangladesh/inflation-cpi))

The high inflation has reduced households purchasing power, limiting households ability to access services including health. Already 52% of children in Burundi are malnourished, while maternal and child mortality remains high at 334 deaths per 100,000 live births, and 78 deaths per 1,000 live births (higher than WHO standards).

title: Escalating cross-border insecurity linked to the Sudan conflict increases protection risks and humanitarian needs in eastern Chad
type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale: Since early 2026, the conflict in Sudan has evolved from a humanitarian crisis affecting Chad into a direct security threat to eastern border areas. Repeated drone strikes, cross-border incursions, and clashes involving fighters aligned with the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) have already caused casualties on Chadian territory, including around Tine and other border regions. These incidents indicate a growing risk that the Sudan conflict could generate sustained military confrontations, proxy violence, or retaliatory attacks inside Chad. This risk is increasingly characterised by the possibility of sustained military confrontation on Chadian territory involving RSF, SAF-aligned groups, and associated proxy forces operating along the Chad–Sudan border. This risk is driven by a convergence of security, economic, and political factors. The Chad–Sudan border has become a strategic corridor for the movement of fuel, arms, gold, and military supplies supporting groups involved in the Sudan conflict. Competition over these routes has transformed border areas into
expectedImpact: Further escalation of cross-border violence linked to the Sudan conflict could expose eastern Chad to new levels of civilian casualties, trauma, and insecurity. Additional drone strikes, shelling, armed incursions, or proxy attacks in border areas such as Adré, Tine, and the surrounding areas may directly affect civilians, trigger new displacement, and increase protection risks in communities already hosting large numbers of refugees and returnee

triggers.title: Expansion of cross-border attacks and insecurity
triggers.description: :Additional drone strikes, shelling, or armed incursions near the Chad–Sudan border, particularly around Adré, Tina, and other eastern border localities, increase civilian casualties, trigger further displacement into Chad, and constrain humanitarian operations in already fragile border areas. Continued insecurity may also disrupt cross-border trade and movement routes relied upon by refugees and host communities

triggers.title: Attacks on strategic infrastructure in Chad
triggers.description: Threats by Sudanese actors against Chadian airports, border facilities, military positions, or transport infrastructure may materialise into direct attacks on strategic assets in eastern Chad. Any strike against airports such as Amdjarass, military installations, or critical transport corridors would increase the risk of direct confrontation between Chad and Sudanese armed actors, disrupt humanitarian and commercial

triggers.title: Renewed proxy mobilisation and cross-border armed group activity
triggers.description: Historical patterns of proxy warfare between Chad and Sudan may re-emerge through the mobilisation, arming, or support of rebel groups and allied militias operating along the border. Increased involvement of SAF-aligned groups, RSF-linked actors, Darfuri armed factions, or Chadian rebel networks could expand the conflict beyond isolated border incidents and increase the likelihood of retaliatory attacks on Chadian te

rationaleUpdates.text: The risk remains active, although no significant new cross-border attacks inside Chad were identified during the second half of September. Humanitarian pressure linked to the Sudan conflict has nevertheless increased sharply as fighting in Darfur and other parts of Sudan drives renewed displacement across the border. By 25 September, more than 400 Sudanese refugees were crossing into Chad each day, around 20 times the rate recorded in previous months, bringing arrivals since the beginning of 2026 to more than 55,000. The acceleration in arrivals is increasing pressure on already overstretched reception areas and services in eastern Chad, while funding constraints affect humanitarian organisations' capacity to provide shelter, food, and relocation assistance. Continued conflict in neighbouring Sudan therefore maintains the risk of further refugee arrivals and humanitarian deterioration in eastern Chad, while the potential for renewed cross-border security incidents remains, given the heightened military presence and tensions established along the border following the August strikes. ([UNHCR 25/09/2026](https://www.unhcr.org/news/briefing-notes/unhcr-its-fourth-year-sudan-conflict-drives-new-displacement-chad-funding-falls), [Reuters 25/09/2026](https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/number-sudanese-fleeing-chad-surges-20-fold-aid-runs-dry-un-says-2026-09-25/))

The risk deteriorated in August 2026 as cross-border violence increasingly affected Chadian territory and prompted stronger security measures. On 21 August, Chad accused Sudanese Armed Forces aircraft and drones of striking a convoy more than 100km inside Ennedi-Est province, prompting authorities to raise the regional alert level to its highest and deploy additional forces. On 28 August, an air strike near the border killed at least 12 people at a fuel market, further increasing civilian protection risks and concerns over escalation. ([Reuters 27/08/2026](https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/chad-accuses-sudan-cross-border-strike-raises-alert-level-2026-08-27/), [AJ 28/08/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/28/chad-accuses-sudan-of-deadly-air-strike-near-shared-border)).

The risk remains active after slightly deteriorating in July. Cross-border insecurity continues along eastern Chad, with new drone attacks reported on 21 July near Tiné amid intensified hostilities in Darfur. One strike in Indour hit a water point, causing livestock losses and possible human casualties, while another damaged an administrative vehicle in Bamina. Between 17 June and 17 July, 23 security incidents were recorded, killing 23 people, nearly half concentrated in Ouaddai and Wadi Fira. Chadian authorities have continued disarmament operations and movement controls in Sila, reflecting persistent concerns over cross-border armed activity. Humanitarian pressures have also increased. Despite the official border closure, 4,126 new refugees arrived in July, while protection conditions during displacement worsened. The proportion of households reporting at least one human rights violation during flight increased from 53% in June to 58% in July, with reported physical violence rising from 22% to 29%. More than 220,000 refugees remain stranded in insecure border areas awaiting relocation, increasing their exposure to insecurity and limited access to services. Over the coming months, further drone strikes, cross-border violence, or proxy mobilisation could further restrict safe movement across eastern Chad and increase protection risks for refugees, returnees, and host communities. The continued backlog of relocations, rainy season access constraints, and the potential suspension of WFP food assistance from September would likely amplify the humanitarian consequences of any further deterioration in border security. ([UNHCR 30/07/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/chad/flash-updates-55-nouvel-afflux-de-refugies-soudanais-au-tchad), [UNHCR 02/08/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/chad/projet-21-tchad-urgence-soudanaise-monitoring-aux-frontieres-tendances-cles-juillet-2026), [WFP 27/07/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/chad/wfp-chad-country-brief-july-2026), [FEWS NET 04/08/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/chad/tchad-mise-jour-des-messages-cles-retard-dinstallation-de-la-saison-dans-les-provinces-de-lest-deja-en-crise-phase-3-de-lipc-juillet-2026-janvier-2027), [ICG 23/07/2026](https://www.crisisgroup.org/vid/africa/chad/sudans-war-risks-fracturing-eastern-chad)).

The risk remains active and has slightly deteriorated. Recent reporting indicates that border insecurity continues to affect eastern Chad, with refugee arrivals from Sudan slowing in May likely because of insecurity around crossing points, including a 26 May drone strike in Al-Tina. This supports the risk logic that violence linked to the Sudan conflict is increasingly affecting Chadian border areas and limiting safe mobility rather than only generating humanitarian spillover. The humanitarian exposure remains high. As of 21 June, 932,771 Sudanese refugees had arrived in Chad since April 2023, while 400,914 Chadian returnees were also recorded. Most new arrivals remain concentrated in Ouaddaï, Wadi Fira, Sila, and Ennedi Est, including 234,499 in Wadi Fira and 509,637 in Ouaddaï. UNHCR also reports that 87% of registered people are women and children and 13% have specific needs.
Protection risks are also increasing. Border monitoring between 1–15 June found that 63% of interviewed households fled Sudan because of insecurity, 42% reported human rights violations during flight, and 49% had family members still blocked in Sudan, mainly because of lack of transport means. In Wadi Fira, continued Zaghawa–Tama tensions and clashes have restricted movement and access to essential SRH and GBV services. UNFPA also reports a 90% funding gap, severely limiting life-saving SRH and protection services.
Over the next one to three months, further drone strikes, cross-border violence, or proxy mobilisation could further restrict movement across the Chad–Sudan border, increase protection risks, and strain humanitarian operations in eastern Chad. The acceleration of refugee relocations from unstable border areas to safer inland sites shows that insecurity remains a direct operational concern. If insecurity persists, humanitarian actors may face greater access constraints while refugees, returnees, and host communities face worsening protection, health, and service-access risks.
([UNFPA 16/06/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/chad/unfpa-situation-report-chad-humanitarian-response-1-31-may-2026), [UNHCR 15/06/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/chad/hcr-tchad-rapport-operationnel-hebdomadaire-du-15-avril-2026), [UNHCR 21/06/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/chad/core-emergency-situation-chad-update-arrivals-sudan-21-june-2026), [UNHCR 17/06/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/chad/p21-tchad-urgence-soudanaise-situation-de-protection-des-nouveaux-arrivants-01-15-juin-2026-fr)).

On 17 September, armed assailants killed at least 15 civilians in Madegoua, near Makary commune in Logone et Chari division. title: Intensified territorial disputes among armed groups over illegal mining corridors in southern Bolívar lead to mass displacement and confinement
type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale: Territorial disputes between non-state armed groups (NSAGs) over the control of strategic corridors and illegal mining activities in southern Bolívar have intensified dramatically since 2023, escalating humanitarian needs. Historically, the National Liberation Army (ELN) maintained territorial control and governance throughout southern Bolívar. The arrival, however, of competing NSAGs – including the Gaitanist Self-Defence Forces of Colombia (AGC), Comandos de la Frontera, dissident groups of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, and others – has fractured this control. This violent competition has triggered frequent armed confrontations, targeted attacks against civilians, population displacement, and confinement, creating acute protection risks. Conflict dynamics have steadily intensified over the past years. In Bolívar, mass displacements have become increasingly frequent. The number quadrupled from three incidents in 2023 to 16 in 2024, with 12 additional conflict-related emergencies recorded by mid-2025. All these events were in municipalities surrounding the Serranía de S
expectedImpact: Escalating armed confrontations among competing NSAGs would lead to mass displacement, confinement, and the systematic recruitment and exploitation of children by armed groups, with rural municipalities including Arenal, Montecristo, Santa Rosa del Sur, and Simití being the most affected. Displacement would primarily affect families in remote rural areas, forcing them to move to municipal centres with limited capacity to host large numbers of IDP

According to official estimates, the EGC increased its membership by 95% between 2018 and 2024, reaching around 7,000 members—including 2,499 combatants and 4,563 support network members—

At the same time, the territorial presence and influence of NSAGs, restrict free political parti

triggers.title: Increase in Military Operations
triggers.description: In response to escalating violence and territorial disputes among NSAGs, the Colombian Ministry of Defense has announced the continuation of offensive and territorial control operations in southern Bolívar. A new military unit of more than 2,500 soldiers has been deployed, with its command base established in Santa Rosa del Sur, to lead operations aimed at dismantling criminal structures operating across the region.

rationaleUpdates.text:
The risk of escalation in southern Bolívar remains sustained, with the continued consolidation of non-state armed group control and the increasing use of explosive devices (such as improvised explosive devices [IEDs]) and drones intensifying protection risks. Armed groups have strengthened their presence across the Serranía de San Lucas, expanding territorial control through recruitment, threats, confinement, killings, and displacement. This reflects a broader loss of state control and the entrenchment of violence across critical mining areas.
The use of IEDs and drone-based attacks has become more prominent in 2026, marking a shift in conflict dynamics compared to 2025. These tactics have caused direct damage to civilian infrastructure, including homes, schools, and rural water systems, while triggering displacement and confinement. This indicates increasing operational capacity and a likely continuation of remote and indiscriminate attacks affecting civilian populations.
In April, two security incidents, including an armed confrontation and an attack, affected at least 133 people. At the same time, the onset of the rainy season is increasing the risk of flooding in already-vulnerable areas, particularly among communities historically exposed to inundations.
In the short term, the combined effects of armed violence and seasonal flooding are likely to increase humanitarian needs, restrict mobility, and further limit access to essential services and assistance. ([OCHA accessed 30/04/2026](https://monitor.unocha.org/colombia), [El Original 29/04/2026](https://eloriginal.co/abril-lluvias-mil-garzas-anuncian-el-diluvio-bolivar-se-prepara-para-un-invierno-peligroso/), [OCHA 14/04/2026](https://www.unocha.org/publications/report/colombia/colombia-informe-de-situacion-humanitaria-2026-datos-acumulados-entre-enero-febrero-de-2026-fecha-de-publicacion-14-de-abril-de-2026), [FIP 22/04/2026](https://ideaspaz.org/publicaciones/investigaciones-analisis/2026-04/las-alertas-detras-del-mapa-de-10-zonas-criticas-en-seguridad-y-control-estatal))

The risk of escalation in southern Bolívar remains sustained, with increased use of explosive-laden drones intensifying conflict dynamics and protection risks. Clashes between the National Liberation Army (ELN), the Gaitanist Army of Colombia (EGC), and dissident groups of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC-EP) continue as they compete for control of illegal mining corridors, triggering displacement and heightened insecurity in rural areas.
In March 2026, armed groups demonstrated growing operational capacity through the use of drones equipped with explosive devices, including an attack on a military helicopter that injured 12 soldiers. The dismantling of a training camp in Cantagallo revealed structured efforts to train combatants in drone-based attacks and explosive ordnance use, indicating increasing technological adaptation and a likely continuation of remote attacks. Simultaneously, the discovery of more than 15 bodies in Santa Rosa del Sur, linked to armed confrontations, highlights the intensity and lethality of current disputes over strategic corridors. These developments coincide with continued displacement in municipalities such as Arenal and persistent territorial contestation, particularly over river routes critical for mobility and supply chains. In the short term, the increased use of drones and explosive devices is likely to expand the geographical reach of violence, heighten risks to civilians and infrastructure, and further restrict movement and humanitarian access, particularly in rural communities.
([RCN 28/02/2026](https://www.noticiasrcn.com/colombia/ataque-a-helicoptero-del-ejercito-en-bolivar-deja-8-militares-heridos-996915), [La FM 01/03/2026](https://www.lafm.com.co/orden-publico/consejo-de-seguridad-en-bolivar-tras-atentado-a-helicoptero-de-ejercito-y-hechos-violentos-392040), [Corrillos 21/03/2026](https://www.corrillos.com.co/hallazgo-de-15-cuerpos-profundiza-violencia-en-santa-rosa-del-sur-bolivar/), [El Frente 20/03/2026](https://elfrente.com.co/terror-en-sur-de-bolivar-hallados-16-cadaveres-en-descomposicion/), [Seguimiento.co 20/03/2026](https://seguimiento.co/colombia/cae-centro-de-drones-y-explosivos-del-clan-del-golfo-en-el-sur-de-bolivar-85054))

The risk of escalation in southern Bolívar remains sustained, with continued armed confrontations, new displacement, and compounding climatic shocks increasing humanitarian needs. In February 2026, mass displacement was reported in Arenal, with families from high lands fleeing to the urban centre following direct threats from non-state armed groups (NSAGs) and fear of being caught in clashes and bombardments. This represents recurrent displacement, as some of the affected population had already been displaced in 2025, indicating protracted vulnerability.
Social and human rights organisations issued an early warning on 12 February 2026 highlighting the intensification of clashes among NSAGs and the severe impact on agro-mining communities, including forced displacement, livelihood disruptions, and violations of international humanitarian law. The security situation has further deteriorated since the groups started using explosive-laden drones. On 6 February, the overflowing of the Caribona River and Santo Domingo Stream affected Montecristo and Arenal, creating a double-impact emergency. Floods, erosion, and climate variability affected over 15,000 people across Bolívar, while local capacities remain saturated.
In the short term, the overlap of conflict and flooding is likely to increase confinement, disrupt livelihoods, heighten protection risks for children, and further constrain humanitarian access. ([Caracol Radio 05/02/2026](https://caracol.com.co/2026/02/05/emergencia-humanitaria-en-arenal-desplazamientos-masivos-en-el-sur-de-bolivar-por-fuertes-combates/), [IFM Noticias 14/02/2026](https://ifmnoticias.com/organizaciones-de-derechos-humanos-denunciaron-escalada-de-violencia-en-el-sur-de-bolivar/), [Alerta Cartagena 04/02/2026](https://cartagena.alerta.com.co/judiciales/desplazamientos-en-arenal-al-sur-de-bolivar-233669), [OCHA 12/02/2026](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Ui8hMAnWs4K-pyZti5reCrsd-q2d8SHW/view), [El Colombiano 18/02/2026](https://www.elcolombiano.com/colombia/bolivar-calamidad-publica-municipios-lluvias-inundaciones-MP33697597))

The risk of a further escalation of violence in southern Bolívar has intensified since December 2025, driven by shifts in non-state armed group financing, expanding territorial disputes, and overstretched state response capacities. As armed groups increasingly turn to illegal gold mining, incentivised by record-high global gold prices amid geopolitical uncertainty, the strategic value of mining corridors in southern Bolívar has increased, heightening competition and the probability of violent confrontation. At the same time, changes in territorial control have led to a rise in direct clashes, with violence becoming more systemic rather than selective. Confinements and forced displacement (both mass and individual) continue to increase, disproportionately affecting rural and riverine communities, while threats increasingly materialise through mobility restrictions rather than isolated acts of intimidation.
In late January 2026, the governor of Bolívar requested urgent national-level intervention, warning that the escalation has exceeded local and departmental response capacities, signalling a shift from a localised security challenge to a crisis requiring coordinated national action. In the short to medium term, continued escalation is likely to drive further displacement, restrict humanitarian access, undermine agriculture- and mining-based livelihoods, as well as deepen protection risks. The risk posed by explosive ordnance remains high, with no new demining programmes identified until January 2026 further limiting safe movement and access to services. [Las Dos Orillas 29/01/2026](https://www.las2orillas.co/la-peligrosa-fiebre-del-oro-amenaza-con-ser-mas-violenta-que-las-guerras-del-narcotrafico/), [3iS/EHP Colombia 05/01/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/colombia/colombia-contexto-humanitario-y-conflicto-armado-magdalena-medio-2025?_gl=1*yeipiw*_gcl_au*MTM1ODQ3NDQyNC4xNzY5MTEyNTg4*_ga*MTgzMDA5Njk2NC4xNzY5MTEyNTc2*_ga_E60ZNX2F68*czE3Njk3ODczMjEkbzckZzAkdDE3Njk3ODczMjEkajYwJGwwJGgw), [El Tiempo 17/01/2026](https://www.eltiempo.com/colombia/otras-ciudades/yamil-pide-a-petro-reunion-urgente-por-escalada-armada-en-el-sur-de-bolivar-y-advierte-riesgo-humanitario-por-disputas-territoriales-armadas-ilegales-3524954), [Semana 15/01/2026](https://www.semana.com/nacion/cartagena/articulo/crisis-de-orden-publico-en-el-sur-de-bolivar-va-en-aumento-gobernador-arana-pide-reunion-urgente-con-el-presidente-petro/202616/))

The humanitarian crisis in southern Bolívar has escalated as non-state armed groups (NSAGs) consolidate territorial control through intensified violent tactics against civilians. Across the Serranía de San Lucas, displacement, confinement, and mobility restrictions have become primary tools for population control, positioning the region as one of Colombia’s most affected areas in 2025. Between January--November, confinement affected 20,894 people, mass displacement affected 5,078, and mass displacement affected 4,616 (OCHA accessed 11/12/2025).  The widespread use of explosive ordnance (EO) – including anti-personnel mines and improvised explosive devices – and the increasing use of weaponised drones aggravate this precarious environment.
The resulting EO contamination of schools, water points, and agricultural land has disrupted essential services and undermined livelihoods, driving acute food insecurity. Beyond physical threats, NSAGs exert control by intimidating community leaders and weakening local governance. These pressures are expected to intensify ahead of the 2026 electoral cycle, heightening risks of political coercion. The region’s difficult geography and poor health and goverment facility infrastructure continue to restrict humanitarian access, delaying life-saving assistance in territories where the Ombudsman’s Office has already issued high-risk early warnings given the expansion of illicit economies. ([OCHA accessed 11/12/2025](https://monitor.unocha.org/colombia), [OCHA accessed 22/12/2025](https://monitor.unocha.org/colombia), [OCHA 24/10/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/colombia/informe-de-tendencias-e-impacto-humanitario-en-2025-datos-acumulados-entre-enero-septiembre-de-2025-fecha-de-publicacion-24-de-octubre-de-2025-enes), [DP 10/02/2025](https://www.defensoria.gov.co/-/defensor%C3%ADa-del-pueblo-alerta-sobre-crisis-humanitaria-en-el-sur-de-bol%C3%ADvar), [PARES 06/03/2025](https://www.pares.com.co/sur-de-bolivar-entre-coca-oro-y-guerra/), 
[El Universal 15/12/2025](https://www.eluniversal.com.co/regional/bolivar/2025/12/15/crisis-de-violencia-en-el-sur-de-bolivar-reiteran-alertas-ante-autoridades/))

The risk trend has deteriorated over the past month as nonstate armed groups have expanded mobility restrictions, attacks against civilians, and territorial control in southern Bolívar. Armed strikes, blockades on food and fuel, and the use of explosive-bearing drones have deepened confinement and disrupted access to services. Around 34,900 people experienced forced displacement, confinement, or mobility restrictions from January–November 2025. Key developments include a 4 November massacre in San Pablo targeting mining workers, increased pressure and threats against civic authorities, and the coercive use of children and adolescents in support roles. Armed groups are also assuming quasi-state functions, arbitrating community disputes and consolidating subregional dependence. Sustained mine contamination in Montecristo and Arenal, attacks on schools, the prolonged suspension of classes affecting 1,370 students, and the kidnapping of a community leader indicate continued escalation. Short- to medium-term impacts include worsening food insecurity as a result of blockades, reduced mobility, contaminated water sources, heightened psychological distress, and major constraints on humanitarian access and safe political participation ahead of 2026. ([OCHA 08/08/2025](https://www.unocha.org/publications/report/haiti/latin-america-caribbean-weekly-situation-update-8-august-2025), [Cambio 06/08/2025](https://cambiocolombia.com/conflicto-armado-en-colombia/articulo/2025/8/ejercito-sur-bolivar-eln-clan-golfo-confinamiento-conflicto-armado/), [Caracol Radio 07/11/2025](https://caracol.com.co/2025/11/07/tres-muertos-dejo-presunta-incursion-armada-del-eln-en-una-mina-de-oro-del-sur-de-bolivar/), [DP 22/09/2025](https://alertasstg.blob.core.windows.net/alertas/013-25.pdf), [EE 06/10/2025](https://www.elespectador.com/colombia-20/paz-y-memoria/guerra-en-sur-de-bolivar-desplazados-vuelven-a-la-zona-donde-hay-minas-antipersonal-y-combates-entre-eln-y-clan-del-golfo/), [OCHA accessed 10/11/2024](https://monitor.unocha.org/colombia), [OCHA accessed 27/11/2025](https://monitor.unocha.org/colombia))

title: La Niña-driven above-normal rainfall and flooding in Colombia cause widespread crop damage, landslides, waterborne diseases, and food insecurity and malnutrition
rationale: An above-average rainy season is forecast for northern and northwestern Colombia through the remainder of 2025 and early 2026 (November–January), as La Niña conditions are expected to persist across the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean until the February–March 2026 period. This will likely lead to abundant rains, increasing the flood risk across Atlántico, northern Bolívar, Córdoba, La Guajira, Magdalena, Sucre, and the islands of San Andrés and Providencia department. The second half of 2025 has already seen above-average rainfall, widespread flooding, and local and national response systems operating at full capacity, leaving the country more vulnerable to La Niña’s impacts. Heavy rainfall has affected almost 25,000 in just Bolívar, Córdoba, and Magdalena. Between November–January, rainfall is forecasted to increase by up to 30% in the regions expected to be affected, aggravating floods and landslides, damaging infrastructure, and destroying public buildings and main roads. Flooding may affect crops and reduce agricultural production, particularly harming communities th
expectedImpact: Above-average rainfall linked to La Niña is expected to affect at least five departments in Colombia, including the Pacific Islands. The rains are likely to reduce both the capacity and volume of food production, limiting availability for farmers and households reliant on local markets. Infrastructure is also at high risk; many roads are unpaved and prone to flooding, while months of heavy rain have already weakened paved routes, increasing the l
materialised: From November 2025 to January 2026, heavy rains, floods, and landslides impacted 115,000 families, affected 24 of the country's 32 departments, and forced the closure of major roads in several departments across the country. This resulted in 600 reported emergencies. The risk materialised both in im

triggers.title: El Niño/La Niña-Southern Oscillation
triggers.description: Climate forecasts predict La Niña conditions through November 2025 to January 2026, increasing rainfall across Haiti, which will bring flooding and landslides.

rationaleUpdates.text:
Between January-June 2026, at least 600 rain-related emergencies have been reported in 24 of Colombia's 32 departments, affecting 155,000 families – five times more than in the first semester of 2025. Floods and rising river levels were concentrated particularly in the departments of Antioquia, Caldas, Córdoba, Cundinamarca, Huila, and Valle del Cauca. The transition from La Niña to El Niño is expected by June, with El Niño reaching its peak in September. As a result, rainfall has already decreased, and above-average temperatures and below-average rainfall are expected in the coming months.
([Marsh 01/05/2026](https://www.marsh.com/es/services/climate-change-adaption/insights/climate-agenda-2026-el-nino-impact.html), [UNGRD 25/03/2026](https://portal.gestiondelriesgo.gov.co/Paginas/Noticias/2026/Asi-se-comportara-el-clima-en-Colombia-IDEAM-UNGRD-y-DIMAR-entregan-predicciones-y-recomendaciones.aspx), [WWF 13/02/2026](https://www.wwf.org.co/?399751/Lluvias-en-Colombia-2026), [El Tiempo 25/03/2026](https://www.eltiempo.com/vida/medio-ambiente/emergencia-nacional-por-lluvias-hay-mas-de-155-000-familias-damnificadas-un-574-mas-que-el-ano-anterior-3542816))

La Niña-associated heavy rainfall and flooding across Colombia appear to have subsided, with neutral conditions and average precipitation maintained throughout April. However, Colombia is now transitioning towards El Niño conditions, with a 60% probability of onset between May and June, rising to 90% between June and November. El Niño is typically associated with elevated temperatures, drought, heatwaves, and below-average rainfall — conditions that are in direct contrast to those produced by La Niña and that carry significant implications for agricultural production, water availability, and food security across already vulnerable communities in the months ahead. ([CPC 09/04/2026](https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/analysis_monitoring/enso_advisory/ensodisc_Sp.shtml); [IDEAM 11/04/2026](https://www.ideam.gov.co/sala-de-prensa/noticia/ideam-y-minambiente-alertan-de-90-de-probabilidad-de-llegada-del-fenomeno-de-el-nino-para-septiembre#:~:text=Existe%20una%20probabilidad%20del%2061%25%20de%20que,en%20un%2090%25%20para%20septiembre%20de%202026.))

Persistent La Niña-associated rainfall across Colombia has shown signs of easing throughout March, indicating a trend toward stabilization and a slight improvement in humanitarian conditions. By late February, more than half a million people across 22 departments had been affected by heavy rainfall since the start of 2026; however, heavy rain recorded during March does not seem to have created climatic events of comparable magnitude or significantly increased the number of people affected. Only in the department of Huila, in southern Colombia, was heavy rainfall recorded, but without resulting in new people affected.
Looking ahead, conditions are expected to shift from above-average rainfall to below-average precipitation, signaling a move toward seasonal drought across affected areas. This poses an additional concern for food production, given that tens of hectares of crops and thousands of animals had already been lost due to the previous flooding — leaving agricultural communities with significantly reduced capacity to recover and sustain livelihoods in the coming months. ([ECHO 10/03/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/colombia/colombia-severe-weather-ideam-meteo-colombia-media-echo-daily-flash-10-march-2026?_gl=1*1hbd590*_gcl_au*MTU4NjgyOTk1MS4xNzY4NTYzNzI4*_ga*NDU4MTg0MzExLjE3Njg1NjMzNjI.*_ga_E60ZNX2F68*czE3NzU0NzgyNTMkbzQkZzEkdDE3NzU0NzgzODckajU5JGwwJGgw); [ECHO 06/03/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/colombia/colombia-floods-and-landslides-update-dg-echo-wfp-ungrd-un-ocha-ideam-echo-daily-flash-6-march-2026?_gl=1*c11nxx*_gcl_au*MTU4NjgyOTk1MS4xNzY4NTYzNzI4*_ga*NDU4MTg0MzExLjE3Njg1NjMzNjI.*_ga_E60ZNX2F68*czE3NzU0NzgyNTMkbzQkZzEkdDE3NzU0Nzg0MTMkajMzJGwwJGgw); [Infobae 25/03/2026](https://www.infobae.com/colombia/2026/03/26/colombia-pasaria-de-inundaciones-a-sequia-en-2026-las-autoridades-lanzan-alerta-por-la-llegada-de-el-nino/))

Persistent heavy rainfall associated with La Niña conditions triggered widespread landslides and flooding across Colombia in January and February 2026, affecting nearly 252,000 individuals across 22 of the country's 32 departments and compounding an already deteriorating humanitarian situation. Córdoba remains the most critically affected department, accounting for 66% of the national caseload, with the majority of its territory inundated. In La Guajira, flooding had reached approximately 32,000 people by early February; the department's capital water network is at risk of overflow, further aggravating chronic drinking water shortages that disproportionately impact Indigenous communities in the area.
Damage to critical infrastructure — including water systems, schools, healthcare facilities, and housing — has been reported across Antioquia, Cauca, Chocó, Córdoba, La Guajira, Nariño, and Sucre. The destruction of road networks continues to constrain both national and humanitarian response capacities, deepening pre-existing vulnerabilities among affected populations. With La Niña conditions expected to persist for March, the situation is expected to deteriorate further with more floods, increasing the risk of compounding impacts on communities already exposed to climatic shocks since late 2025. ([Copernicus Accessed 27/02/2026](https://mapping.emergency.copernicus.eu/activations/EMSR865/reporting/); [OCHA 20/02/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/colombia/latinoamerica-y-el-caribe-resumen-de-situacion-semanal-al-20-de-febrero-2026?_gl=1*1a04k3b*_gcl_au*MTU4NjgyOTk1MS4xNzY4NTYzNzI4*_ga*NDU4MTg0MzExLjE3Njg1NjMzNjI.*_ga_E60ZNX2F68*czE3NzE4NDY0NjUkbzcyJGcxJHQxNzcxODQ2Njk1JGo2MCRsMCRoMA); [OCHA Emergency Tracker Accessed 23/02/2026](https://colombia-emergency-response-tracker.consorcioevidem.org/))

title: Peace talk end and military offensive against armed groups in Colombia escalate conflict and increase civilian casualties and displacement
rationale: After the elections in June 2026, Abelardo de la Espriella’s win as Colombia's new President signalled a major change in the country's stance towards non-state armed groups (NSAGs) and drug trafficking organisations. The President-elect has since announced an end to peace negotiations and a nationwide military offensive to begin once he takes office on 7 August, including a 90-day security crackdown involving military deployments, aerial operations, and coca eradication measures. This shift may increase the risk of clashes, civilian casualties, displacement, and confinement, particularly in Pacific Coast departments, including Cauca, Chocó, Nariño, and Valle del Cauca, as well as in Norte de Santander and Putumayo, which were among Colombia’s most conflict-affected areas in 2025. This risk is compounded by the significant strengthening of NSAGs in recent years. Armed group membership has grown substantially since 2022. Armed groups have simultaneously expanded into new territories, adopted new warfare tactics, including the use of explosive drones, and extended social control against
expectedImpact: The expected impact of intensifying NSAG activity and a state military offensive extends to the entire population of the departments highlighted, approximately 10.6 million people, who face risks of forced displacement, confinement, and attacks against civilians. Military operations and armed group retaliation are also expected to increase risks of civilian casualties, attacks against communities, and humanitarian access restrictions in affected

triggers.title: Launch of the 90-Day Security Crackdown
triggers.description: The incoming government’s planned military offensive against NSAGs from 7 August, including bombing campaigns against armed group camps, aerial coca fumigation, deployment of Joint Task Forces to Cauca, Chocó, and Nariño, and increased defence investment, is expected to provoke armed group retaliation against security forces and civilians perceived to be cooperating with the State.

triggers.title: NSAG consolidation and territorial expansion
triggers.description: The significant strengthening of NSAGs since 2022, including a reported increase in membership, territorial expansion, adoption of new tactics, and increased reliance on illicit economies such as coca cultivation and illegal mining, increases the likelihood that armed groups will seek to consolidate control over contested territories and demonstrate operational capacity ahead of and during the anticipated offensive.

triggers.title: Formal termination of peace negotiations
triggers.description: A decision by the incoming government to end the outgoing administration’s “Total Peace” talks with NSAGs would remove an important mechanism for dialogue and de-escalation. The breakdown of ELN talks preceding the escalation of fighting in Catatumbo (Norte de Santander) in January 2025 illustrates how quickly violence and displacement can increase following the collapse of negotiations.

triggers.title: Bureaucratic cuts and public sector purges
triggers.description: Implementation of the pledged 40% reduction in the state apparatus and removal of officials linked to the outgoing administration could trigger sustained protest mobilisation, adding a civil unrest dimension to the security risk through potential clashes with security forces and increased protection concerns.

rationaleUpdates.text: In September, intensified state operations and continued armed group activity sustained conflict-related protection risks in Colombia. Between January–August, 23,931 people were affected by mass displacement and 80,369 by confinement, with Cauca, Chocó, Norte de Santander, and Putumayo among the most affected departments. In August alone, 5,976 people were displaced and 6,201 confined. The Government’s shift towards military pressure has increased the lethality of operations against armed groups, while attacks using explosive drones remain a concern, particularly in Cauca and Norte de Santander. Further military pressure may redirect armed group activity towards state forces in the short term, while territorial competition, retaliatory attacks, and incursions into contested areas could sustain violence over the following months. Civilians in rural and Indigenous communities remain exposed to displacement, confinement, movement restrictions, and disrupted access to markets and livelihoods. ([El País 29/09/2026](https://elpais.com/america-colombia/2026-09-29/la-ofensiva-del-gobierno-contra-los-pachenca-deja-a-santa-marta-en-una-fragil-calma.html), [ACLED 02/09/2026](https://acleddata.com/expert-comment/total-peace-prison-or-death-de-la-espriellas-offensive-colombia), [FEWS NET accessed 02/10/2026](https://fews.net/latin-america-and-caribbean/colombia/key-message-update/september-2026))

The risk deteriorated during August 2026 as the new Government’s military offensive coincided with intensified armed group violence and growing civilian exposure. In Sipí and Nóvita municipalities, Chocó department, fighting between the Clan del Golfo and National Liberation Army (ELN) since 10 August has restricted mobility and livelihoods, displaced hundreds of families, and confined other communities; a 23 August drone attack injured three civilians and displaced 90 families to Barranco, Charco Hondo, and Charco Largo. The Government conducted air strikes against the ELN in Tibú and San Calixto municipalities, Norte de Santander, on 10 August and against dissident groups of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia in El Retorno and Miraflores municipalities, Guaviare, on 27 and 30 August. The first two operations killed at least four minors. In El Patía municipality, Cauca, suspected Carlos Patiño members attacked security forces, while five improvised explosive devices were found on the Pan-American Highway. These events indicate that the anticipated escalation is materialising through simultaneous non-state armed group violence, intensified state operations, and increased risks to civilians and key transport routes. ([El Tiempo 01/09/2026](https://www.eltiempo.com/colombia/cali/ejercito-evita-una-tragedia-mayor-tras-ataque-con-camion-bomba-en-via-panamericana-en-cauca-vehiculo-tenia-otros-5-explosivos-y-fueron-neutralizados-3582611); [El Espectador 01/09/2026](https://www.elespectador.com/judicial/aumentan-a-16-los-heridos-tras-ataque-terrorista-del-eln-con-carro-bomba-en-los-patios/); [El Pais 31/09/2026](https://elpais.com/america-colombia/2026-09-01/tres-bombardeos-en-tres-semanas-la-primera-estrategia-de-seguridad-del-gobierno-de-de-la-espriella.html); [Eje21 26/08/2026](https://www.eje21.com.co/2026/08/defensoria-del-pueblo-de-colombia-alerta-sobre-combates-en-zona-afectada-por-el-terremoto/), [ACLED 27/08/2026](https://acleddata.com/report/drones-are-re-shaping-armed-group-warfare-latin-americhttps://acleddata.com/report/drones-are-re-shaping-armed-group-warfare-latin-america)).

Since the election of right-wing politician Abelardo de la Espriella as President of Colombia, the activities of non-state armed groups (NSAGs) in Colombia's peripheral departments have increased especially in July 2026, intensifying the likelihood of rising humanitarian impacts. In Norte de Santander, a department in eastern Colombia on the border with Venezuela, the NSAG known as the National Liberation Army (ELN) attacked with explosive-laden drones the main airport in Catatumbo subregion; in the department of Chocó, west of the country, the ELN kidnapped 39 people while they were travelling along a main departmental road. Other NSAGs also stole armoured vehicles, set up illegal checkpoints, and engaged in combat against the armed forces in departments such as Cauca and Valle del Cauca, south of Chocó in western Colombia. In response, the new de la Espriella Government has announced an offensive against illicit crops and illegal mining, the main source of financing for NSAGs, as well as an operation to reassert state control over territories in the departments of Cauca, Chocó, Nariño, and Norte de Santander, where these groups are the strongest. ([NTN 24 23/07/2026](https://www.ntn24.com/noticias-actualidad/combates-entre-el-ejercito-nacional-y-las-disidencias-de-las-farc-dejaron-siete-militares-heridos-y-dos-disidentes-muertos-en-el-tambo-cauca-635769); [France 24 14/07/2026](https://www.france24.com/es/minuto-a-minuto/20260714-la-guerrilla-del-eln-secuestra-a-39-personas-en-colombia); [DW 10/07/2026](https://www.dw.com/es/el-eln-atenta-con-explosivos-contra-aeropuerto-en-colombia/a-77898317); [Insight Crime 08/07/2026](https://insightcrime.org/news/new-president-hard-line-approach-coca-colombia/))

title: Worsening energy shortages and U.S. pressure lead to essential service disruptions and rising humanitarian needs in Cuba
type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale: The reduction in Cuba’s oil imports – following the suspension of Venezuela’s daily supply of approximately 30,000 barrels and the continued pressure to prevent alternative sourcing from Mexico – has created an energy deficit equivalent to at least 30% of the country’s daily needs. Given Cuba’s reliance on imported fuel to operate even at reduced capacity, this shortfall is already contributing to prolonged power outages and fuel scarcity. Over the next six months, unless alternative fuel supply arrangements materialise rapidly, the convergence of acute fuel supply disruption and structural economic fragility is likely to drive rapid and compounding humanitarian deterioration across Cuba. Power outages of 12–20 hours daily are already cascading across health, water, food, and social protection sectors in mutually reinforcing ways: hospitals losing electrical backup, ambulances unable to refuel, and refrigeration failures disrupting food imports collectively represent systemic stress – not isolated shocks – across interconnected service delivery chains. This trajectory is expected to
expectedImpact: The crisis is expected to cause severe humanitarian impacts across multiple interconnected sectors. Direct mortality risks are high, particularly among the five million people with chronic illnesses. Treatment interruptions for cancer patients requiring radiotherapy or chemotherapy, disrupted dialysis services, compromised obstetric care for pregnant women, and failing life-support equipment in hospitals experiencing prolonged power outages make
materialised: Three major nationwide blackouts in March 2026 – the direct consequence of a critical oil import deficit – have left almost all of Cuba's 10 million inhabitants without reliable access to electricity, producing cascading humanitarian impacts across the country. Disruptions to healthcare services, tr

triggers.title: Prolonged inability to secure fuel imports at market rates
triggers.description: If Cuba cannot obtain licenses or afford commercial fuel purchases under new U.S. licensing policies within the next 4–8 weeks, the energy deficit will persist through summer 2026. This would maintain or intensify current service disruptions, worsening the humanitarian situation.

triggers.title: Depletion of strategic fuel reserves
triggers.description: If Cuba has been drawing on stockpiles since January, these reserves may be exhausted within 2–4 months. Reserve depletion would trigger more severe rationing and could force complete shutdown of non-essential services.

triggers.title: Extreme weather events (hurricane season June–November 2026)
triggers.description: Hurricanes or tropical storms affecting fuel supply lines, damaging electrical infrastructure, or disrupting already fragile food production systems. Cuba is particularly vulnerable given deteriorated infrastructure and reduced maintenance capacity.

rationaleUpdates.text:
Cuba continues to suffer the consequences of fuel production that barely met 40% of national needs by 2025, as well as the effects of the US embargo, which prevents it from importing fuel from Venezuela, formerly its main supplier. As a result, June saw the third nationwide blackout, affecting 9.5 million people – almost the entire population. The effects ranged from paralysed transportation and the inability to work at night to delays in public health services. Meanwhile, there has been no progress in talks between the Cuban and US Governments to lift the embargo, as the latter demands that the current rulers step down, fully open the Cuban economy, and hold elections supervised by US authorities and international organizations – something that does not appear likely to happen in the near future.
([AJ 11/06/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/6/11/trump-administration-sanctions-cubas-national-oil-company-blasts-castros), [El Financiero 10/06/2026](https://www.elfinanciero.com.mx/mundo/2026/06/10/se-avecina-un-verano-oscuro-para-cuba-apagones-le-quitan-el-sueno-a-los-cubanos/), [El Comercio 10/06/2026](https://www.elcomercio.com/actualidad/mundo/cuba-enfrenta-apagones-severos-crisis-energetica/))

The collapse of Cuba's national electricity grid – driven by a critical deficit in oil imports – has affected almost all ten million people living on the island, with three major or nationwide blackouts recorded in March 2026. The outages have caused widespread disruptions to transportation systems, healthcare services, energy production, essential public services, and the broader economy. The fuel deficit has also constrained the capacity of both the Government and international organisations to offer humanitarian aid to the more than 4.2 million people in need given power outages and the impacts of Hurricane Melissa, which caused significant destruction across the eastern provinces in October 2025. The oil deficit is expected to persist and potentially worsen given the sustained US-imposed trade blockade on Cuba, meaning that power outages and their associated humanitarian consequences are likely to continue. Of particular concern is the risk of compounding damage to the national electricity infrastructure itself, which would result in longer periods of power outages than the 48 hours the power grid was down in March, as well as worse humanitarian impacts. ([OCHA 02/04/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/cuba/plan-action-united-nations-system-cuba-response-energy-and-hurricane-melissa-emergencies-march-2026), [CNN 21/03/2026](https://edition.cnn.com/2026/03/21/americas/cuba-second-nationwide-blackout-latam-intl), [The Guardian 22/03/2026](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/mar/22/cubas-power-grid-collapses-in-third-nationwide-blackout-amid-us-oil-blockade))

The electricity deficit in Cuba continues a gradual but steady deterioration, linked to reduced oil imports from key suppliers such as Mexico and Venezuela and the cumulative impact of recurrent nationwide blackouts. By March 2026, two national‑level outages had been reported, temporarily affecting most of the country’s approximately ten million inhabitants and representing a marked increase compared with the late‑2025 blackout that affected around three million people across the country. In parallel, negotiations between the US and Cuban authorities under President Miguel Díaz‑Canel have continued, including measures by the Cuban Government to facilitate greater private investment and engagement with parts of the Cuban diaspora, which has historically included prominent critics of the current administration. Despite these talks, the US has maintained and in some areas stepped up political and economic pressure on Cuba, while some public statements by US officials and commentators have raised questions about potential future courses of action. A significant further escalation – including any move towards the use of force – would carry substantial protection risks for civilians, including increased risks of violence, displacement, and constraints on safe movement and access to essential services.

rationaleUpdates.text: The risk has partially deteriorated. A sustained collapse in Suez Canal traffic has still not materialised, but regional maritime and energy security threats have increased. In late July 2026, renewed Houthi attacks and threats against shipping in the Bab Al Mandab Strait prompted some tankers to reroute or reverse course, while Saudi Arabia increasingly relied on Egypt's Suez–Mediterranean pipeline and Suez corridor to maintain oil exports, increasing the strategic importance of Egyptian transit infrastructure. On 30 July, a drone strike damaged two gas tankers at Egypt's Damietta port, highlighting that regional conflict has expanded to Egyptian energy infrastructure, although Suez Canal operations were not disrupted. Inflationary pressures remained elevated despite some easing. Annual urban headline inflation declined slightly to 14.3% in June, while annual food inflation slowed to 5.4% after reaching 7.6% in May. ([Reuters 30/07/2026](https://www.reuters.com/business/energy/drone-strike-egypt-sparks-security-concerns-about-suez-oil-exports-2026-07-30/), [Reuters 31/07/2026](https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/imf-completes-egypt-reviews-unlocks-18-billion-2026-07-31/), [CBE 09/07/2026](https://www.cbe.org.eg/en/news-publications/news/2026/07/09/17/02/mpc-press-release-9-july-2026))

The risk continued to deteriorate as regional conflict-related economic pressures persisted, although a renewed Red Sea blockade and major Suez Canal disruption did not materialise. Instead, Egypt remained exposed to higher energy and agricultural input costs, with inflationary pressures affecting food access and production. Food inflation increased to 7.6% year-on-year in May 2026, while fertiliser markets remained affected by regional energy disruptions given the sector’s dependence on natural gas. The Government continued measures to secure fuel supplies and manage electricity demand during the summer, reflecting persistent concerns over energy availability and costs. These pressures are likely to continue affecting agricultural production costs and household purchasing power, particularly among lower-income households. ([Daily News Egypt 20/06/2026](https://www.dailynewsegypt.com/2026/06/20/annual-urban-inflation-eases-to-14-6-in-may-as-non-food-price-pressures-moderate-cbe/), [Daily News Egypt 10/06/2026](https://www.dailynewsegypt.com/2026/06/10/egypts-headline-inflation-eases-to-14-6-in-may-core-rate-steady-at-13-8/), [SIS 30/06/2026](https://sis.gov.eg/en/media-center/news/electricity-petroleum-ministers-review-joint-summer-plan-to-meet-rising-power-demand/))

Fertiliser prices increased from around USD 400 per tonne before the war to USD 700–750 per tonne by May. This represents an increase of approximately 75–87.5%, while fuel prices increased by up to 30%, contributing to higher agricultural input costs and reduced cultivation. Farmers in rural areas south of Cairo reduced cultivated land, laid off agricultural workers, and shifted away from fertiliser-intensive crops such as wheat, maize, and rice. Egypt produces 7–8 million tonnes of nitrogen fertiliser annually but remains exposed to global price volatility because of uneven domestic distribution and reliance on imported energy inputs. The country also imports 12–14 million tonnes of wheat annually to sustain its subsidised bread system, increasing macro-level vulnerability to food and input price shocks. ([TNA 15/05/2026](https://www.newarab.com/news/egypts-farmers-hit-iran-war-price-surge?amp), [RFI 15/05/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/en/international-news/20260515-egypt-farmers-hit-by-iran-war-price-surge))

title: Forecast below-average Kiremt rains in Ethiopia threaten food production and livelihoods
rationale: El Niño conditions are forecast to develop by July 2026 and strengthen through the second half of the year. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration puts the probability of El Niño from May–July at around 61%, rising to 87–92% between July 2026 and January 2027. Severe localised deficits are likely in the northeast and central areas, with at least 50% probability of deficits reaching 50% or more. Kiremt is the primary rainy season for Ethiopia's northern and central cropping areas, governing the Meher harvest – the country's most important crop season, which produces the most teff, maize, sorghum, wheat, and barley across Amhara, Central Ethiopia, Oromia, the Southern regions, and Tigray.
