rationaleUpdates.text:
The risk remained stable in September, with conditions continuing to follow the drought-then-flood pattern expected under El Niño. Rainfall deficits during the June–September Kiremt rains exceeded 50% of average across much of the country, and the Meher harvest, which provides over 85% of national crop production, could be up to 30% below average, with the worst-affected areas being Tigray, eastern Amhara, Afar, and eastern Oromia regions. Slight late-season improvements in rainfall are unlikely to help earlier planted crops substantially, although later planted crops may benefit. In northeastern pastoral areas, deficits have rapidly depleted surface water and increased distances to watering points, while pasture in the southeast is deteriorating after the rains ended. Crisis (IPC Phase 3) outcomes are expected to persist through January 2027 across many drought-affected areas, with some households facing Emergency (IPC Phase 4). October–December rainfall is forecast to be above average, with up to a 90% probability of enhanced rainfall in southern Ethiopia. In September, the Ethiopian Meteorological Institute warned of flash flooding and landslides in southwestern, southern, and southeastern lowlands, with rainfall up to 75% above normal in parts of the south. The institute also cautioned that unseasonal rains in northern, northeastern, and eastern areas could damage mature crops ready for harvest, meaning drought and flood impacts could occur at the same time in different parts of the country.
([FEWS NET accessed 29/09/2026](https://fews.net/east-africa/ethiopia/food-security-outlook-update/august-2026), [FEWS NET 11/09/2026](https://fews.net/east-africa/seasonal-monitor/september-2026) [The Reporter Ethiopia 19/09/2026](https://www.thereporterethiopia.com/52897))

The risk deteriorated in August 2026 as parts of central and northern Ethiopia experienced a very poor start to the June–September Kiremt season, with persistent rainfall deficits accompanied by soil-moisture and vegetation stress. These conditions have increased concerns over reduced agricultural production and productivity, as well as pressure on pasture and water resources. El Niño is forecast to strengthen through late 2026. ([ICPAC 11/08/2026](https://www.icpac.net/publications/climate-watch-advisory-the-evolving-dry-conditions-in-the-northern-parts-of-eastern-africa-august-2026-update), [ICPAC/FSNWG 19/08/2026](https://www.icpac.net/fsnwg/fsnwg-special-report-on-el-ni%C3%B1o/)).

rationaleUpdates.text: Rainfall patterns across Haiti over the past month have remained erratic, with slightly above-average precipitation recorded in central areas of the country and slightly below-average rainfall in the northwest. This has kept the overall risk trend broadly stable. However, the island's primary rainy season is expected to commence in late March or early April, with the potential to rapidly deteriorate conditions through an increase in flooding and landslide events. While no significant new flood events have been recorded in recent weeks, populations affected by early 2026 rainfall and those still recovering from the impacts of Hurricane Melissa in October 2025 continue to present unmet emergency humanitarian needs. Should rainfall increase above average levels from April and onwards, these populations face the risk of compounded humanitarian impact, with pre-existing needs to access health services and food, exacerbated by new shocks generated by the incoming rainy season.([PAHO,UNFCCC, WHO 19/03/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/haiti/health-and-climate-change-country-profile-2025-haiti?_gl=1*gxar1b*_gcl_au*MTU4NjgyOTk1MS4xNzY4NTYzNzI4*_ga*NDU4MTg0MzExLjE3Njg1NjMzNjI.*_ga_E60ZNX2F68*czE3NzUwMTI4MjEkbzgzJGcxJHQxNzc1MDE0MDc3JGoyNSRsMCRoMA..); [Britanica Accessed 31/03/2026](https://www.britannica.com/place/Haiti/Climate); [Fews Net 03/03/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/haiti/haiti-seasonal-monitor-above-average-vegetation-health-across-most-areas-haiti-march-2-2026))

During the first two months of 2026, Haiti experienced above-average cumulative rainfall across parts of the country, a result of La Niña conditions forecast for the first semester of the year. However, these anomalies were driven primarily by episodic heavy rainfall events interspersed with dry spells, reflecting significant intra-seasonal variability. La Niña conditions are expected to transition to ENSO-neutral by late March this year, increasing the scale of dry spells and reducing rainfall.
The humanitarian impact of recent rainfall has compounded the effects of Hurricane Melissa in late October last year, which caused widespread destruction of roads, houses, health facilities, and schools. These consecutive shocks, layered on the ongoing consequences of gang violence — which has displaced millions of people internally — have significantly deepened the vulnerability of affected populations. Those exposed to both crises face heightened susceptibility to the humanitarian consequences of the February flooding and the drought conditions forecast from April to June. Additionally, a sustained increase in cholera cases has been recorded across Haiti since 2025, a trend that is likely to be exacerbated by the recent rainfall and the deterioration of water, sanitation, and hygiene conditions associated with flooding events. ([Copernicus Accessed 27/02/2025](https://climate.copernicus.eu/charts/packages/c3s_seasonal/products/c3s_seasonal_spatial_mm_rain_3m?area=area06&base_time=202601010000&type=tsum&valid_time=202602010000); [Haitian Times 25/02/2026](https://haitiantimes.com/2026/02/25/cap-haitien-tries-to-bounce-back-after-heavy-rains-flood-downtown-disrupt-city-life-photos/); [CPI 19/02/2026](https://periodismoinvestigativo.com/2026/02/haiti-farmers-build-community-irrigation-network/))

The seasonal forecast for February–April 2026 indicates a likelihood of above-average rainfall across most of Haiti, except the Nord-Ouest department, marking a stabilization of the trend risk highlighted in December. La Niña conditions are expected to transition to ENSO-neutral by the second trimester of 2026, decreasing overall climate risk across the country.
Although no extreme rainfall has been reported by January, communities are still recovering from landslides and flooding caused by Hurricane Melissa in late October 2025. Rural populations already displaced by gang violence and affected by the hurricane remain particularly vulnerable to further flooding, as water and sanitation infrastructure have been destroyed, and local response capacities are already strained. In parallel, Haiti is experiencing a resurgence of cholera cases, reversing recent improvements; above-average rainfall and flooding could further exacerbate transmission, given the waterborne nature of the disease. ([Fews Net 15/01/2026](https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/international/FEWS_REPORT/Haiti/Current.pdf); [Copernicus Accessed 30/01/2025](https://climate.copernicus.eu/charts/packages/c3s_seasonal/products/c3s_seasonal_spatial_mm_rain_3m?area=area06&base_time=202601010000&type=tsum&valid_time=202602010000); [UN 21/01/2026](https://news.un.org/en/story/2026/01/1166801)).

title: El Niño-driven above-average temperatures and below-average precipitation cause widespread drought in the Central American Dry Corridor (El Salvador, Guatemala, and Honduras), increasing food and health needs
type: Future impact of a hazard which has already taken place
rationale: El Niño is very likely to emerge by July 2026 and persist until December 2026 to February 2027. Between June–August 2026, seasonal forecasts anticipate a high probability of above-average temperatures and below-average precipitation associated with El Niño across the Central American Dry Corridor, an arid region that spans from eastern Guatemala, northern El Salvador, and southern and southwestern Honduras. The region is highly vulnerable to climate shocks, with 21 million people living in rural areas – over 20% of them employed in agriculture, and more than one-third living below the poverty line. While dry and warm conditions in Central America are typical of El Niño events, current forecasts indicate a stronger-than-average El Niño in 2026, with higher temperatures and significantly reduced or irregular rainfall compared to past years. The effects of El Niño in 2026 may be particularly severe as they could affect both the primary and secondary crop seasons, leading to reduced maize, beans, and cash crop yields. Drought may also reduce the availability of water for domestic use, in
expectedImpact: In 2023, the El Niño event had severe consequences in the region, as 7.7 million people in El Salvador, Guatemala, and Honduras (almost a quarter of their combined population) experienced moderate to severe food insecurity. Between 500,000 and 700,000 people are projected to require humanitarian assistance related to food access by September 2026, based on assessments of populations living within the Dry Corridor in Honduras. As this figure cover
materialised: El Niño-associated drought is increasing humanitarian needs across Central America’s Dry Corridor, particularly in food security, livelihoods, and WASH. In Honduras, WASH accounts for 708,000 people in need in red-alert municipalities, followed by food security and nutrition (622,000), health (617,0

triggers.title: El Niño
triggers.description: El Niño is a climate variability phenomenon characterised by the anomalous warming of ocean surface temperatures across the central and eastern tropical Pacific, accompanied by a weakening of trade winds and a significant shift in global weather systems. Its effects are highly variable by region: it typically brings below-average rainfall to Central America and drought conditions across the Dry corridor

rationaleUpdates.text: Food insecurity in Central America’s Dry Corridor is deepening as primera crop losses are confirmed and El Niño strengthens. In Honduras, 1.88 million people (18% of the analysed population) are projected to face Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse between August–October, around 108,500 more than projected in March. Eight departments are classified in IPC 3. Over708,000 people in 103 red-alert municipalities could require assistance. In Guatemala, delayed planting is preventing the poorest households in the Dry Corridor, Alta Verapaz, and the Western Highlands from accessing primera harvests, which normally begin in September. These households are projected to face IPC 3 outcomes through September. In 354 assessed communities across El Salvador, Guatemala, and Honduras, 78.6% of maize-growing households reported crop losses of 75–100%, while 64.2% have maize reserves lasting three weeks or less. A weak postrera harvest could prolong food needs into 2027. ([OCHA 22/09/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/honduras/honduras-llamamiento-urgente-sequia-sep-2026-resumen), [IPC 18/09/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/honduras/honduras-analisis-de-inseguridad-alimentaria-aguda-de-la-cif-agosto-octubre-2026-publicado-el-17-de-septiembre-de-2026), [Educo 04/09/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/el-salvador/educo-flash-update-and-appeal-1-el-salvador-meteorological-and-agricultural-drought-september-2026), [FEWS NET 18/09/2027](https://reliefweb.int/report/guatemala/guatemala-food-security-outlook-update-harvest-delays-and-losses-dry-corridor-will-prolong-market-dependence-august-2026-january-2027), [OCHA 01/10/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/guatemala/el-nino-2026-2027-climate-risk-humanitarian-outlook-latin-america-and-caribbean-september-2026))

The risk of drought and elevated temperatures across El Salvador, Guatemala, and Honduras has deteriorated during August 2026, as the impacts of the El Niño phenomenon continue to affect the Dry Corridor agricultural zone shared by the three countries. At least five million people across Honduras and Guatemala currently face the threat of food insecurity, driven in part by reduced rainfall and elevated temperatures linked to El Niño. In Guatemala, above-average temperatures and irregular rainfall in July 2026 have reduced food production in the departments of Alta Verapaz, Huehuetenango, Jalapa, Jutiapa, Quiché, and Zacapa. A similar situation has unfolded in Honduras, where communities across 75 municipalities were placed on yellow drought alert in August as a result of reduced rainfall linked to El Niño. A heat wave has also been affecting El Salvador since 11 August, with six weather stations recording heatwave conditions across the country. Historical temperature records have been broken at multiple stations, including San Francisco Gotera (40.6° C on 13 August) and San Andrés in La Libertad (40° C, the highest in 43 years). Temperatures in the eastern zone are forecast to reach between 38–41° C, with the heatwave expected to persist and potentially spread to additional areas before gradually decreasing from 20 August.
([NOAA13/08/2026](https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov), [FEWS NET 07/2026](https://fews.net/latin-america-and-caribbean/guatemala), [SWI/EFE 06/07/2026](https://www.swissinfo.ch), [El Libertador 14/08/2026](https://ellibertador.hn/2026/08/14/viene-agua-75-municipios-hondurenos-alerta-amarilla-por-sequia-larga-48-verde-y-111-en-vigilancia/),[La Prensa Gráfica/EFE 09/08/2026](https://www.revistaeyn.com/centroamericaymundo/guatemala-el-nino-amenaza-con-dejar-sin-alimento-a-32-millones-de-personas-EA31648419), [El Salvador 14/08/2026](https://www.elsalvador.com/?p=1289063))

The risk has deteriorated. El Niño weather patterns have begun to affect the Dry Corridor region in Central America, driving up temperatures and reducing rainfall by up to 50% compared to typical levels for the season that normally begins in June. In Guatemala, Alta Verapaz and Western Highlands regions have experienced irregular rainfall and elevated temperatures since June, resulting in reduced harvests and a decline in agricultural labour opportunities, which in turn have reduced household income for families dependent on seasonal agricultural employment. As a result, the number of people in need of food assistance in Guatemala is projected to reach up to 2.49 million by August. A similar impact is expected in Honduras, particularly in Choluteca region and along the Dry Corridor, where El Niño impacts have reduced agricultural production and labour demand, exposing 750,000 people to food insecurity by August. Erratic, below-average rainfall and high temperatures brought by El Niño have also affected the western and Dry Corridor areas of El Salvador, depleting food reserves among smallholder farmers and agricultural workers and diminishing their food purchasing capacity. That said, the number of people expected to face food insecurity needs in El Salvador is not projected to reach the same scale as in Guatemala. Compounding these impacts, food prices have risen across most of the Dry Corridor in all three countries, driven by a combination of reduced food supply, increased demand as agricultural households are forced to purchase food they would otherwise produce, and price increases linked to rising inflation. ([FEWS NET accessed 03/08/2026](https://fews.net/es/latin-america-and-caribbean/guatemala/perspectiva-de-seguridad-alimentaria/junio-2026/print); [Fews Net 31/06/2026](https://fews.net/latin-america-and-caribbean/el-salvador/key-message-update/may-2026/print), [FEWS NET accessed 03/08/2026](https://fews.net/latin-america-and-caribbean/honduras/food-security-outlook/june-2026/print), [NOA 11/07/2026](https://www.noaa.gov/news-release/el-nino-forms-expected-to-strengthen-say-noaa-forecasters))

The risk has deteriorated as El Niño weather patterns have begun to produce measurable humanitarian impacts across the Dry Corridor. In Guatemala, irregular rainfall has caused crops to dry out before harvest, forcing Indigenous communities to draw on food reserves or financial resources to meet their nutritional needs. In El Salvador, authorities have confirmed that the entire country, including Dry Corridor provinces, is already under El Niño influence, with below-average rainfall and above-average temperatures forecast for July 2026. The most recent manifestation was a 12-day heat wave that sustained abnormally elevated temperatures across the country. In Honduras, El Niño-associated drought, compounded by dependence on staple crops such as maize and beans, has already reduced both planting areas and harvest yields during the primary mid-year agricultural season.
These developments are unfolding across a region that is home to ten million people, of whom approximately 80% depend directly on agricultural production for their livelihoods. As El Niño conditions persist and drought intensifies, declining food production is expected to place severe pressure on subsistence farming households in the Dry Corridor and all others across the three countries who rely on the market purchase of staple crops to meet their daily food needs. ([Canal 26 YouTube 05/06/2026](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yzz6fBOKmU0), [SWI 06/07/2026](https://www.swissinfo.ch/spa/gobierno-de-el-salvador-confirma-influencia-de-el-ni%C3%B1o%2C-con-m%C3%A1s-calor-y-menos-lluvias/91707068), [Infobae 30/06/2026](https://www.infobae.com/el-salvador/2026/06/30/corredor-seco-en-alerta-sequias-por-el-nino-violencia-y-un-recorte-del-59-de-la-ayuda-empujan-a-guatemala-y-honduras-al-limite/), [NOAA 11/06/2026](https://www.noaa.gov/news-release/el-nino-forms-expected-to-strengthen-say-noaa-forecasters))

title: Intensifying forest and peatland fires across Indonesia cause prolonged hazardous haze, health impacts, and education, transport, and livelihood disruptions
type: Future impact of a hazard which has already taken place
rationale: Indonesia's annual forest and peatland fire season has intensified sharply during the 2026 dry season. Nearly 95,000 hectares burnt in July alone, almost doubling the area burnt during the first six months of the year and bringing the January–July total to more than 202,000 hectares. By late August, around 285,000 hectares had burnt, and thousands of hotspots were being detected across Kalimantan and Sumatra. West Kalimantan, including Ketapang and Pontianak, is among the areas most affected, while fires are also concentrated in Central Kalimantan and parts of Sumatra, particularly Jambi, Riau, and South Sumatra. The risk could deteriorate over the next one to three months as El Niño conditions intensify and prolong hotter, drier weather. Fire risk normally peaks during the late dry season, while peatland fires can burn underground, spread beyond visible fire lines, and remain difficult to extinguish. Agricultural land clearing and fires within company concessions are also contributing to the ignition and spread. More than 9,000 hotspots were recorded in August, exceeding the number
expectedImpact: If the risk materialises, prolonged hazardous haze would primarily affect health, education, transport, and livelihoods across fire-prone areas of Kalimantan and Sumatra. Repeated exposure to PM2.5 and other pollutants could increase acute respiratory infections, asthma attacks, eye and skin irritation, and cardiovascular complications. Children, older people, pregnant women, outdoor workers, and people with pre-existing heart or lung conditions

triggers.title: Sustained increase in hotspots and peatland fires
triggers.description: A continued rise in hotspots and burned area across West and Central Kalimantan, South Sumatra, Riau, and Jambi, particularly where fires spread into deep peat, would indicate that suppression operations are not containing the fire season. Fires persisting underground or reigniting after initial suppression would increase the likelihood of prolonged smoke exposure.

triggers.title: Prolonged dry conditions and peak El Nino
triggers.description: Below-average rainfall, extreme heat, declining water availability ahead of El Nino peak towards the end of 2026 could dry vegetation and peat further. This would allow fires to spread more rapidly and simultaneously across several provinces, stretching firefighting capacity.

rationaleUpdates.text: The risk increased during September, with haze continuing to disrupt education and transport despite a decline in fire activity. By 9 September, more than 250,000 pupils across 1,030 schools in Palembang, South Sumatra, had shifted to remote learning, while around 12,800 schools were closed across Sumatra and Borneo. Over 1.4 million students were learning online across affected areas of Indonesia. Since 11 September, haze has reduced visibility in Pontianak, West Kalimantan, to below 1km, disrupting flights for several days and hampering firefighting operations. Although high-confidence fire hotspots declined significantly in Central and West Kalimantan by 14 September, and none were recorded in Riau, fires continued in parts of Kalimantan. Smoke transported from other provinces has also sustained haze in affected areas. Continued fires and cross-provincial smoke are likely to prolong exposure to hazardous air pollution, disrupt transport and education, and constrain firefighting efforts. ([AP 09/09/2026](https://apnews.com/article/indonesia-forest-fires-south-sumatra-haze-16095c9a33ff1653f74a3445645c8b8a), [AP 14/09/2026](https://apnews.com/article/indonesia-forest-fires-haze-borneo-flights-kalimantan-bb64405033429c1de557bb8f0cf6a5f9), [Reuters 23/09/2026](https://www.reuters.com/investigates/special-report/asia-weather-indonesia-wildfire-women/))

title: Rising water scarcity in Iran leads to a deterioration in health, food security, and livelihood needs
type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale: Iran’s current water crisis is expected to worsen, with warnings that Tehran could face severe water shortages affecting large parts of the city by October 2025 if water consumption is not drastically reduced. The country has endured a five-year drought, and reservoirs supplying major cities have fallen to their lowest levels in a century. In Tehran, key reservoirs dropped to roughly 14% capacity during peak heat periods, causing widespread water service cuts and outages lasting 12–18 hours in some districts. Critically low reservoir levels have also hampered hydroelectric power generation, aggravating electricity shortages already driven by fuel constraints and extreme heat. Between June–August, temperatures exceeding 50° C in provinces including Khuzestan, Sistan-Baluchestan, and Yazd led to power and water outages disrupting cooling systems, medical facilities, and water pumping networks. Hospitals report difficulties in maintaining refrigeration for medicines and stable operations during rolling blackouts. At the same time, heat-related mortality has spiked among vulnerable popul
expectedImpact: The worsening water crisis in Iran is set to have profound impacts on health, food security, livelihoods, and social stability. Critical water and electricity shortages threaten to worsen health risks, including heat-related mortality, waterborne diseases, and healthcare service disruptions, especially for vulnerable populations, such as older and displaced people. Food security is also likely to deteriorate as water shortages impair agricultural

Rising temperatures have accelerated evaporation and reduced snowpack in key mountain ranges, diminishing surface runoff that feeds rivers and reservoirs. rationaleUpdates.text: The risk continues to deteriorate based on data up to 18 July 2026. US strikes have damaged the Bunji desalination plant west of Jask in Hormozgan governorate, southern Iran, destroying the seawater intake pump and electrical transformer and disrupting the facility's operations. According to the Hormozgan Water and Wastewater Company, the damage has cut water supplies to at least 20 villages with a combined population of approximately 10,000 people. Continued insecurity and further attacks are likely to delay repair works, prolonging disruptions to safe water access. Prolonged water shortages are likely to increase reliance on unsafe water sources, heightening the risk of waterborne diseases, such as acute diarrhoea and cholera, while reducing water available for drinking, cooking, and hygiene. The disruption is also likely to increase household spending on water trucking, further straining coping capacities. Iran’s water scarcity situation deteriorated further in May–June 2026 amid persistent drought, depleted reserves, and growing pressure on urban water supplies and agriculture. On 3 May, authorities reported that the five dams supplying Tehran were only 18% full, with reservoir levels remaining significantly below historical averages despite some rainfall during the 2025–2026 water year. On 11 May, Iranian officials estimated that around 35 million people were experiencing water shortages across several provinces, including Tehran, Isfahan, Yazd, Qom, Alborz, and Qazvin. Authorities intensified water conservation measures and warned that rainfall remained approximately 35% below the long-term average. In June, concerns increased that conflict-related damage to infrastructure and electricity disruptions could worsen water shortages and affect irrigation systems, with agricultural representatives warning of potential crop production losses of 25–30%. The crisis is increasing risks to livelihoods, agricultural production, food security, and social stability, particularly in drought-affected areas. ([Iran Intl 11/05/2026](https://www.iranintl.com/en/202605111643), [Iran Intl 03/05/2026](https://www.iranintl.com/en/202605035394), [Iran Wire 15/05/2026](https://iranwire.com/en/features/152433-tehran-faces-harsh-summer-as-irans-water-crisis-deepens/), [AJ 09/06/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/6/9/irans-lakes-are-vanishing-satellite-images-show-a-deepening-water-crisis-2), [NY Post 28/05/2026](https://nypost.com/2026/05/28/world-news/iranians-warned-to-conserve-water-amid-ongoing-sanctions/))

World Resources Institute ranks Iran as the 14th most water-stressed country, with 26 of 31 provinces under extreme stress. Water supply is projected to fall by 11% by 2080, while demand could rise 30% by 2050, deepening long-term scarcity. The crisis has accelerated sharply due to conflict, prolonged drought, and decades of mismanagement, pushing water systems toward collapse, particularly in Tehran and other major cities. Recent strikes have exposed the vulnerability of water and energy infrastructure, with reports of pollution affecting urban water channels. However, due to information gaps amid ongoing conflict, obtaining accurate, real-time assessments of water conditions remains challenging. ([NSB 02/04/2026]( https://www.newsecuritybeat.org/2026/04/complicating-long-term-stability-water-security-and-the-iran-war/), [Fanack Water 16/03/2026]( https://water.fanack.com/iran-war-water-crisis/), [WRI 20/03/2026]( https://www.wri.org/insights/iran-war-water-crisis-middle-east))

Iran’s water crisis has continued to deteriorate, with little meaningful recovery despite isolated rainfall events earlier in the season. While some precipitation has occurred, it has not significantly replenished reservoirs or groundwater, and inflows remain below normal. Water availability in major urban centres – including Tehran – continues to face severe stress, with authorities confirming concerns about potential rationing in 2026 as storage levels remain far below historical averages.
The situation is worsened by the conflict and heightened regional insecurity, which have strained governance capacity, disrupted infrastructure maintenance, and diverted public resources away from long-term water management. In conflict-affected and strategically sensitive areas, the risk of damage to water systems and energy supply networks has increased, while emergency preparedness and repair response times have slowed.
Overall, until March 2026, Iran stood to face critical water shortages, weak hydrological recovery, and an elevated risk of supply disruptions in the coming months. ([WRI 20/03/2026](https://www.wri.org/insights/iran-war-water-crisis-middle-east), [Resilience 05/03/2026](https://www.resilience.org/stories/2026-03-05/water-and-security-in-the-middle-east-lessons-from-the-iranian-crisis/), [Iran Focus 23/02/2026](https://iranfocus.com/economy/57198-rainfall-in-iran-has-been-higher-than-last-year-but-64-of-dam-reservoirs-are-still-empty/), [Atlantic Council 18/03/2026](https://www.atlanticcouncil.org/dispatches/attacks-on-desalination-plants-in-the-iran-war-forecast-a-dark-future/), [AJ 30/03/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/3/30/schools-water-industry-what-civilian-targets-have-us-israel-iran-hit))

As of February 2026, Iran’s water crisis remains severe, despite some reports of slightly higher rainfall this season. Recent data show that around 64 % of the country’s dam reservoirs are still effectively empty, reflecting persistently low inflows and prolonged drought conditions across major basins. In Tehran and surrounding regions, water resources continue to be under acute stress: key dams that supply the capital, such as the Amir Kabir and Karaj Reservoirs, remain critically low, with storage far below historical averages and still insufficient to meet urban demand if drought persists. Officials in Alborz and Hormozgan provinces have warned that decreased rainfall and lower reservoir levels could lead to water rationing and shortages later in 2026, affecting both household supplies and agricultural use. Overall, limited seasonal rainfall so far has provided only marginal relief, and Iran continues to face serious risks to water security, public health, sanitation, and livelihoods as drought conditions endure. ([Iran Focus 23/02/2026](https://iranfocus.com/economy/57198-rainfall-in-iran-has-been-higher-than-last-year-but-64-of-dam-reservoirs-are-still-empty/), [Geopolitical Monitor 12/02/2026](https://www.geopoliticalmonitor.com/irans-water-crisis-a-national-security-imperative/), [The conversation 02/02/2026](https://theconversation.com/drastic-water-shortages-and-air-pollution-are-fuelling-irans-protests-274554)

In January 2026, Iran’s water crisis remained acute and continued to worsen, following extremely limited rainfall in December 2025. Reservoir levels in Tehran and across several regions have declined sharply owing to prolonged drought and record-low precipitation. Key reservoirs, including the Amir Kabir Dam, remain near critically low capacity, severely constraining the supply of drinking water to Tehran’s population of more than ten million. Although sporadic winter rainfall in December offered marginal relief, it has been insufficient to reverse declining storage levels, leaving the risk of prolonged water shortages high. The continued drought and depleted water infrastructure continue to undermine public health, sanitation, and livelihoods, particularly in urban centres reliant on piped water systems. Water scarcity has also emerged as a key grievance during recent mass protests and is expected to further intensify social tensions in the coming months. ([CNN 01/12/2025](https://edition.cnn.com/2025/12/01/climate/iran-water-crisis-evacuate-tehran), [AJ 01/01/2026](https://studies.aljazeera.net/en/analyses/tehran%E2%80%99s-%E2%80%9Cday-zero%E2%80%9D-threat-or-opportunity-revive-water-governance-and-adaptive-water), [UNDRR 04/12/2025](https://www.preventionweb.net/news/irans-record-drought-and-cheap-fuel-have-sparked-air-pollution-crisis-real-causes-run-much), [The Guardian 15/01/2026](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/jan/15/how-day-zero-water-shortages-in-iran-are-fuelling-protests), [Euro News 15/01/2025](https://www.euronews.com/green/2026/01/15/water-shortages-blackouts-and-air-pollution-how-environmental-damage-fuelled-irans-protest))

The water crisis has intensified over the past month and worsened further in the last week. Rainfall remains roughly 85% below average in many basins, several major reservoirs have plunged to single-digit capacities, and officials report more dams at critical lows than in prior months. Reservoir levels have fallen below 3% in Mashhad and many other dam systems, government announcements include rotating cuts and partial rationing for Tehran, and satellite imagery shows rapidly shrinking river flows and exposed riverbeds. Some officials have discussed water bankruptcy and even temporary relocation or emergency measures for urban areas.
Climate-driven drought and long-term mismanagement (the overdrilling of wells, water-intensive cropping, and the proliferation of dams) continue to shrink surface and groundwater stocks in the country. Economic strains, sanctions, budget limits, and fuel/energy pressures reduce authorities’ ability to fund emergency water-trucking or large-scale infrastructure fixes. Political choices, such as continuing subsidised, water-hungry agricultural policies, remain an aggravating factor.
Because of this crisis, worsening public health risks (e.g. reduced drinking water quality and higher disease risk) are expected, along with acute impacts on food security from failed crops and livestock losses, job and income losses for rural households, and increased urban stress from rationing and possible mass migration from the hardest-hit provinces. Strained municipal services and competition for scarce water raise the risk of local unrest and increased protection needs. ([Reuters 12/11/2025](https://www.reuters.com/sustainability/land-use-biodiversity/tehran-taps-run-dry-water-crisis-deepens-across-iran-2025-11-12/), [The Guardian 09/11/2025](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2025/nov/09/water-levels-below-3-percent-in-dam-reservoirs-for-iran-second-city-say-mashhad-reports), [BBC 17/11/2025](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cj4172yl0l1o), [AJ 24/11/2025](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2025/11/24/tehran-shrouded-in-thick-smog-as-iran-burns-dirty-fuel-amid-energy-crisis), [ABC 24/11/2025](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2025-11-24/iran-facing-worst-drought-in-60-years/106035210), [Iranian International 25/11/2025](https://beta.iranintl.com/en/202511250070))

The water crisis has significantly deteriorated since September 2025. Tehran faces an imminent humanitarian crisis with its main drinking water reservoir at critical depletion. By 2 November, the Amir Kabir Dam held only 14 million cubic metres of water (just 8% capacity) – sufficient for only two weeks of supply for the city's over ten million residents. This represents a catastrophic decline from 86 million cubic metres one year prior, driven by a 100% drop in precipitation. Nationally, the crisis has intensified dramatically. 19 major dams across Iran are near total depletion, with three already reaching zero capacity. Hydroelectric generation remains severely compromised, perpetuating electricity shortages alongside water rationing. At the same time, the fall rainfall (November–December) is predicted to remain below normal through early December, with precipitation delays suggesting a continuation of the water crisis. ([Essydo 03/11/2025](https://essydo.com/2025/11/03/tehran-water-crisis-only-two-weeks-of-supply/), [Daily Sabah 02/11/2025](https://www.dailysabah.com/world/mid-east/tehrans-main-reservoir-has-only-2-weeks-of-water-left-official), [Circle of Blue 04/11/2025](https://www.circleofblue.org/newsletter/the-stream-november-4-2025-tehran-two-weeks-away-from-day-zero-scenario-sees-largest-dam-at-8-percent-capacity/), [Iran HRM 13/10/2025](https://iran-hrm.com/2025/10/13/environmental-and-human-rights-crisis-in-iran-under-the-mullahs-regime/))

This would trigger US counter-retaliation against Iranian military assets and command structures, potentially expanding the conflict through an escalatory spiral involving Iranian proxies in Yemen, Gulf states facing missile and drone threats, and Israel conducting strikes on Iranian targets, ultimately transforming bilateral US–Iran confrontation into a protracted regional war with multi-front humanitarian consequences. Strikes on strategic targets within densely populated urban centres, such as Isfahan, Mashhad, and Tehran – cities where military installations and government facilities are deeply embedded in civilian environments – would produce direct civilian casualties dependin

Initial US–Israeli airstrikes on strategic military and nuclear sites quickly triggered Iranian retaliation through missile and drone attacks, leading to a sustained, multi

rationale: A US–Iran confrontation triggered by a ten-day ultimatum issued by the US administration for Iran to reach a nuclear and regional agreement (placing a potential military trigger in late February or early March 2026) could increase humanitarian needs in Iraq through two compounding mechanisms: direct Iranian proxy escalation via the Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) and broader regional economic disruption, including potential closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Following the fall of Bashar Al Assad's regime in Syria and Israel's weakening of Hezbollah in Lebanon and Syria, Iraq has become a significant regional asset for Iran. The PMF, an official Iraqi security institution composed largely of Iran-backed militias, represents Iran's likely vector for retaliation against US interests in Iraq. Kata'ib Hezbollah, the largest militia within the PMF, has publicly warned of military response if Iran is attacked. Iraq's political trajectory compounds this risk. Government formation remains contested between the US administration and Iraq's Coordination Framework over the composition of leaders

The demographic faces barriers to PDS access, including inability to claim rations without valid civil docume

The leader of Kata'ib Hezbollah has explicitly warned of "total war" in this scenario, and Iran's Revolutionary Guard has reportedly discussed activating alternative support arenas in Iraq in the event of a direct confrontation. Unlike Jordan and Yemen, Iraq's risk is dri

rationaleUpdates.text: During May, risk levels have slightly improved because the Strait of Hormuz disruption has renewed efforts to restore Iraq's northern oil export corridor through Türkiye, which could modestly enhance export diversification and reduce some of the country's vulnerability to future maritime disruptions, although significant structural risks remain. The Strait of Hormuz disruptions have highlighted Iraq’s continued vulnerability to regional disruptions while exposing the limitations of its current oil export infrastructure. Although efforts to restore the Ceyhan pipeline could modestly reduce dependence on the Strait of Hormuz and improve export resilience, the route is unlikely to offset major disruptions to southern exports. The situation has also increased Baghdad’s reliance on cooperation with the Kurdistan regional government, potentially strengthening Erbil’s political leverage amid disputes over revenue sharing and governance. The crisis may shift some risks from economic exposure towards heightened political tensions between Baghdad, Erbil, and Iran-aligned actors, while leaving Iraq broadly vulnerable to further regional escalation. ([CNBC 09/06/2026](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/06/09/iraq-uae-hormuz-oil-pipelines-oil-iran-war.html), [ISPI 21/05/2026](https://www.ispionline.it/en/publication/caught-in-the-middle-iraq-amid-the-us-iran-power-struggle-238263), [Chatham House 10/06/2026](https://www.chathamhouse.org/2026/06/can-iraqs-new-prime-minister-finally-rein-its-armed-factions))

The risk for Iraq continues to be stable, as the ceasefire agreed from 7–8 April 2026 between Iran and the US did not effectively improve the flow of goods through the Strait of Hormoz but did restore relative security. Reports indicate that in April, Iraq’s oil exports had collapsed by up to 80% following disruptions to tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, reducing production to around 1.2 to 1.3 million barrels per day. Humanitarian implications include reduced public spending capacity, service delivery disruptions, and a potential deterioration in livelihoods. ([Oil Price 21/04/2026](https://oilprice.com/Energy/Energy-General/Iraq-Turns-to-Risky-Overland-Routes-as-Oil-Exports-Collapse.html))

The risk has deteriorated, with Iranian-backed armed groups intensifying attacks against US and Israeli assets since 1 March 2026. In response, US and Israeli forces are striking their positions in central and southern Iraq, while Iran is targeting Kurdish groups in the north, turning Iraq into a battleground of attacks and counterattacks. Prior to the escalation, over 90% of Iraq’s oil was exported through the Strait of Hormuz. The rest was exported through the Ceyhan pipeline, connected to Türkiye via Iraq’s autonomous Kurdish region, which has been closed as a safety measure in response to the conflict. With storage facilities mostly full and production halts being announced, an Iraqi government adviser has warned that suspending exports would cause losses of USD 6–7 billion per month, threatening the Government’s total income, which comprised 93% oil receipts in 2025. A sustained export halt would also threaten the Public Distribution System, an expense dependent on Iraq’s oil revenues and the primary food safety net for 39 million people (84% of the population). ([ACAPS 20/03/2026](https://www.acaps.org/fileadmin/Data_Product/Main_media/20260320_ACAPS_Ripple_effects_and_scenarios_of_the_Middle_East_conflict_.pdf))

title: Contested electoral process ahead of Côte d'Ivoire’s October 2025 elections leads to political violence and protection risks
rationale: Côte d’Ivoire is preparing for presidential elections scheduled for 25 October 2025. Although recent elections have been relatively peaceful, the political environment is becoming increasingly tense. The Independent Electoral Commission (CEI) released the final electoral roll on 4 June, confirming the exclusion of four prominent opposition leaders: Laurent Gbagbo, Tidjane Thiam, Charles Blé Goudé, and Guillaume Soro. While Thiam was excluded based on nationality concerns, the others were barred because of past judicial convictions. All four are also prohibited from voting. The exclusion of these high-profile figures has triggered strong criticism from their parties, which have withdrawn from the CEI and denounced a lack of institutional independence. Some, such as Thiam and his party, have appealed to international bodies such as the UNHRC. Others, including former first lady Simone Gbagbo, have warned that the conditions are not in place for peaceful elections. Some parties have announced protests, and public calls for boycotts or civil disobedience could escalate in the coming mont
expectedImpact: The most likely scenario is a series of protests or boycotts, potentially escalating into violent confrontations in major cities including Abidjan, Bouaké, and Yamoussoukro. The excessive use of force by security forces, targeted arrests of opposition figures, and violent clashes between rival groups are likely. Urban populations may face mobility restrictions, service disruptions, and protection risks, especially youth and opposition sympathiser

The move would likely trigger opposition reactions, public protests, and heighten political tensions in the pre-electoral period.

triggers.title: Protests or civil disobedience called by opposition parties

triggers.title: Spread of disinformation through social media
triggers.description: Misleading narratives regarding candidates’ eligibility, foreign interference, or electoral fraud could fuel anti-government sentiment and trigger unrest, especially among disenfranchised voters.

rationaleUpdates.text:
The 25 October 2025 presidential election in Côte d’Ivoire concluded with the re-election of President Alassane Ouattara for a fourth term, with 89.77% of the vote. Although the electoral context remained highly contested — particularly following the exclusion of opposition leaders Thiam and Gbagbo — the voting day was largely peaceful, with no widespread unrest.
The government had banned protests in early October and deployed 44,000 security forces across the country, leading to a tightly controlled election environment. Participation remained low in traditional opposition strongholds, especially in the south and west, where turnout fell below 35% in some areas. In contrast, northern regions showed near-unanimous support for the incumbent, with some turnout levels exceeding 95%.
Despite reports of isolated incidents — including intercommunal violence and at least ten deaths linked to the electoral process — the elections unfolded without the large-scale violence anticipated in earlier risk assessments. Opposition parties have rejected the legitimacy of the results and called for new elections, but no major mobilisations have occurred so far. ([RFI 25/10/2025](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20251025-pr%C3%A9sidentielle-en-c%C3%B4te-d-ivoire-%C3%A0-abidjan-une-journ%C3%A9e-de-vote-dans-le-calme), [DW 27/10/2025](https://www.dw.com/fr/alassane-ouattara-reelu-quatrieme-mandat-avec-89-des-voix/a-74517060), [TV5 Monde 27/10/2025](https://information.tv5monde.com/direct/presidentielle-en-cote-divoire-les-resultats-attendus-dans-la-journee-2796017), [Le Monde 27/10/2025](https://www.lemonde.fr/afrique/article/2025/10/27/en-cote-d-ivoire-le-crepuscule-du-pouvoir-d-alassane-ouattara-reelu-pour-un-quatrieme-mandat_6649860_3212.html)).

Tensions remain high ahead of the 25 October presidential election in Côte d’Ivoire. On 8 September, the Constitutional Council published the final list of approved candidates, excluding opposition leaders Tidjane Thiam and Laurent Gbagbo. Both the Democratic Party (PDCI) and the African People's Party (PPA-CI) condemned the decision and announced joint protests. On 3 October, the Government formally banned all demonstrations contesting the Council’s ruling and mobilised 44,000 security personnel nationwide. Several opposition leaders and youth activists have been arrested since June. Meanwhile, the government and judiciary have warned media outlets against the spread of hate speech and misinformation online, threatening legal action against non-compliant publishers. Despite mounting restrictions, the opposition remains mobilised and has called for further action. The electoral campaign officially opens on 10 October. ([Le Monde 03/10/2025](https://www.lemonde.fr/afrique/article/2025/10/03/presidentielle-ivoirienne-du-25-octobre-le-gouvernement-interdit-les-manifestations-contre-l-exclusion-de-candidats-d-opposition_6644248_3212.html), [RFI 03/10/2025](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20251003-pr%C3%A9sidentielle-ivoirienne-les-manifestations-contre-l-exclusion-de-candidats-de-l-opposition-interdites), [Le Monde 19/09/2025](https://www.lemonde.fr/afrique/article/2025/09/19/presidentielle-en-cote-d-ivoire-laurent-gbagbo-ineligible-exclut-de-soutenir-un-autre-candidat_6641822_3212.html), [RFI 27/09/2025](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20250927-c%C3%B4te-d-ivoire-les-m%C3%A9dias-appel%C3%A9s-%C3%A0-la-vigilance-quant-aux-contenus-haineux-avant-la-pr%C3%A9sidentielle)).

The political situation in Côte d’Ivoire remains tense following President Alassane Ouattara’s confirmation in late July 2025 that he will run for a fourth term. His decision has been strongly contested by the opposition, particularly the Democratic Party of Ivory Coast - African Democratic Rally and African People's Party - Côte d'Ivoire, whose leaders Tidjane Thiam and Laurent Gbagbo remain barred from the electoral roll. Despite their ineligibility, both parties submitted candidacies for Thiam and Gbagbo before the 26 August deadline, further escalating tensions. Internal divisions emerged, as alternative opposition figures attempted to enter the race and were subsequently expelled from their parties. Protests organised by the Front Commun on 9 August drew thousands, signalling popular resistance to perceived democratic backsliding. At the same time, the Independent Electoral Commission received over 50 candidacies, though only a fraction is expected to be validated by the Constitutional Council. Civil society responders warn of rising repression, including arrests of opposition youth leaders, and growing public disillusionment, especially among the country’s youth. The lack of dialogue between the ruling party and opposition continues to undermine confidence in the electoral process. ([RFI 27/08/2025](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20250827-pr%C3%A9sidentielle-en-c%C3%B4te-d-ivoire-plus-de-50-dossiers-ont-%C3%A9t%C3%A9-d%C3%A9pos%C3%A9s-%C3%A0-la-commission-%C3%A9lectorale-ind%C3%A9pendante), [DW 30/07/2025](https://www.dw.com/fr/alassane-ouattara-est-candidat-%C3%A0-sa-r%C3%A9%C3%A9lection/a-73460127), [DW 01/08/2025](https://www.dw.com/fr/guerres-succession-partis-politiques-ivoiriens/a-73502509), [JA 09/08/2025](https://www.jeuneafrique.com/1713187/politique/en-cote-divoire-pro-thiam-et-pro-gbagbo-manifestent-contre-un-4e-mandat-de-ouattara/))

rationale: Kenya’s refugee camps, particularly Dadaab and Kakuma, are facing an increasingly fragile situation owing to severe underfunding, overstretched infrastructure, and surging new arrivals. Cuts in humanitarian aid have already led to reductions in food rations, the closure of essential services, and growing frustration among both refugees and host communities. In 2025, WFP was only able to provide 60% of the minimum food basket by midyear, with responders reporting critical gaps in healthcare, education, and WASH services. The camps, which host more than 600,000 refugees, are still absorbing new displacements from conflict-affected areas of Ethiopia, Somalia, and Sudan. These arrivals further strain already limited resources and contribute to tensions over land, water, and security. Escalating tensions have already led to ethnic clashes, protests, and police interventions within camps including Kakuma and Dadaab. triggers.description: If humanitarian funding gaps persist through late 2025, food rations may fall below survival thresholds, while key services such as maternal health, water trucking, or protection casework may be scaled back or halted entirely. rationaleUpdates.text: Since June 2025, over 9,300 South Sudanese refugees have returned from Kakuma and Kalobeyei camps in Kenya, with daily arrivals peaking at over 220 in August. The movement is prompted by food ration cuts that have left 85,000 (45% of camp populations) without assistance, triggering protests. Kakuma and Kalobeyei were hosting nearly 191,000 South Sudanese refugees prior to the new arrivals. Two-thirds of the returnees are children, many arriving through Nadapal town into eastern Equatoria before moving to Budi, Ikotos, Kapoeta, and Torit towns. Families face ambush risks, lack of reception facilities, unsafe sanitation, and exposure to gender-based violence and disease at the border. While many returnees rejoin relatives, host households are increasingly overstretched, leading to overcrowding, food insecurity, and limited health and shelter access. Urgent needs include food, safe water, health services, and protection support especially for children and women, alongside assistance for host communities. ([UNHCR 11/09/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/south-sudan/emergency-update-returns-kenya-south-sudan), [TRT Afrika 29/08/2025](https://www.trtafrika.com/english/article/7d3492517a31), [Radio Tamazuj 14/08/2025](https://www.radiotamazuj.org/en/news/article/over-350-refugees-arrive-torit-following-food-cuts-in-kenyan-camp#:~:text=Over%20350%20refugees%20arrive%20Torit,in%20Kenyan%20camp%20%2D%20Radio%20Tamazuj))

Worsening socioeconomic conditions heightened by funding shortfalls are fuelling a rise in crime, heightening tensions between refugee and host communities, and triggering renewed protests over limited access to essential services. On 28 June 2025, a protest in Kalobeyei settlement turned violent following clashes between refugees and police. Across all camps, malnutrition is increasing, especially among children, pregnant or lactating women, and individuals with chronic illnesses, as a result of severe reductions in food rations. Gender-based violence, including intimate partner violence and early or forced marriage, remains widespread as a result of economic hardship, entrenched social norms, and overcrowded living conditions. In Kakuma and Kalobeyei, water shortages and service interruptions have led to internal relocations, disproportionately affecting vulnerable populations. Access to protection, shelter, and education remains inadequate, with girls at heightened risk of early marriage and boys pushed into informal labour. At the same time, dengue fever outbreaks in Ifo and Dagahaley camps in Dadaab have been linked to poor waste management, rising temperatures, and constrained healthcare access. ([ECHO 29/07/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/kenya/kenya-humanitarian-situation-refugee-camps-dg-echo-drc-echo-daily-flash-29-july-2025), [Radio Ergo 22/07/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/kenya/job-losses-and-aid-cuts-leave-dadaab-refugees-uncertain-their-future))

title: Forecast El Niño conditions threaten crop production and worsen food insecurity in Kenya
rationale: El Niño conditions are forecast to develop by July 2026 and strengthen through the second half of the year. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration estimates a 61% probability of El Niño from May–July, rising to 87–92% between July 2026 and January 2027. The Intergovernmental Authority on Development Climate Prediction and Applications Centre forecasts below-normal June–September (JJAS) rainfall across western and northern Kenya alongside above-normal temperatures nationwide, closely resembling the 2023 El Niño, when below-normal JJAS rainfall affected western Kenya. The forecast threatens Kenya's principal food-producing areas during a critical stage of the long rains season. Over 70% of the country's annual crop production depends on the long rains, which extend into August–September in the North Rift and western Kenya. These areas had already recorded below-average rainfall in April and early May despite favourable national rainfall totals. Combined with delayed fertiliser deliveries, below-average rainfall and above-average temperatures from June–September are likely
expectedImpact: Below-average JJAS precipitation and above-average temperatures would directly threaten the October–November harvest of maize, beans, sorghum, and sweet potato across the North Rift and western Kenya – crops that represent the primary source of domestic food production. Reduced yields would tighten household food stocks at a time when they are already depleted, drive staple prices higher in already-stressed markets, and erode incomes for farming

During the 2023 El Niño, wetter-than-normal OND conditions across eastern Kenya materialised as severe and damaging flooding. With seasonal forecast anticipating high probability of above-average precipitation between October and December 2026, a comp

rationaleUpdates.text: El Niño has driven a dry spell that has cut Kenya's harvest and is now expected to bring above-average short rains and flooding, with Lamu county projected to reach Crisis (IPC Phase 3) and Dadaab camp Emergency (IPC Phase 4) between October–January. The dry spell caused a poor long rains harvest, with maize production estimated at 22–28% below the five-year average and losses of up to 43% anticipated in high potential North Rift counties including Trans Nzoia, Uasin Gishu, and Nakuru. The Ministry of Agriculture has acknowledged widespread crop failure in the North Rift, which produces over 60% of Kenya's maize. Wholesale maize prices in Nairobi are expected to remain 9–19% above the five-year average until January 2027, limiting food access for poor households. The October–December rains are expected to improve pastoral conditions, but in Dadaab flooding is likely to last for weeks, limiting humanitarian access and increasing waterborne disease. IPC 3 outcomes are expected to persist in Garissa, Mandera, Tana River, Wajir, and Turkana counties through January, where flooding is likely to damage transport infrastructure and displace households. A national assessment has identified 18 counties and 5,660 health facilities in areas at risk of flooding. ([FEWS NET accessed 29/09/2026](https://fews.net/east-africa/kenya/food-security-outlook-update/august-2026), [FEWS NET 11/09/2026](https://fews.net/east-africa/seasonal-monitor/september-2026), [The EastAfrican 15/08/2026](https://www.theeastafrican.co.ke/tea/sustainability/climate/east-africa-braces-for-prolonged-food-crisis-5558506), [Milling Middle East & Africa 13/08/2026](https://millingmea.com/kenya-anticipates-maize-deficit-of-nearly-486000-tonnes-by-late-september/), [WHO 28/09/2026](https://afro.who.int/countries/kenya/news/kenya-readies-its-military-medical-team-protect-communities-ahead-el-nino-rains))

title: A rising number of Syrian refugees opt for an unsafe return to Syria to avoid a deepening economic crisis in Lebanon and the repercussions of the 2020 Beirut explosion
rationale: Inflation, rising prices, and the depreciation of the Lebanese lira threaten the livelihoods of Syrian refugees, who struggle to survive on cash assistance (delivered in Lebanese liras) or receive low to no salary from their employers in the informal sector. Because of these factors, as well as Lebanese governmental policies on return, an increasing number of refugees might opt for an unsafe return to Syria. While the severity of people’s needs has worsened, during 2020, the number of voluntary refugees returning to Syria was only 9,351 – half of the figure registered in 2019. The refugees' decisions to return to Syria were influenced mainly by the security and safety situation, economic growth, public service availability, and personal relationships in their place of origin, while refugees’ poor living conditions in Lebanon were less likely to be an influence. Unless the situation significantly improves in Syria, refugees are unlikely to return.

title: Diplomatic tensions between Lebanon and the Gulf states affect Lebanon's economy and aggravate humanitarian needs
type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale: Political tension between Lebanon and some Gulf countries caused a risk of deterioration of Lebanon’s economy and increased humanitarian needs across all sectors for the most vulnerable. The diplomatic crisis threatened the job security of the Lebanese diaspora in the Gulf states, potentially affecting remittances and decreasing the flow of foreign currency into Lebanon, as Lebanon had been exporting basic goods and materials to some Gulf states. Following Information Minister George Kordahi’s comments on the role of the United Arab Emirates and the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in the war in Yemen – including implications that the Houthis had the right to defend themselves against foreign attacks – Bahrain, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates expelled Lebanese ambassadors from their countries. The Gulf states perceived these comments as antagonising. Saudi Arabia also banned Lebanese imports to the kingdom and asked the minister to resign as a condition to lift the ban.

title: Increased intensity and spread of the conflict between Hezbollah and Israel increases humanitarian needs in Lebanon
type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale: Since 8 October, the exchange of airstrikes between Hezbollah and Israel following the start of the conflict in Gaza has been mainly near the Blue Line area (southern Lebanon) and mostly targeting military locations. Recent attacks since mid-February 2024 have been expanding into more areas in Lebanon and affecting more civilians. Israel carried out at least two airstrikes in Ghaziyeh town, five kilometres outside a key Lebanese city (Saida), on 19 February. This attack was considered the largest airstrikes carried out near a major population centre since 8 October. A factory producing electrical generators was targeted. On 26 February, an Israeli air strike targeted the outskirts of Buday village near Baalbek city, eastern Lebanon for the first time since 8 October 2023. The attacks targeted a convoy of trucks carrying food, killing at least two people. Hezbollah has also been responding with expanding the geographical area targeted in Israel, increasing the likelihood of further clashes and impacting more areas in Lebanon.
expectedImpact: It is likely that more civilian casualties will be recorded in southern Lebanon, leading to an escalation of clashes into more areas. It is also likely that more people will be displaced, not only from southern cities, but also from areas close to the south such as Nabatieh and Beqa’a. Livelihood needs are likely to increase as more farmers are being displaced to safer areas, leaving their lands behind. Many agricultural lands are also becoming i
materialised: Before the ceasefire agreement was reached in November, the conflict had displaced nearly 900,000 people in Lebanon, with many seeking refuge in temporary shelters or with host families. Southern Lebanon's agricultural sector has been severely affected, with over 1,240 hectares of land damaged and a

triggers.description: The airstrikes has been mainly targeting southern Lebanon. However, it is likely that more attacks will be affecting cities such as Sida or Baalbak that were already targeted one time each in February.

title: Attempts to politically marginalise and militarily weaken Hezbollah in Lebanon leads to internal tensions, protests, and displacement
rationale: Since the escalation of conflict with Israel on 8 October 2023, Hezbollah has experienced military setbacks, resulting in its political and military marginalisation. A new Lebanese Government was formed on 9 January 2025, with a prime minister appointed on 8 February. While the leadership tries to balance power, it faces pressure from Israel and the US to exclude Hezbollah, which they label a ‘terrorist’ organisation. The 27 November 2024 ceasefire agreement included implementing UNSC Resolution 1701, requiring Hezbollah’s withdrawal from south of the Litani River and blocking arms transfers to the group. The resolution also strengthens the role of the Lebanese Armed Forces and UNIFIL in southern Lebanon, which Hezbollah sees as an effort to weaken its military role. The deadline for Israel’s withdrawal from southern Lebanon was on 18 February 2025, but their troops continue to occupy five border areas. Despite the ceasefire, Israeli air space violations and air strikes continue, resulting in casualties. The Lebanese army has not responded, leaving civilians in southern Lebanon (most
expectedImpact: If the risk materialises, protests and riots are likely to take place in Beirut areas with higher Shia presence, such as its southern suburbs. Other areas exposed to the escalation of tensions are likely to include mixed-population areas where social friction is already high, such as central Beirut neighbourhoods and parts of the Bekaa Valley, besides southern Lebanon which is predominantly inhabited by the Shia community. The escalation of viole

triggers.title: Military setbacks weakening Hezbollah
triggers.description: The assassination of Hassan Nasrallah on 27 September 2024 and the pager attack on 17 September 2024 significantly undermined Hezbollah’s operational capabilities. Additionally, the fall of the Assad regime on 8 December 2024 disrupted the supply routes for arms and funds from Iran, further weakening the group. These events have collectively contributed to the perception that Hezbollah’s military strength is in decli

triggers.title: Foreign pressure and ceasefire conditions
triggers.description: Foreign governments, notably the United States and Israel, are pressuring the Lebanese government to marginalize Hezbollah by excluding it from power. The ceasefire agreement signed on 27 November 2024 includes conditions such as the enforcement of UN Security Council Resolution 1701, which mandates the withdrawal of Hezbollah fighters from south of the Litani River and prevents further arms transfers.

triggers.title: Ongoing Israeli military activity
triggers.description: Despite the ceasefire, Israeli forces continue to conduct air strikes and infiltrations into Lebanese territory, creating a persistent security threat. Israel is actively working to blockade Hezbollah via land, air, and sea to cut off the flow of arms and funds from Iran.

triggers.title: Growing frustration among the Shia population
triggers.description: The Shia community, which makes up over 30% of Lebanon’s population, is increasingly frustrated by the government's failure to prevent Israeli attacks on their villages and to support the reconstruction of their homes. Protests and riots, such as those that occurred on 14–15 February 2025 over the ban on Iranian airplanes at Rafic Hariri International Airport, reflect their frustration. This growing discontent risks

rationaleUpdates.text: The risk has greatly deteriorated. On 2 March 2026, the November 2024 ceasefire collapsed, triggering a re-escalation of hostilities between Israel and Hezbollah that has displaced nearly 1.2 million as of 19 March. Israeli ground operations in southern Lebanon began on 16 March. The Lebanese Government has banned Hezbollah's military activities, deepening sectarian tensions among Shia communities who bear the greatest displacement burden. Civil war is unlikely, but large-scale displacement and social tensions between the IDPs and the host community are actively materialising. According to the Tension Monitoring System, anti-IDP rhetoric is increasing following continued military strikes affecting “safe areas”. ([TMS 13/03/2026](https://admin.tms-lebanon.com/StaticFiles/Files/TMS_Tensions_Pulse_-_13_March_2026.pdf), [OCHA 21/03/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/lebanon/lebanon-flash-update-10-escalation-hostilities-lebanon-19-march-2026), [AJ 02/03/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/3/2/lebanese-pm-nawaf-salam-announces-ban-on-hezbollah-military-activities)).

The risk continues to be stable overall but with a slight intensification regarding Israeli military air strikes. Between 20–21 February 2026, Israeli forces conducted multiple air strikes and drone operations across Lebanon, targeting densely populated civilian areas and Hezbollah-affiliated sites. Strikes hit the Ein Al Hilweh Palestinian refugee camp in Sidon city, killing at least ten civilians and six Hezbollah combatants, including senior commanders, and injuring 24 other civilians, including children. The attack also killed a residential building in Bekaa Valley, causing civilian casualties. The escalation raised the national threat level to ‘high’, increasing regional tensions. There are no reports of displacement, but needs for shelter and healthcare assistance are recorded. ([SARI Global 23/02/2026](https://img1.wsimg.com/blobby/go/048e81f0-4f39-47ce-9ac6-0ff113a00a60/downloads/ea552e93-d668-4176-ba37-890c86bc6137/Bekaa%20Airstrikes%20and%20Regional%20Tension%20Dynamics.pdf?ver=1771682578376))

In January 2026, the Lebanese Armed Forces (LAF) completed the first phase of a U.S-backed plan to disarm Hezbollah and other groups south of the Litani River. While this has cleared some weapons from the border, Hezbollah warns that expanding the disarmament further north could trigger civil conflict as they refuse to disarm elsewhere. With increasing US and Israeli threats to attack Iran, the situation is becoming more volatile, and a renewed escalation of clashes between Hezbollah and Israel is likely, with Hezbollah being perceived as a proxy of Iran and already stating that it will not remain neutral if Iran is attacked, at the same time that Israel continues to consider Hezbollah a major threat to its national security. [(AJ 08/01/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/1/8/lebanons-mission-to-complete-disarmament-plan-of-hezbollah#:~:text=dismantle%20Hezbollah's%20weapons.%E2%80%9D-,Litani%20River,Secretary%2DGeneral%20Naim%20Qassem%20said), [Geopolitical Monitor 07/11/2025](https://www.geopoliticalmonitor.com/israeli-hezbollah-strikes-toward-a-new-conflict/), [FDD 27/01/2026](https://www.fdd.org/analysis/2026/01/27/hezbollah-we-will-not-remain-neutral-if-islamic-republic-endangered/), [TV7 27/01/2026](https://www.tv7israelnews.com/vod/series/18738/?episode-id=RTr7v66vvD4))

Lebanon is at a crossroads as Israel has set a deadline for disarming Hezbollah on 31 December, threatening renewed military action if Lebanon fails. The Lebanese Government is facing two difficult choices: attempt to forcibly disarm Hezbollah, potentially triggering internal conflict/civil war, or to fail to do so, increasing the likelihood of renewed war with Israel. The Lebanese State lacks the political and military capacity to impose disarmament on Hezbollah, which remains influential among Shia communities, despite having been significantly weakened by Israeli strikes and leadership assassinations in 2024 and 2025. Foreign pressure from the US to disarm Hezbollah continues alongside Israeli air strikes mainly targeting southern Lebanon. That said, some analysts suggest that this ultimatum is being used as political pressure rather than an imminent invasion, given Israel’s military fatigue and Lebanon’s inability to forcibly disarm Hezbollah without risking civil conflict. ([The Conversation 09/12/2025](https://theconversation.com/with-a-deadline-looming-lebanon-is-under-pressure-to-disarm-hezbollah-or-risk-another-war-271523), [SCMP 02/12/2025](https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/politics/article/3334841/israel-sets-deadline-hezbollah-disarmament-can-lebanon-deliver), [TNA 10/12/2025](https://www.newarab.com/analysis/lebanon-and-israel-will-direct-talks-change-status-quo))

Israel’s military interference in Lebanon and the disarming of Hezbollah increase the risk of rising social tensions in Lebanon. Since the ceasefire between Hezbollah and Israel on 27 November 2024, Israeli forces have continued to violate the ceasefire and kept control of five border areas. The UNIFIL also reports a concrete T-wall erected by Israeli forces in October crossing the Blue Line, rendering more than 4,000sq.m. of Lebanese territory inaccessible. On 23 November 2025, an Israeli air strike on the southern suburbs of Beirut killed Haitham Ali Al Tabtabai, Hezbollah's chief of staff, marking a serious breach of the ceasefire and possibly leading to a re-escalation of clashes between Israel and Hezbollah. On the other hand, the Lebanese army remains largely uninvolved in the Israeli attacks on Lebanon, and the Lebanese Government continues to call for the disarming of Hezbollah. This is increasing sectarian tensions, as Shia Lebanese, especially who live in southern Lebanon, feel ignored by their Government and fear being left unprotected if Hezbollah is disarmed. ([UNIFIL 14/11/2025](https://unifil.unmissions.org/unifil-statement-14-november-2025), [BBC 23/11/2025](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cn81j54xjx1o), [GIS 31/10/2025](https://www.gisreportsonline.com/r/hezbollah-disarmament-lebanon/))

In September 2025, the risk of internal tensions, protests, and displacement in Lebanon related to attempts to politically marginalise and militarily weaken Hezbollah continues to materialise and remained relevant. The situation has led to growing frustrations within Lebanon’s Shia community. The Lebanese Government aims to complete Hezbollah disarmament by the end of 2025, but Hezbollah strongly opposes this, threatening potential unrest. While a full civil war remains unlikely, localised protests, social tensions, and displacement risks persist as Hezbollah is increasingly sidelined and the needs of affected Shia communities remain unmet. ([AJ 28/09/2025](https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2025/9/28/after-war-with-israel-how-is-lebanons-hezbollah-regrouping), [ACLED 05/09/2025](https://acleddata.com/update/middle-east-overview-september-2025), [AP 06/10/2025](https://apnews.com/article/lebanon-israel-army-hezbollah-disarmament-haikal-gabriel-5e41f719da37c61517955752374fe3e5))

On 7 August 2025, Lebanon’s cabinet, led by Prime Minister Nawaf Salam, approved a US- and Gulf-backed agreement to disarm Hezbollah by the end of 2025, with the Lebanese Army due to submit an implementation plan by late August and begin phased operations immediately after. The deal includes Israeli troop withdrawals, the dismantling of Hezbollah’s missile and drone stockpiles, and an international donor conference for reconstruction. The decision sparked protests on 8 August in Beirut’s southern suburbs, where hundreds of Hezbollah supporters gathered, chanting, “Disarming will happen in your dreams,” while Hezbollah ministers walked out of the cabinet session, calling the move a “grave sin” and vowing to treat it “as if it did not exist”. Iran is likely to increase its involvement in Lebanon, as marginalising and militarily weakening Hezbollah could destabilise regional power balances.

Until July 2025, Israeli military operations against Hezbollah continued to be reported, targeting both its leadership and infrastructure, further weakening the group’s military posture. Between 14–20 July alone, Israeli forces carried out 16 air strikes, eight ground raids, and two artillery assaults across 18 Hezbollah-linked locations, killing at least 17 people, including around ten operatives. In parallel, the US has intensified diplomatic pressure to negotiate a four-month disarmament plan for Hezbollah in exchange for a full Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanon. Despite these efforts, Hezbollah has refused to disarm until Israeli forces fully withdraw and halt all military operations.

Israel conducted over 50 air strikes in Lebanon in April 2025 claiming to target Hezbollah positions and infrastructure, but at least 190 deaths and 485 injuries among civilians had been recorded since the start of the ceasefire agreement on 27 November 2024.

Israel continues to violate the ceasefire agreement, with little response from the Lebanese Government. On 22 March 2025, Israel conducted air strikes in southern Lebanon in response to rockets fired towards the Israeli town of Metula. The air strikes resulted in casualties and infrastructure damage. Hezbollah has denied involvement in the rocket attacks, raising concerns about the stability of the existing ceasefire. The air strike killed at least eight Lebanese.

title: Hezbollah–Israel escalation related to Israeli/United States attack on Iran results in increased internal displacement, cross-border movements, and worsening food insecurity
rationale: A renewed escalation of clashes between Hezbollah and Israel is likely to happen in parallel with US and Israeli attacks on Iran. Hezbollah is perceived as a proxy of Iran and has already stated that it will not remain neutral if Iran is attacked, and Israel considers Hezbollah a major threat to its national security. The conflict dynamics in a future escalation may be largely similar to the September–November 2024 escalation, with some key differences. First, Hezbollah has been significantly weakened following the assassination of several senior leaders, disrupted arms and funding routes from Iran through Syria after the fall of Al Assad on 8 December 2024, and reduced service provision capacity within Hezbollah’s area of influence, increasing civilian reliance on humanitarian assistance. Second, the Lebanese Government, under international pressure, continues to attempt to disarm Hezbollah, increasing the likelihood of an internal conflict. Third, displacement dynamics will likely differ from previous escalations. Displaced Lebanese people may not consider crossing to Syria, since

The most affected areas are likely governorates with a high Shia presence that are perceived as under Hezbollah’s influence, mainly Al Nabatieh, south Leba

By 22 April, about 268,900 Syrians and a smaller number of around 53,000 Lebanese had crossed to Syria.
