triggers.description: Following the 12-Day War in June 2025 and a military buid up by the United States in the Middle East since December 2025, it is likely that a war on Iran will take place in February or March.

triggers.title: Intensified attempts to disarm Hezbollah
triggers.description: As of early 2026, Lebanon is pursuing a phased, multi-month plan to disarm Hezbollah. While the Lebanese Armed Forces (LAF) have made limited progress in the south, Hezbollah is actively resisting, calling these efforts, backed by U.S. and Israeli pressure, a "grave sin".

rationaleUpdates.text: This risk has largely deteriorated. The re-escalation of hostilities between Israel and Hezbollah on 1 March 2026 had displaced about 1.2 million people by 19 March, with Syria receiving an influx comprising Syrian returnees (132,186 by 18 March) and Lebanese refugees (15,618). Tensions are heightening between the host community and IDPs because of pressure over services and sectarian-related triggers, partly rising from the Lebanese Government banning Hezbollah military activities. Food insecurity is likely to deteriorate as around 25% of agricultural output originates from southern Lebanon, which has become isolated after the systematic destruction of bridges and key roads connecting the southern governorates to the rest of Lebanon. [(OCHA 21/03/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/lebanon/lebanon-flash-update-10-escalation-hostilities-lebanon-19-march-2026), [UNHCR 20/03/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/syrian-arab-republic/regional-flash-update-69-syria-situation-20-march-2026), [AJ 02/03/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/3/2/lebanese-pm-nawaf-salam-announces-ban-on-hezbollah-military-activities))

title: Intercommunal tensions between IDPs and host communities in Lebanon result in localised clashes and further displacement
rationale: Rising intercommunal tensions between host communities and IDPs in Lebanon have intensified by late March 2026 amid large-scale displacement and mounting socioeconomic pressure. The re-escalation of hostilities between Hezbollah and Israel since 1 March has displaced an estimated 1.2 million people, mostly from southern Lebanon. Reports indicate growing host community fatigue, with increasing complaints over overcrowding, pressure on basic services, and the repurposing of schools and public buildings into collective shelters, disrupting education and raising concerns over some IDP sites becoming permanent sites rather than temporary ones. Besides the high number of IDPs, many other factors drive the tensions, including economic deterioration, rising fuel and commodity prices, and a highly polarised information environment that is fuelling sectarian tensions between Shia and Christian/Sunni populations. Misinformation, especially on social media, including security-related rumours and anti-IDP rhetoric are fuelling tensions. Host communities also express security concerns, fearing tha
expectedImpact: The escalation of intercommunal tensions is likely to disproportionately affect high-density urban and peri-urban areas hosting large numbers of IDPs, particularly in Beirut, its southern suburbs, and parts of Mount Lebanon, as well as coastal and central areas where collective shelters are concentrated. According to the Tension Monitoring System, Ain Al Remmeneh, Aramoun, Beirut, Bwarej, Choueifat, Hadath, Hazmieh, Saida, and Tripoli districts a

triggers.title: Additional internal displacement
triggers.description: Additional influxes of IDPs into already saturated urban areas will further strain housing, services, and labour markets. Sudden increases in population density are likely to heighten competition over resources and amplify host community resentment.

triggers.title: Expansion of Israeli military operations in southern Lebanon
triggers.description: Wider ground operations or intensified hostilities in the south may prolong displacement and reduce prospects for return. This would reinforce perceptions among host communities that displacement is becoming protracted, increasing resistance to hosting arrangements.

triggers.title: Increased airstrikes on areas perceived as “safe” for IDPs
triggers.description: Strikes in Beirut and Mount Lebanon between 12 and 13 March, including on residential areas hosting IDPs, have undermined the notion of safe zones. Such incidents heighten host community fears that hosting IDPs exposes them to direct security risks, increasing hostility and rejection.

rationaleUpdates.text: The risk has deteriorated. While mass displacement from southern Lebanon had decreased from approximately 499,800 IDPs on 1 July 2026 to around 375,100 by 22 July, the nature of displacement dynamics shifted in ways that are increasing rather than reducing intercommunal pressure. Returns were driven by the inability to sustain displacement costs rather than improved conditions. Most residents who briefly returned to pilot zones in Zawtar Al Gharbiya village, Nabatiye governorate, have left again owing to extensive destruction and the absence of services, generating repeated movement between host communities and areas of origin, sustaining pressure on host areas. Host community fatigue is shifting into concrete restrictive measures, with Rmeish and Ain Ebel villages, Bint Jbeil district, South governorate, introducing registration mechanisms to monitor IDP movement, and Saida city, South governorate, identified as an emerging intercommunal hotspot. Fuel prices rising again on 25 July, with 95-octane petrol at LBP 2.414 million (USD 26.96) per 20L container, and the availability of electricity averaging only three to six hours daily are compounding economic pressure on host communities already carrying a disproportionate burden. ([IOM 02/07/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/lebanon/lebanon-displacement-tracking-matrix-mobility-snapshot-round-106-2-july-2026), [IOM 23/07/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/lebanon/lebanon-mobility-snapshot-round-109-23-july-2026), [Al-Sifr 08/07/2026](https://alsifr.org/displaced-lebanese), [TMS Lebanon 10/07/2026](https://tms-lebanon.com/product/report/276), [UNDP Tensions Pulse 17/07/2026](https://tms-lebanon.com/product/report/278), [Al Araby 25/07/2026](https://www.alaraby.co.uk/economy/%D8%BA%D9%84%D8%A7%D8%A1-%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%85%D8%AD%D8%B1%D9%88%D9%82%D8%A7%D8%AA-%D9%8A%D8%B2%D9%8A%D8%AF-%D9%85%D8%B9%D8%A7%D9%86%D8%A7%D8%A9-%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%84%D8%A8%D9%86%D8%A7%D9%86%D9%8A%D9%8A%D9%86), [Attaqa 22/07/2026](https://attaqa.net/2026/07/22/%D8%A3%D8%B2%D9%85%D8%A9-%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%83%D9%87%D8%B1%D8%A8%D8%A7%D8%A1-%D9%81%D9%8A-%D9%84%D8%A8%D9%86%D8%A7%D9%86-%D8%AA%D8%AA%D8%B1%D9%82%D8%A8-%D8%AF%D8%B9%D9%85-%D8%AA%D8%B1%D9%83%D9%8A%D8%A7/#google_vignette))

The risk remained stable as the de-escalation of hostilities since 20 June 2026 triggered significant return movements towards southern Lebanon, reducing immediate pressure on some host communities and collective shelters. These returns remain highly uncertain, however, with many displaced families travelling to assess conditions rather than permanently returning given extensive housing destruction, infrastructure damage, limited services, and continued security incidents. Sporadic Israeli strikes and security incidents, including air strikes in Nabatiye and Bint Jbeil on 26 June, continue to undermine confidence in safe and sustainable returns. Until 26 June, around 57,700 IDPs remained in 514 collective shelters, more than 47% of which were operating at full capacity. The evolving displacement dynamics may continue to generate tensions over shelter availability, access to services, and recovery support, particularly if households are forced to repeatedly move between areas of origin and host communities. ([TMS 26/06/2026](https://tms-lebanon.com/product/report/272))

Sectarian and intercommunal tensions in Lebanon increased in May 2026 because of growing political disputes, displacement pressures, and deteriorating social conditions in conflict-affected areas. Widespread destruction in southern Lebanon and Nabatieh, including damage to more than 94,000 buildings, increased shelter needs and forced the continued use of schools as collective shelters. By 14 May, 448 schools remained non-operational, contributing to frustration among communities and tensions between parents and private schools over tuition fees and disrupted education access in conflict-affected areas. Sectarian tensions were also compounded by debates over the General Amnesty Law that deepened divisions among religious and political groups, as parties disagreed over which detainees should benefit from amnesty, creating perceptions of sectarian favouritism and unequal treatment. [(Now Lebanon 13/05/2026](https://nowlebanon.com/lebanons-general-amnesty-law-becomes-stage-for-sectarian-fighting/), [TMS 11/05/2026](https://tms-lebanon.com/product/report/256), [Sifr 14/05/2026](https://alsifr.org/lebanese-schools-shelters))

The risk has improved slightly thanks to a ten-day ceasefire between Israel and Lebanon, brokered by the US, that took effect on 16 April 2026. The risk remains stable as only 26% of the displaced people in collective shelters have attempted to temporarily return, while most IDPs continue to stay in shelters and open areas, mostly in Beirut. Tensions between IDPs and host communities are still reported, especially following the Government’s decision to resume in-person schooling at a time when many IDPs still use schools as shelters. On 23 April, it was announced that the temporary truce would be extended by an additional three weeks to facilitate further negotiations, but Israeli air strikes on southern Lebanon still occur, and insecurity remains high. ([TMS 27/04/2026](https://tms-lebanon.com/product/report/251), [BBC 24/04/2026](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cwy32277e58o), [UNHCR 20/04/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/lebanon/middle-east-situation-lebanon-flash-update-7-13-19-april-2026))

title: Economic instability and a threat to the UN-brokered peace deal amid Libya's oilfield shutdown and Central Bank dispute

The disruption has already caused liquidity issues, delayed public salaries, and rising prices, worsening the public's economic hardships. With this situation lasting longer, people's access to essential needs of food, water, and healthcare will lik

It also means that banking services and oil production will continue to be halted, affecting Libyan citizens and harming the country's economy.

title: Russia's increased military presence in eastern Libya leads to a return to conflict, displacement, and increased humanitarian needs
rationale: On 18 December 2024, Russia transferred approximately 1,000 military personnel, including former Syrian soldiers, from Hmeimim airbase in Lattakia governorate in Syria to Benghazi airport in Libya, which is under the control of the Haftar Affiliated Forces. The personnel included officers from Syria’s 5th Corps and 25th Special Tasks Division, along with dismantled S-400 air defence systems. The move appears to be Russia’s strategic aim to strengthen its military presence in Libya, a key asset for its operations in Africa and the Mediterranean. It is also likely an opportunity to compensate for the loss that Russia experienced in Syria following the fall of Bashar Al Assad regime on 8 December. Since 2008, Russia has sought to expand its influence in Libya, using bases near Benghazi and Al Jufra districts to support operations across the Sahel region (Mali, Burkina Faso) and Sudan. Libya's location near NATO's southern border and its shorter access to the Sahel region make it key for Russia's strategic goals. An increased Russian presence will likely empower Khalifa Haftar to dominat
expectedImpact: This escalation of clashes will increase civilian casualties and displacement. Historically, such escalations have resulted in an increase in humanitarian needs and mass displacement, especially from key areas such as Misrata, Sirte, Tripoli, and parts of southern Libya. triggers.title: Increased Russian military presence
triggers.description: Following the fall of Al Assad regime on 8 December 2024, the loss of Syria as a strategic foothold is likely to prompt Russia to redirect focus to Libya to compensate for its position in the region. On 18 December, Russia moved approximately 1,000 military personnel, including former Syrian soldiers, and air defense systems to Benghazi Airport, strengthening its military presence in Libya.

triggers.title: Increased movement of Haftar's forces
triggers.description: An increased Russian presence could strengthen Khalifa Haftar’s position. Already on 31 December, reports indicated that Haftar's forces had taken control of a camp affiliated with the Presidential Council, though it did not trigger further clashes as of 8 January 2025

rationaleUpdates.text: Russia continues to strengthen its presence in Libya, extending from troop and air-defence deployment in December to a full logistics and weapons hub. Advanced systems are now in play, raising the risk of an escalated proxy confrontation with Turkish-aligned forces. In June 2025, Haftar’s Libyan National Army (LNA) reportedly used advanced Russian-supplied weapons, such as Smerch rocket launchers and Tor air-defense systems, in clashes that took place in or near populated areas. This raises concern because these heavy weapons can cause significant civilian harm, and their use shows a growing Russian military role in Libya.

Russian presence continues to be reported in Libya, but it has not led to clashes between the two rival governments in Libya. On 26 May 2025, the Libyan National Army displayed a significant array of new Russian heavy weaponry for the first time during a military parade in Benghazi. Reports also indicate a sustained air bridge between Russia and eastern Libya since December 2024, including flights to Al Khadim Air Base.

Russia continues to expand its military presence in Libya, focusing on modernising the Maaten Al Sarra airbase near the Chadian and Sudanese borders. The base, developed in coordination with the Libyan National Army (LNA), is likely to serve as a logistics hub for operations in Mali, Burkina Faso, and Sudan, instead of escalating conflict in Libya. 
This shift likely reflects Russia's strategic reorientation toward the Sahel and has significant geopolitical implications, including increased regional conflict, strengthened Russian influence in Africa, and weakened Western security efforts.

title: The consolidation of power by Dbeibeh's forces across Libya provokes counteractions from other factions, renewing clashes and protection risks
rationale: On 12 May 2025, Tripoli security forces announced the killing of Abdel Ghani al-Kikli (also known as Ghnewa), commander of the Stability Support Apparatus (SSA). His assassination immediately triggered armed clashes in southern Tripoli. Militia units loyal to the SSA fought the 444th Combat Brigade forces (aligned with Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibah), resulting in intense gun battles and killing eight civilians. By 14 May, a ceasefire was declared. As part of the political impacts, Tripoli saw large protests with demonstrators demanding Dbeibah’s resignation. By mid-May, at least three ministers announced their resignations in solidarity with the protesters. In eastern Libya, the Libyan National Army (LNA) remains under the control of General Khalifa Haftar, with his son, Lieutenant General Saddam Haftar, taking on an increasingly central operational role. In April 2025, Saddam held meetings in Ankara and Washington, signalling growing diplomatic outreach. Domestically, he has overseen new military deployments and Russian arms deliveries since December 2024. On 20 May 2025, LNA p
expectedImpact: The escalation of clashes in May destroyed homes and killed at least eight civilians, indicating that armed groups indiscriminately used heavy weapons in populated areas. If fighting further escalates, especially in new areas, more civilian casualties, displacement, and service disruptions are likely. IDPs are likely to need emergency shelter, NFIs, and protection services. The disruption of supply chains and agricultural activities in conflict-a

triggers.title: Dbeibah’s consolidation of power in Tripoli
triggers.description: The recent defeat of rival factions (like Ghnewa) and Dbeibah’s expanding control could be perceived by the LNA as a threat or provocation, prompting a response.

triggers.title: Tripoli's perceived weakness
triggers.description: Saddam may see the internal reshuffling or instability in western Libya as an opportunity to reassert LNA influence.

rationaleUpdates.text: The political situation in Libya has been relatively calm since the brief clashes reported in September 2025. It is likely that no further escalation will occur.

While no major new offensive has erupted since the May 2025 clashes, localised incidents and militia skirmishes continue, especially near Tripoli’s southern outskirts, sustaining protection risks for civilians. Abdulhamid Al Dbeibah’s Government has sought to consolidate control, exemplified by a recent preliminary accord with the powerful Radaa Force that controls Mitiga airport, brokered through Turkish and UN mediation efforts to reduce tensions in the capital’s west. In the east and south, Saddam Haftar has intensified military deployments, notably strengthening Libyan National Army presence in Sabha and surrounding southern areas. These moves are interpreted as a strategic preparation for potential escalation, supported by continued Russian arms supplies. ([Arab News 13/09/2025](https://www.arabnews.com/node/2615212/middle-east), [The Soufan Center 08/09/2025](https://thesoufancenter.org/intelbrief-2025-september-8/), [ISPI 11/09/2025](https://www.ispionline.it/en/publication/libyas-crisis-persists-amid-tripoli-tensions-and-renewed-international-role-216835), [Agenzia Nova 02/09/2025](https://www.agenzianova.com/en/news/Libya:-Haftar's-forces-strengthen-military-presence-in-Sabha/))

Following the major clashes in May 2025, Tripoli experienced additional but more localised armed confrontations in June. On 9 June, fighting broke out between the Special Deterrence Force (SDF) and the Public Security Service, after the latter established a checkpoint in a disputed area within the zone set by the May ceasefire. The SDF responded by expanding its positions, triggering several hours of clashes. This incident indicates the fragility of the ceasefire and underlying tensions over territorial control. While no large-scale or prolonged battles were reported in July, the risk of renewed violence remains likely given unresolved rivalries and the continued presence of heavily armed factions competing for influence in Tripoli. No significant clashes were reported in July. ([Reuters 14/05/2025](https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/most-intense-fighting-years-rocks-libyan-capital-2025-05-14/), [Agenzia Nova 28/04/2025](https://www.agenzianova.com/en/news/saddam-haftar-ispeziona-le-forze-di-sicurezza-al-confine-con-lalgeria/#:~:text=The%20Chief%20of%20Staff%20of,the%20troops%20in%20border%20surveillance))

title: A contested April 2026 electoral process in Libya heightens localised armed clashes, displacement, and service disruptions
rationale: Amid a stalled UN-backed political process and deep institutional fragmentation, political tensions in Libya will likely increase over the next three to six months around the April 2026 presidential and parliamentary elections and ensuing impacts. The immediate political context is marked by institutional paralysis. Disputes between the east-based House of Representatives (HoR) and the Tripoli-based High Council of State (HCS) over the reconstitution of the High National Election Commission (HNEC) board have stalled the electoral timeline. On 29 December 2025, the HoR voted to fill vacant HNEC board seats, prompting the HCS head to accuse the HoR speaker of violating the UN-backed political agreement. On 5 January 2026, the HCS elected a new HNEC president, triggering objections from eastern authorities. UNSMIL publicly warned on 6 January that these escalatory steps risk undermining the political process. By mid-February, UNSMIL reported “no meaningful progress” on agreeing to election rules or forming a unified Government. Several triggers could spark election-related violence. Fir
expectedImpact: If elections take place but the results are contested, resulting political tensions and clashes will likely have negative humanitarian consequences. Renewed instability would disrupt basic services and restrict humanitarian access, particularly in Tripoli, parts of eastern Libya, and southern border areas. Localised clashes and targeted violence would likely trigger short-term, localised displacement, especially from urban neighbourhoods affected

triggers.title: Contested election timeline
triggers.description: As of 24 February, presidential and parliamentary elections are planned for mid-April, while little agreement regarding the elections process, timeline, and rules have been made.

triggers.title: Unilateral decisions on electoral institutions
triggers.description: Unilateral moves by either the House of Representatives or the High Council of State on election rules or the composition of the High National Election Commission may provoke armed responses from rival authorities and affiliated militias, further undermining trust in the electoral process.

triggers.title: Perceived bias in the UNSMIL Structured Dialogue
triggers.description: The proposed UNSMIL Structured Dialogue may reinforce existing power imbalances if seen as bypassing key actors or legitimising contested authorities, potentially triggering resistance among excluded political and armed groups.

triggers.title: Worsening economic conditions
triggers.description: The devaluation of the Libyan dinar by approximately 14.7% on 18 January, combined with fuel shortages and declining living standards, is intensifying public frustration and lowering tolerance for political disputes, increasing the risk of unrest.

rationaleUpdates.text: Risk levels are stable as elections in Libya remain uncertain despite renewed political momentum and multiple initiatives aimed at ending the country’s political deadlock. The UN is advancing a “structured dialogue” process and facilitating “4+4” talks between eastern and western Libyan representatives to resolve disputes over electoral laws and appointments within the electoral commission. ([A. Awsat 30/05/2026](https://aawsat.com/%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B9%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%85-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B9%D8%B1%D8%A8%D9%8A/%D8%B4%D9%85%D8%A7%D9%84-%D8%A7%D9%81%D8%B1%D9%8A%D9%82%D9%8A%D8%A7/5278705-%D8%B9%D9%88%D8%AF%D8%A9-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A7%D9%86%D8%AA%D8%AE%D8%A7%D8%A8%D8%A7%D8%AA-%D8%A5%D9%84%D9%89-%D9%88%D8%A7%D8%AC%D9%87%D8%A9-%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%86%D9%82%D8%A7%D8%B4-%D8%AA%D8%AE%D8%AA%D8%A8%D8%B1-%D9%82%D8%AF%D8%B1%D8%A9-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A3%D9%81%D8%B1%D9%82%D8%A7%D8%A1-%D8%B9%D9%84%D9%89-%D8%A5%D9%86%D9%87%D8%A7%D8%A1))

Risk levels are stable as there is still no agreement regarding the election’s framework or date. On 27 April 2026, Prime Minister Abdulhamid Al Dbeibah met the UN envoy to discuss the UNSMIL political road map aimed at ending institutional fragmentation and advancing elections. The UN proposed a ‘mini dialogue phase’ focused on finalising electoral laws and restructuring the High National Elections Commission. The political process in Libya remains stalled because of the influence of rival eastern and western authorities, competing governance structures, and the weak implementation of the August 2025 road map. ([Libya Observer 27/04/2026](https://libyaobserver.ly/news/dbeibah-backs-un-mini-dialogue-urges-swift-move-elections#google_vignette), [JP 25/04/2026](https://www.jpost.com/international/article-894087))

title: El Niño drives drought conditions, increasing food insecurity and heightening humanitarian needs in Madagascar in 2027
rationale: Current models indicate a very high probability for El Niño to develop by July 2026 and persist into early 2027. In Madagascar, El Niño typically drives precipitation and temperature anomalies, with dry conditions in southern parts of the country and heavy rainfall in the north and east. In 2015–2016 and 2023–2024, El Niño caused prolonged drought conditions and crop failure, resulting in increased food insecurity that particularly affected the country's south. Seasonal forecasts anticipate near-average precipitation in July–September and below-average precipitation across most of the country in October–December. The same forecasts indicate a very high probability of above-average temperatures across the entire country in July–December. Drier and hotter-than-average conditions may affect the start of the rainy season, which runs October–April and is essential for producing Madagascar's main staple cereals, such as maize and rice, harvested in April–June. This may lead to below-average yields, with severe consequences for the population's access to food in 2027, widening food consumpt
expectedImpact: The effects of El Niño-induced drought are expected to result in deteriorating food security, increased malnutrition, and heightened humanitarian needs. In the south, rainfall deficits are likely to lead to the most severe impacts, as the region already experiences prolonged dry conditions and a poor 2025–2026 rainy season. Across the country, similarly poor conditions in 2026–2027 may lead to reduced agricultural production, depletion of househo

triggers.title: Rainfall deficits and above average precipitation affecting agricultural production
triggers.description: Dry conditions are likely to lead to reduced soil moisture, crop failure, and declining pasture availability, which in turn limit household food production and income from agriculture. This reduces food availability at the household level and increases reliance on markets at a time of constrained purchasing power.

rationaleUpdates.text: The risk has further increased in September 2026 as forecasts indicate a strong to very strong El Niño from October 2026 to February 2027, with below-average rainfall expected across parts of southern Madagascar (Androy, Anosy, and Atsimo-Andrefana regions) during the October–November start of the rainy season. Assessments indicate that the lean season has already started earlier than usual in the Grand South, with poor households exhausting food stocks in September following below-average 2025/26 harvests and increasingly relying on markets and negative coping strategies. Conditions are expected to deteriorate further from October, with around 3.7 million people (11% of the analysed population) projected to face Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse between October 2026 and February 2027, including nearly 426,000 in Emergency (IPC Phase 4). El Niño-related rainfall deficits could further reduce 2027 crop production and household incomes, particularly in the Grand South, increasing food insecurity and humanitarian needs through early 2027, though past El Niño events had limited effects on national paddy output. ([WMO 03/09/2026](https://public.wmo.int/media/news/el-nino-set-become-very-strong-raising-risks-of-extreme-weather-2027), [FEWS NET accessed 05/10/2026](https://fews.net/southern-africa/madagascar/key-message-update/september-2026), [Meteo Madagascar accessed 05/10/2026](https://www.meteomadagascar.mg/prevision/previsions-saisonnieres-hiver-meteo-madagascar), [IPC 15/07/2026](https://www.ipcinfo.org/ipc-country-analysis/details-map/es/c/1165106/?iso3=MDG), [FAO 23/09/2026](https://www.fao.org/giews/countrybrief/country.jsp?code=MDG))

The risk has deteriorated since July 2026 as confidence in a strong El Niño event has increased, and forecasts continue to indicate elevated drought risks across southern Madagascar through late 2026 and early 2027. El Niño is projected to strengthen further and persist into early 2027, increasing the likelihood of below-average rainfall and above-average temperatures during the critical agricultural season. Recent food security assessments indicate worsening conditions in Grand Sud starting in October, with below-normal harvests, reduced household food stocks, and expectations of an early and more severe lean season. The number of people facing Crisis (IPC Phase 3) and Emergency (IPC Phase 4) food insecurity is likely to increase between late 2026 and early 2027. ([NOAA 09/07/2026](https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/analysis_monitoring/enso_advisory/ensodisc.shtml), [AGH 29/07/2026](https://www.actioncontrelafaim.org/en/news/press/super-el-nino-2026-food-and-nutrition-crises-on-the-horizon-according-to-action-against-hunger/), [WMO 31/07/2026](https://wmo.int/news/media-centre/strong-el-nino-expected-intensify), [FEWS NET 30/07/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/madagascar/madagascar-food-security-outlook-early-lean-season-and-el-nino-challenge-food-security-grand-south-june-2026-january-2027), [IPC 15/07/2026](https://www.ipcinfo.org/ipc-country-analysis/details-map/en/c/1165106/?iso3=MDG))

title: Deterioration of humanitarian situation in Mali
rationale: On 18 August, troops in Bamako conducted a mutiny and arrested the country's president, Ibrahim Boubacar Keita, and vice-president. Late in the night between 18-19 August, IBK resigned dissolving the parliament and the government. Men claiming to be the spokespeople of the "National Committe for the Salvation of the People" gave an address on the country's public TV station where they announced that the country's borders were now closed and a curfew was in place. They also promised that the Malian armed forces would honour all of their current commitments (G5 Sahel and Barkhane, 2015 peace deal), and that elections would be organized in a "reasonable" amount of time. People have been protesting since a controversial ruling by the country's Constitutional Court flipped 31 legislative seats, including 10 that went to IBK's party. The protests were organized by the M5-RFP coalition under the guidance of Immam Dicko. So far, there is no evidence of coordination between the coup plotters and M5-RFP. The main difference between this coup and the one in 2012, which makes predicting outcomes

title: An increase in security incidents lead to displacement in Niono circle.
type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale: Since July, clashes have resumed in the Niono circle (Ségou region) between the Katiba Macina armed group linked to Al-Qaeda in the Islamic Maghreb (Aqmi) and the traditional dozo hunters militia in the area, who tried to face them. The ceasefire agreement that was reached in March 2021 has been broken. The situation has deteriorated particularly since the end of September with daily attacks targeting civilians but also clashes between armed groups and militia. Dozens of deaths are reported even though there is no reliable figures yet. The Dozo militiamen are also accused of extortion, forced recruitment and cattle theft. These incidents occur during the harvest period, preventing farmers from going to the fields. Many people have started to flee to safer places, especially in Ségou. With the violence continuing, the risk of increased attacks on civilians and displacement seems very likely in the weeks to come. The needs for essential goods and food security are likely to increase.

title: Economic sanctions lead to the loss of livelihoods and increased food insecurity.
rationale: On 9 January 2022 the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) decided to apply several economic sanctions against Mali, including the closure of land and air borders with member countries, the suspension of all commercial and financial transactions between ECOWAS countries and Mali, and the freezing of Malian assets in the Central Banks of ECOWAS. These sanctions were applied in reaction to the decision of the Transition authorities to postpone the presidential election, initially scheduled for February 2022, and following the submission of a timetable for a transition period of five years at the end of the Assises Nationales de la Refondation −consultations with the population with the objective to fix the date of the next elections and to guarantee the return of civilians to power. The five-year period was judged too long by ECOWAS.
expectedImpact: These sanctions are likely to cause loss of livelihoods and increased food insecurity, aggravated by the persistent conflict and the economic consequences of COVID-19, including difficulties in the supply of food products and agricultural inputs, rising prices, and job losses (IRC 19/01/2022). Even though the authorities try to resort to other neighboring non-ECOWAS countries to circumvent the effects of the sanctions, the transport of essential
materialised: This risk has partially materialised in terms of rising food prices, but the impact of sanctions on humanitarian access has been very limited. The same can be said for the impact of sanctions on livestock farming. The increase in food insecurity has materialised, but food security was expected to de

title: Failure of essential services owing to the blockade in Mali leads to civil unrest and destabilisation and aggravates needs
type: Future impact of a hazard which has already taken place
rationale: Since September 2025, Jama'a Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM), an Al Qaeda–affiliated group, has expanded its blockade strategy from the traditional conflict zones in northern and central Mali (Gao, Mopti, Tombouctou) to southern and southwestern regions, including Kayes, Koulikoro, and Ségou. This expansion signals a shift towards a strategy of coercive governance, with JNIM using economic strangulation – via targeted attacks on fuel convoys and the imposition of checkpoints along critical trade routes – to undermine state legitimacy and force power-sharing negotiations. The blockade marks the first large-scale attempt to encircle Bamako, Mali’s capital, and demonstrates the group’s increasing operational reach. The blockades have resulted in acute shortages of fuel, electricity, and essential goods across the country. Fuel prices in Bamako surged by over 400% in October, with queues lasting hours and some car owners abandoning vehicles at petrol stations. Major public services, including health and education, have been severely disrupted. The Government closed schools and univer
expectedImpact: Blockades will continue to erode state authority and legitimacy throughout 2026, with JNIM consolidating control over additional rural areas and possibly seizing more towns. As a result, acute food insecurity is expected to worsen as transportation costs and food prices continue rising. Inflation and food shortages will undermine household purchasing power and increase hunger, particularly in urban areas where informal labour is the main income s
materialised: The blockade caused recurrent fuel shortages, electricity cuts, transport disruptions, school closures, increased prices, and constraints on humanitarian operations. Access to healthcare, markets, and essential services deteriorated in several regions. While large-scale civil unrest did not material

triggers.title: Exhaustion of strategic fuel reserves
triggers.description: If strategic fuel reserves held by the Malian army and state institutions fall below critical thresholds, the suspension of non-emergency services—such as power generation, water treatment, and public transportation—will become likely. This could spark widespread public unrest and intensify pressure on the transitional government.

triggers.title: Breakdown of essential services in urban centres
triggers.description: If power outages become prolonged and water treatment plants cease operations due to lack of fuel or technical maintenance, urban populations may face acute public health risks, including waterborne disease outbreaks and sanitation system failures.

triggers.title: Collapse of government–JNIM negotiations
triggers.description: If informal negotiations between JNIM and Malian authorities collapse or result in the government accepting destabilising conditions (e.g. prisoner releases or expanded social control measures), this could further erode state legitimacy and increase risks of political instability

triggers.title: Escalation of civil unrest and anti-government protest
triggers.description: If fuel, food, and service shortages persist in Bamako and other cities, spontaneous or organised protests may erupt, particularly among marginalised or economically vulnerable groups. Such unrest could trigger government crackdowns or be exploited by JNIM to further destabilise the regime

rationaleUpdates.text: The risk remains high and increasingly volatile. While there were indications of a partial easing in the intensity of the fuel blockade earlier in April 2026, recent large-scale coordinated attacks across multiple cities highlight a renewed deterioration in the security environment. Attacks targeting key locations, including Kati near Bamako, and the reported death of the Minister of Defence underscore the extent of armed groups’ operational reach. These developments are likely to further undermine the State’s ability to secure key transport corridors and ensure the continuity of fuel supply, which remains heavily dependent on military-escorted convoys. The reported loss of control over areas such as Kidal and the withdrawal of allied forces also point to weakening state authority in strategic regions. As a result, the risk of renewed disruptions to fuel supply and essential services remains high. Combined with continued fuel price increases and inflationary pressures, this may further constrain access to electricity, healthcare, and markets, while increasing the likelihood of social tensions. Overall, recent events suggest that earlier improvements were fragile and that the structural drivers of the risk remain firmly in place. ([RFI 27/04/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260427-attaques-au-mali-apr%C3%A8s-la-mort-du-ministre-de-la-d%C3%A9fense-les-populations-inqui%C3%A8tes-malgr%C3%A9-un-certain-calme), [RFI 02/04/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260402-mali-autorit%C3%A9s-accusent-des-entreprises-utiliser-crise-carburant-pour-gonfler-leurs-prix), [BBC 24/04/2026](https://www.bbc.com/afrique/articles/cyv1rpn4753o), [Ledjely 01/04/2026](https://ledjely.com/2026/04/01/mali-la-hausse-du-carburant-fait-craindre-une-spirale-des-prix/), [Timbuktu Institute 17/04/2026](https://timbuktu-institute.org/index.php/toutes-l-actualites/item/1509-le-mali-entre-chocs-externes-et-defis-internes))

The risk has slightly deteriorated, with more fuel shortages reported. On 28 March 2026, the Government of Mali raised diesel prices by nearly 30% and petrol prices by 13% in response to supply disruptions by the Jama'at Nasr Al Islam wal Muslimin blockade. The heightened impacts of the fuel shortages increase the likelihood of civil unrest. On 25 March, diesel shortages in Bamako intensified as limited fuel imports were further redirected to support electricity generation during a heat wave. Several fuel stations ran out of diesel, leading to long queues at remaining supply points and disrupting urban mobility. At least 100 public transport vehicles were taken out of service, while construction-related transport (e.g. sand and gravel trucks) halted. ([TRT 10/03/2026](https://www.trtafrika.com/article/27f0213a3997), [Bloomberg 28/03/2026](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-03-28/mali-raises-petrol-diesel-prices-and-cuts-some-fuel-subsidies))

Since January, the risk linked to the fuel blockade and related insecurity has remained high and volatile, with continued attacks despite temporary supply improvements in Bamako. While fuel availability in the capital improved in early February, the broader trend points to sustained operational disruption and geographic expansion of insecurity.  Key developments include renewed large-scale JNIM attacks on fuel convoys near Kayes, leading to the killing of drivers and military escorts and prompting a nationwide transport strike on 9 February. In central Mali, state forces conducted airstrikes in Macina (Ségou Region) following reported insurgent activity in Sikasso, while in Kidal region, a convoy was targeted by both JNIM and Azawad Liberation Front elements, suggesting overlapping armed actor pressure in the north. Continued road blockades affecting multiple localities and persistent electricity shortages (6–8 hours per day in Bamako) indicate structural fragility. In the short to medium term, continued convoy insecurity and transport disruptions risk renewed fuel shortages, rising prices, reduced market access, and further constraints on electricity supply, livelihoods, and humanitarian access, particularly outside the capital. ([DW 10/02/2026](https://www.dw.com/fr/focus-sahel-plus-villes-sous-blocus-du-jnim-au-mali/a-75901357), [RFI 03/02/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260203-au-mali-l-approvisionnement-en-carburant-plie-mais-ne-rompt-pas), [RFI 10/02/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260210-mali-cibles-d-attaques-jihadistes-des-chauffeurs-routiers-appellent-%C3%A0-un-arr%C3%AAt-de-travail), [RFI 20/02/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260220-mali-une-frappe-de-drone-des-rebelles-du-fla-contre-l-arm%C3%A9e-fait-des-morts-des-deux-c%C3%B4t%C3%A9s)).

Since the previous update, the risk associated with the fuel blockade has remained elevated but volatile, with short-lived improvements followed by renewed disruption. While some fuel circulation has resumed intermittently, shortages persisted throughout January 2026, indicating neither clear escalation nor stabilisation. Key developments point to a broadening of the blockade’s scope. In Bamako, electricity supply remains limited to around five to seven hours per day, and fuel availability continues to be intermittent, with long queues and growing reliance on informal markets. In the southwest, Nioro du Sahel remains under a near-total blockade since early September 2025, with movement restrictions, reported abductions, and the increasing scarcity of food, medicines, fuel, and water. In parallel, attacks linked to Jama'at Nasr Al Islam wal Muslimin have expanded beyond fuel convoys to economic infrastructure, including mid-January 2026 attacks on industrial sites in Kayes and late January attacks on fuel convoys. Authorities have announced tighter fuel controls and reinforced escorts ahead of Ramadan, but continued incidents suggest a persistent risk of disruption to essential services, rising living costs, constrained access to markets, and increasing humanitarian needs in affected urban and blockaded areas. ([RFI 10/01/2026)[https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260110-mali-des-habitants-de-nioro-du-sahel-racontent-le-blocus-jihadiste-qui-dure-depuis-cinq-mois), [RFI 14/01/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260114-mali-la-fourniture-d-%C3%A9lectricit%C3%A9-et-de-carburant-reste-tr%C3%A8s-insuffisante-les-bamakois-se-r%C3%A9signent), [RFI 14/01/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260114-mali-le-manque-de-carburant-%C3%A0-l-a%C3%A9roport-de-bamako-perturbe-certaines-liaisons), [RFI 16/01/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260116-mali-blocus-jihadiste-%C3%A0-nioro-du-sahel-la-situation-est-sous-contr%C3%B4le-selon-les-autorit%C3%A9s-de-transition), [RFI 12/01/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260112-mali-comment-et-pourquoi-des-jihadistes-ont-attaqu%C3%A9-trois-sites-industriels-de-la-r%C3%A9gion-de-kayes), [RFI 02/02/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260202-au-mali-les-autorit%C3%A9s-veulent-s%C3%A9curiser-l-apprivisionnement-de-carburant-pour-le-mois-de-ramadan))

Since early December, the JNIM has resumed attacks on fuel convoys after a temporary slowdown observed in late November. The initial lull allowed some fuel deliveries to reach Bamako and Mopti, briefly reducing shortages and restoring limited electricity and public services. However, renewed ambushes in Bougouni, Ouélessébougou, and Ségou, including the destruction of over 15 fuel tankers and the killing of drivers, have reinstated supply chain disruptions and public anxiety. In Bamako, queues at petrol stations have grown again, diesel has become scarce, and intermittent power cuts have returned. While 300 trucks were received ahead of the AES summit in mid-December, the improvement remains temporary. In Mopti and surrounding areas, fuel convoys have resumed under heavy military protection, but the quantities remain insufficient to meet the demand. Electricity has returned for around nine hours per day, and some economic activity has restarted, though fuel prices on the black market remain triple the official rate.  The blockade continues to affect humanitarian operations and access to essential services. In areas such as Koulikoro, Sikasso, and Koutiala, fuel scarcity persists, with limited electricity, inaccessible health services, and rising transport costs. The JNIM’s strategy has evolved beyond physical control, aiming to delegitimise the state through economic strangulation and selective violence. The group is reportedly consolidating control over rural areas by offering basic services (such as justice and security) under Islamic governance, gradually normalising its authority. 
([Echoes of the Sahel 17/12/2025](https://mailchi.mp/9406facccf81/sahel-news-round-up-21010886?e=fe2a2db667), [RFI 17/12/2025](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20251217-mali-%C3%A0-bamako-l-approvisionnement-en-carburant-est-fluctuant), [RFI 12/12/2025](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20251212-mali-retour-du-carburant-et-du-courant-%C3%A0-mopti-une-am%C3%A9lioration-notable-mais-encore-trop-r%C3%A9duite), [Revue Conflicts 26/11/2025](https://www.revueconflits.com/jnim-au-mali-letranglement-de-bamako-et-la-strategie-du-califat-par-consentement/))

title: Continued coordinated JNIM–FLA attacks and blockades increase protection risks, displacement, and humanitarian access constraints in Mali
type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale: Since late April 2026, the unprecedented operational coordination between Jama’at Nasr Al Islam wal Muslimin (JNIM) and the Front de libération de l’Azawad (FLA) has significantly increased pressure on Mali’s security apparatus and exposed vulnerabilities in state control across northern, central, and western regions. Over the next one to three months, three converging escalation dynamics will likely worsen humanitarian conditions significantly across Mali. The assassination of Defence Minister Gen. Sadio Camara on 25 April 2026 created a command vacuum in Mali's security apparatus leadership. As the junta’s chief military strategist and the primary architect of the partnership with Russia’s Africa Corps, his death is likely to severely hamper coordination of counter-offensive operations, make Malian-Russian tactical responses less cohesive, and embolden further advances by armed groups at a critical juncture of territorial contestation. JNIM and the FLA are both targeting urban supply chains, favouring economic attrition strategies over military objectives. With the FLA explicitly s
expectedImpact: Continued conflict escalation is expected to significantly worsen humanitarian conditions across Mali over the next one to three months, compounding pre-existing vulnerabilities among an estimated 5.1 million people already needing assistance. Mali already hosts more than 414,000 IDPs, and the number is likely to surge as fighting intensifies in Gao and Tombouctou regions and spreads southward into Sikasso and Kayes regions. The conflict also thr

triggers.title: Expansion of coordinated JNIM–FLA operations
triggers.description: Coordinated attacks by JNIM and the FLA against military bases, urban centres, and strategic infrastructure may continue or expand into additional regions, increasing territorial contestation and exposing civilians to heightened insecurity. Although likely tactical and temporary, continued operational coordination between both actors could allow simultaneous attacks across multiple regions and increase pressure on Ma

triggers.title: Intensification of military operations and retaliatory violence
triggers.description: In response to the coordinated attacks, Malian forces and allied armed actors may increase military operations, aerial strikes, and security measures in contested areas. Expanded military deployments around strategic towns, transport corridors, and urban centres may increase movement restrictions and insecurity for civilians. Escalating confrontations and the militarisation of strategic urban centres and transport ro

rationaleUpdates.text: The risk continued to increase during the second half of September as JNIM sustained high-intensity operations in central Mali, further challenging state control and security along strategic corridors. Following its 10 September attack on the Dioura military camp, which killed more than 100 soldiers and resulted in more than 100 being captured, JNIM shelled the Sévaré air base for six consecutive nights between 14–19 September and attacked a forward operating base in Konna on 20 September. The attacks indicate JNIM's continued capacity to target major military positions and transport corridors in Mopti region, while supply routes to Bamako remain exposed to disruption by armed groups. Although no significant new joint operation by JNIM and the Azawad Liberation Front was identified after the previous update, the sustained pressure by JNIM, alongside the continued presence and coordination capacity of both groups in northern Mali, maintains the risk of further territorial and humanitarian deterioration. Continued insecurity is likely to constrain population movement, trade, and humanitarian access, particularly across central and northern Mali. ([Reuters 21/09/2026](https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/al-qaeda-linked-militants-kill-more-than-100-malian-soldiers-attack-this-month-2026-09-21/), [CT 24/09/2026](https://www.criticalthreats.org/analysis/ethiopia-tigray-tplf-fano-china-prc-djibouti-jnim-mali-sudan-saf-rsf-somalia-aussom), [AJ 22/09/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/9/22/mali-marks-independence-amid-a-worsening-security-crisis))

The risk deteriorated in August 2026 as continued operations of Jama'at Nasr Al Islam wal Muslimin and the Azawad Liberation Front sustained pressure on state control in northern and central Mali. Fighting around Kidal contributed to the displacement of nearly 40,000 people, including around 15,000 who sought refuge in Gao and Ménaka regions, increasing pressure on already-strained services. Conflict involving non-state armed groups continued to disrupt markets, livelihoods, and supply routes, worsening food insecurity. From June–August, 1.56 million people faced Crisis (CH Phase 3) or worse food insecurity, including nearly 57,000 in Emergency (Phase 4). ([Global Watch 13/08/2026](https://globalwatch.info/en_GB/articles/gc7/features/2026/08/13/feature-02/Nearly-40-000-displaced-following-Mali-fighting-surge-sources), [FAO 27/08/2026](https://www.fao.org/giews/countrybrief/country.jsp?code=MLI&lang=en&), [DW 17/08/2026](https://amp.dw.com/fr/laide-humanitaire-aux-d%C3%A9plac%C3%A9s-internes-sorganise-%C3%A0-gao-et-menaka-mali-jnim/a-78392740)).

The risk deteriorated further in July 2026. Although Malian and African Corps forces regained Anéfis following the fighting of 4–9 July, subsequent attacks show that they have not secured the surrounding territory or key transit routes. Jama'at Nasr Al Islam wal Muslimin (JNIM) and the Front de libération de l'Azawad (FLA) continued joint operations against military positions and convoys in northern Mali, while JNIM intensified pressure in central Mali, including by taking the Kouakourou military camp and forcing the locality’s approximately 5,000 residents to flee. These developments confirm that the JNIM–FLA operational cooperation remains active and that armed groups retain the capacity to isolate strategic locations, disrupt military resupply, and generate new displacement. Humanitarian conditions have worsened alongside the escalation. More than half of Kidal’s population has moved towards Gao, Ménaka, or Algeria, while markets are operating at reduced capacity, and Emergency (IPC Phase 4) food insecurity is expected to persist in Kidal and Ménaka. Attacks on civilians and vehicles continue to disrupt trade and movement elsewhere, while blockaded communities, such as Diafarabé, remain at risk of renewed shortages despite limited food deliveries. Humanitarian operations remain suspended in Kidal, and insecurity continues to restrict access in Gao, Mopti, and Tombouctou. Over the next one to three months, continued JNIM–FLA operations, insecurity along strategic corridors, and retaliatory military strikes are likely to generate further displacement and civilian protection risks while constraining trade and humanitarian assistance. Limited funding and access will further reduce the capacity to respond as food needs increase during the lean season. ([FEWS NET 06/08/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/mali/mali-mise-jour-des-messages-cles-persistance-de-linsecurite-alimentaire-durgence-phase-4-de-lipc-dans-les-regions-de-kidal-et-de-menaka-juillet-2026-janvier-2027), [ACLED 20/07/2026](https://acleddata.com/expert-comment/malian-military-losing-against-jnim), [RFI 22/07/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/podcasts/revue-de-presse-afrique/20260722-%C3%A0-la-une-au-mali-mbareck-ag-akli-figure-clef-de-la-r%C3%A9bellion-ind%C3%A9pendantiste), [RFI 25/07/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260725-mali-apr%C3%A8s-la-d%C3%A9route-de-l-arm%C3%A9e-malienne-face-aux-jihadistes-du-jnim-kouakourou-s-est-vid%C3%A9-de-ses-habitants), [WFP 22/07/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/mali/wfp-mali-country-brief-july-2026), [RFI 30/07/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260730-mali-la-ville-de-diafarab%C3%A9-enfin-ravitaill%C3%A9e-mais-en-faible-quantit%C3%A9-apr%C3%A8s-un-an-de-blocus-du-jnim)).

The risk has deteriorated further. Since 4 July 2026, Jama'at Nasr Al Islam wal Muslimin and the Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) have launched a new wave of coordinated attacks across northern and central Mali, including Aguelhok, Anéfis, Gao, and Sévaré. Armed groups have seized Anéfis town and continue to besiege the military camp, while clashes, shelling, drone attacks, aerial strikes, and attempts to reinforce the camp continue. The attack on a military convoy travelling from Gao towards Anéfis on 9 July indicates that the armed groups are sustaining pressure on strategic routes and military positions in Kidal region. The escalation confirms that coordinated JNIM–FLA operations remain active and are likely to further disrupt movement along key routes linking Gao, Kidal, and other northern areas. This increases risks of civilian exposure to armed violence, movement restrictions, new displacement, and humanitarian access constraints in areas already facing severe needs. Around 683,000 people live in the affected towns and surrounding regions, including approximately 363,000 already in need of humanitarian assistance. The deterioration comes amid persistent blockade-related impacts. Tombouctou has faced severe fuel shortages, disrupting electricity and water services, while there are reports of serious abuses by all conflict parties since the April escalation, including civilian killings, vehicle burnings, and abusive counter-insurgency operations. ([RFI 09/07/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260709-mali-le-convoi-militaire-en-route-vers-an%C3%A9fis-attaqu%C3%A9-par-le-fla-et-le-jnim-pr%C3%A8s-de-tabankort), [RFI 06/07/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260706-mali-l-arm%C3%A9e-et-l-africa-corps-russe-tiennent-le-camp-d-anefis-assi%C3%A9g%C3%A9-et-bombard%C3%A9), [RFI 04/07/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260704-mali-des-localit%C3%A9s-dans-le-nord-et-une-prison-dans-le-sud-vis%C3%A9es-par-des-attaques), [France 24 29/06/2026](https://www.france24.com/en/africa/20260629-all-warring-parties-in-mali-committed-grave-abuses-against-civilians-report-says))

The risk remains active. While some local agreements have eased movement restrictions in specific areas, recent developments indicate that coordinated JNIM–FLA operations continue to generate significant humanitarian consequences through displacement, access constraints, market disruptions, and the progressive isolation of northern and central regions. The humanitarian impact of the April escalation remains evident in Kidal and neighbouring regions. Food security conditions in Kidal are expected to deteriorate from Crisis (IPC Phase 3) to Emergency (IPC Phase 4) from June onwards as insecurity, military bombardments, reduced trade flows from Algeria, and the absence of escorted convoys further isolate the region during the lean season. Access to humanitarian assistance remains severely constrained, while worsening market shortages, high prices, and restrictions on livestock movements are reducing household access to food and income.
Displacement and service disruptions continue to increase humanitarian needs. WFP reported 2,328 newly displaced people from Kidal to Gao following the April crisis, while all 16 schools in Kidal remained closed through May, disrupting education for more than 2,900 students. At the same time, insecurity continues to affect key transport corridors and access to essential goods. Although a locally negotiated agreement led JNIM to lift its nearly two-year blockade of the road linking Bamako to Nara and Mourdiah, other areas remain affected by movement restrictions, insecurity, and fuel shortages. In Tombouctou, prolonged fuel shortages linked to JNIM's blockade have contributed to disruptions in electricity and water services, forcing residents to rely on limited alternative water sources. Similar disruptions to trade flows and fuel supplies continue to affect purchasing power and access to basic goods across northern and central Mali.
Over the next one to three months, continued JNIM–FLA pressure on transport corridors, urban supply chains, and contested territories is likely to sustain displacement, restrict humanitarian access, and worsen food insecurity, particularly in Kidal, Ménaka, Gao, and parts of Mopti and Tombouctou. While local agreements may temporarily reduce violence in some areas, they do not address the broader deterioration in state control, humanitarian access, and civilian protection conditions across northern and central Mali.
([FEWS NET 11/06/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/mali/mali-key-message-update-food-insecurity-deteriorates-emergency-ipc-phase-4-kidal-amid-severe-conflict-may-september-2026), [WFP 18/06/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/mali/wfp-mali-country-brief-june-2026), [Education Cluster 24/06/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/mali/mali-compte-rendu-reunion-mensuelle-du-mois-de-juin-2026-meeting-minutes), [RFI 26/06/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260626-mali-tombouctou-priv%C3%A9e-d-%C3%A9lectricit%C3%A9-et-d-eau-depuis-quatre-jours-de-carburant-depuis-un-mois), [RFI 25/06/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260625-au-mali-le-blocus-jihadiste-lev%C3%A9-sur-la-route-menant-%C3%A0-mourdiah-et-nara)).

rationale: As of July 2025, pressure over limited resources continues to increase, especially in Hodh Ech Chargui wilaya, where the number of Malian refugees continues to increase, while drought and seasonal dry conditions continue in depletion of water and grazing resources, which may trigger tensions and localized clashes. The southeastern Hodh Chargui wilaya, which borders Mali, now hosts over 160,000 Malian refugees as of 30 June 2025, compromising over 25.5% of the total population of the wilaya, up from 19% in 2024. The refugee-to-host population ratio in some areas exceeds 1:4, straining access to local sources of water, fuel wood, and grazing land. Competition for scarce water, land, and grazing resources is intensifying between refugees, local communities, and Mauritanian returnees, who were previously displaced from Mali due to insecurity and violence. Localised tensions over access to farmland and grazing areas are often reported and is likely, as was the case in 2022 following a large influx of Malian refugees into Mauritania. Tensions could erupt between ethnic groups such as Haratin, Fulani, and Arab-Berber Mauritanians, and Malian refugees (mainly Bambara, Tuareg, and Fulani) as well as among livelihood groups like pastoralists, agropastoralists, and farmers. If tensions over limited water and grazing resources continues between refugees and the host community, this will likely trigger localised clashes.

triggers.title: Lean season (June–September)
triggers.description: As food stocks deplete and pasture scarcity peaks during the lean season (June–September), competition over land, water, and grazing areas intensifies, increasing the risk of localised clashes between refugee, host, and returnee communities.

rationaleUpdates.text: The risk continues to be stable overall, but the influx of refugees from Mali remains ongoing. Between October 2025 and March 2026, more than 13,302 refugees have arrived in southern Mauritania. There are no reports indicating tensions due to competition over scarce water and food sources, however, the risk remains valid, especially as refugees continue to arrive in large numbers in Mauritania. [(UNHCR 18/03/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/mauritania/refugee-influx-hodh-chargui-mauritania-11-march-2026)).

The risk continues to be stable overall, but the influx of refugees from Mali remains ongoing. Between October 2025 and February 2026, more than 10,429 refugees have arrived in southern Mauritania. There are no reports indicating tensions due to competition over scarce water and food sources, however, the risk remains valid, especially as refugees continue to arrive in large numbers in Mauritania. ([UNHCR 17/02/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/mauritania/refugee-influx-hodh-chargui-mauritania-17-february-2026)).

The risk continues to be valid and relevant as more Malian refugees are arriving in Mauritania, further straining the already limited resources in Hodh Ech Chargui wilaya. Between 24 October-25 November, an additional 3774 refugees arrived in Mauritania due to the escalation of violence in Mali. Arrivals are expected to increase further. Most new refugees are women and children, and humanitarian responders anticipate rising needs in food, shelter, and disease prevention. In Mbera camp, they grapple with overcrowding, a weak health infrastructure, and concurrent outbreaks of diphtheria and Rift Valley fever, all of which are straining basic services. ([UNHCR 26/11/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/mauritania/refugee-influx-hodh-chargui-mauritania-25-november-2025), [IFRC 06/11/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/mauritania/mauritania-emergency-operation-update-1-emergency-appeal-no-mdrmr017), [PANA 27/08/2025](https://panafricanewsagency.com/mbera-refugee-camp-a-miniature-mali-in-mauritanias-remote-borderlands/))

title: The implementation of the Migrant Protection Protocol leads to an increased number of migrants stranded at the border lacking protection, shelter, and services.
type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale: The Migrant Protection Protocol (MPP) in the United States will be back in force from Monday 6 December. Through this programme, initially implemented by Trump's administration, the aim is for migrants to wait in Mexican border cities while asylum applications to the United States are processed. This policy works alongside Title 42, which means that, in addition to preventing asylum seekers from passing through, the US government will be able to return asylum seekers already in the US to Mexico's borders. This represents a risk for the migrant population, due to the high levels of xenophobia at the borders. In addition, the Protocol would increase the number of migrants at Mexico's borders, where most shelters are almost at capacity (as is the case in Tamaulipas and Reynosa). There is also a risk to the sectoral needs of the migrant population, as many of the border cities are heavily controlled by drug cartels. To date, 1,544 assaults against MPP asylum seekers have been recorded. Legal representation for MPP asylum seekers is limited (only 10% have access).

triggers.title: Migration crisis in the USA - Mexico border

title: Dzud-related extreme weather conditions leading to decreased livelihoods.
rationale: The “dzud” is a multiple natural disaster comprising summer drought resulting in inadequate pasture and production of hay, followed by severe winter conditions consisting heavy snow cover, winds, and lower-than-normal temperatures. The phenomenon prevents livestock from accessing pasture or from receiving adequate hay and fodder, resulting in high mortality levels, especially in steppe (dry and grassy plain), vast grassland, devoid of trees and with little diversity in vegetation. The frequency of severe winters has doubled in the past 20 years, making only 1% of the steppe suitable for growing crops. These conditions are commonly preceded by a dry summer with equally scant grazing. Livestock struggle to build up the stores of fat they need for winter, and farming families risk losing their main source of income. A quarter to a third of the national herd population were lost in the past two dzud events. title: Drought across Morocco leads to water shortages, decreased agricultural production, and increased food and vegetable prices
rationale: In 2022, Morocco faced its most acute drought in 40 years, aggravated by climate change. The country received little rain that year, 64% less than the standard, and authorities announced that they could reserve only 11% of what they would save in an average year. The most affected cities were Marrakesh and Oujda. The Government supported the agricultural sector with EUR 1 billion (over USD 1 billion) to address the problem. In Morocco, agriculture is the biggest employer, accounting for 17% of output in 2021.

triggers.title: Drought
triggers.description: Drought significantly reduces water availability, which is critical for Morocco's agriculture-dependent economy, impacting crop yields and livelihoods. Prolonged dry conditions also exacerbate food price inflation and strain water resources, increasing vulnerabilities for communities reliant on agriculture and domestic water supply.

title: Escalating civil unrest leads to increased protection risks and poverty
rationale: On 9 October 2024, Mozambique held general elections featuring three main presidential candidates: the Frelimo party’s Daniel Chapo, successor to outgoing President Filipe Nyusi; Venâncio Mondlane of the new Podemos party; and Ossufo Momade of the Renamo party. Allegations of vote tampering, restricted access for opposition representatives and observers, and the misuse of state resources marred the election process Though Chapo led early results, Mondlane alleged victory on 10 October based on parallel vote counts. On 21 October, protests erupted after Mondlane called for demonstrations and a nationwide general strike. The police’s heavy-handed response – including firing live ammunition at demonstrators; the targeted killing of two senior opposition figures, including Mondlane’s lawyer, who was preparing a case claiming electoral fraud; and the declaration by the National Election Commission on 24 October of Chapo as the winner with 71% of the votes– intensified the protests across the country, including in Beira, Maputo, Nacala, Pemba, Nampula, Zambezia, and Chimoio. expectedImpact: Mortality and protection risks will increase as violent confrontations between protesters and police lead to casualties and heightened risks of unlawful arrests, extortion, and attacks on civilians. Young men, women, and children are particularly vulnerable. Criminal activities, including looting, are likely to rise amid the breakdown of law and order. Livelihoods and poverty will deteriorate further, especially in urban centres like Maputo and N

By March 2025, over 350 people had been killed, thousands injured – including gunshot victims – and nearly 4,000 arrested or detained, including children. There

The ongoing dispute over election results and the unyielding positions of both Mondlane and the government (Frelimo) could lead to further polarization and violence

title: La Niña-induced heavy rainfall and enhanced cyclonic activity from October–March in central and northern Mozambique increase flooding and displacement
rationale: Forecasts indicate that weak La Niña conditions will persist through the October 2025 to March 2026 rainy season, typically bringing above-average rainfall to parts of southeastern Africa, including Mozambique. La Niña phases have historically coincided with heightened flood and cyclone risk, particularly along the Zambezi, Licungo, and Pungue River basins, as well as in low-lying coastal areas. The negative Indian Ocean Dipole further reinforces the likelihood of heavy and prolonged rainfall across the region. ([WMO 02/09/2025](https://wmo.int/media/news/la-nina-may-return-temperatures-are-likely-be-above-average), [WFP 15/10/2025](https://docs.wfp.org/api/documents/WFP-0000169538/download/), [FEWS NET 16/10/2025](https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/international/FEWS_REPORT/Mozambique/FEWSNET_Mozambique_September2025.pdf))
expectedImpact: If La Niña-driven rainfall intensifies across Mozambique between October 2025 and March 2026, widespread flooding and displacement are likely, particularly in central and northern provinces, including Manica, Nampula, Sofala, Tete, and Zambézia. rationaleUpdates.text:
The risk of flooding and weather-induced displacement in Mozambique has intensified since December 2025 as La Niña–driven rainfall has translated into sustained, on-the-ground impacts. During January 2026, above-average rainfall persisted across central and northern provinces, with repeated heavy rain episodes falling on already saturated catchments. This has driven further rises in the Zambezi, Licungo, Pungue and Save rivers and expanded flooding in Zambézia, Sofala, Tete, Manica and Nampula.
Cyclonic disturbances and active low-pressure systems in the Mozambique Channel have acted as key aggravating factors, generating short-duration but high-intensity rainfall that has overwhelmed drainage systems and weakened flood defences. Localised infrastructure damage, crop losses and continued population displacement indicate an escalation from forecast risk to realised impact.
In the short to medium term, continued flooding through the remainder of the rainy season is likely to deepen humanitarian needs, disrupt access to affected communities, increase food insecurity due to crop destruction, and strain basic services, particularly in low-lying river basins and coastal districts.
([ECHO 29/01/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/mozambique/mozambique-severe-weather-and-floods-update-ingd-noaa-cpc-echo-daily-flash-29-january-2026), [ECHO 20/01/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/mozambique/mozambique-severe-weather-and-floods-update-ingd-copernicus-emsr-dg-echo-noaa-southern-africa-echo-daily-flash-20-january-2026), [UNFPA 19/01/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/mozambique/unfpa-mozambique-heavy-rains-and-flooding-flash-update-19-january-2026), [IOM 19/01/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/mozambique/mozambique-heavy-rains-and-flooding-displacement-update-18-january-2026), [OCHA 18/01/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/mozambique/flash-update-no3-heavy-rains-and-floods-central-and-southern-mozambique-18-january-2026))

rationale: Climate projections indicate a high likelihood of El Niño conditions developing in July 2026 and persisting into the 2026/2027 rainy season, coinciding with Mozambique's main agricultural period. El Niño will drive contrasting rainfall patterns, with drier conditions in southern and central regions and wetter conditions in the north. The anticipated event is driven by abnormal warming of equatorial Pacific sea surface temperatures, which disrupts global atmospheric circulation and rainfall patterns. Seasonal forecasts for the October–December period anticipate these typical El Niño patterns, indicating a moderate probability of above-average precipitation in the north and below-average precipitation in the south. rationaleUpdates.text: The risk has further increased in September 2026 as forecasts indicate a strong to very strong El Niño from October 2026 to February 2027, with below-average rainfall expected across parts of southern Madagascar (Androy, Anosy, and Atsimo-Andrefana regions) during the October–November start of the rainy season. Assessments indicate that the lean season has already started earlier than usual in the Grand South, with poor households exhausting food stocks in September following below-average 2025/26 harvests and increasingly relying on markets and negative coping strategies. Conditions are expected to deteriorate further from October, with around 3.7 million people (11% of the analysed population) projected to face Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse between October 2026 and February 2027, including nearly 426,000 in Emergency (IPC Phase 4). Humanitarian organisations and government stakeholders have intensified preparedness efforts, with anticipatory action triggers already activated in several districts owing to the heightened climate risk. Conflict-related displacement in Cabo Delgado province and funding shortfalls for humanitarian operations further compound existing vulnerabilities. rationaleUpdates.text:
Since the December 2025 elections in Myanmar, conflict and protection risks have not decreased but instead remain acute. The elections were widely criticised as neither free nor fair. Association of Southeast Asian Nations declined to endorse or observe the polls, citing the exclusion of major opposition parties and the inability to conduct voting in conflict-affected areas. The United Nations and international rights groups also raised concerns over intimidation, arrests, and coercive practices ahead of the vote, while over 300 civil society organisations urged the international community to reject the process as a military entrenchment exercise. In contrast, countries such as China and India maintained engagement, reflecting geopolitical divisions over recognition.

Post-election dynamics have reinforced humanitarian risks. Continued aerial bombardments in Rakhine and Sagaing have caused civilian casualties and disrupted essential services. UNICEF has warned that children are increasingly affected, while the World Food Programme has cautioned that funding gaps and access constraints could worsen hunger and malnutrition in 2026. Ongoing conflict, displacement, and restricted humanitarian access indicate that the elections have not contributed to de-escalation, and civilian protection risks remain high nationwide.

The risk of escalating armed conflict ahead of Myanmar’s elections on 28 December has intensified since October. Political repression has deepened, with over 30,000 opponents detained since 2021 and new laws criminalising dissent. Military offensives and air strikes have surged in Magway, Mandalay, and Sagaing, killing civilians and destroying infrastructure, while opposition forces have vowed to block polling stations. Indicators of escalation include reinstated compulsory military service, expanded drone warfare, and coercive measures forcing civilians to return to insecure areas to vote. Humanitarian conditions have deteriorated sharply; displacement has risen beyond 3.6 million, food insecurity has worsened, and aid access has collapsed. Short- to medium-term impacts include heightened civilian casualties, mass displacement, and the severe disruption of relief operations, particularly in contested regions where violence and intimidation tactics are expected to intensify.
([HRW 16/11/2025](https://www.hrw.org/news/2025/11/16/myanmar-elections-a-fraudulent-claim-for-credibility), [GI 28/11/2025](https://www.globalissues.org/news/2025/11/28/41769), [OCHA 17/11/2025](https://www.unocha.org/publications/report/myanmar/ocha-myanmar-humanitarian-update-no50-17-november-2025), [FR 19/11/2025](https://www.fortifyrights.org/mya-inv-2025-11-19/), [MoeMaKa Media 30/10/2025](https://moemaka.net/eng/2025/10/myanmar-military-news-updates-oct-30-2025-morning/), [VOH 18/11/2025](https://www.visionofhumanity.org/election-plans-amid-myanmars-humanitarian-crisis-and-ongoing-conflict/))
