Some Druze may attempt to cross into northern Jordan given its geographical proximity to the conflict-affected areas in southern Syria. The displaced will likely seek to reach Al Azraq governorate in Jordan, as it hosts the majority of the Druze community in the country. Most of Syria’s Druze are likely to remain internally d

High protection needs are also reported as a result of localised clashes, moveme

triggers.title: Weak control over Sunni armed groups
triggers.description: The transitional Government’s weak control over Sunni armed groups has been a key trigger for renewed clashes with the Druze, as some militias operate independently and target minority communities. This lack of oversight undermines state authority and fuels sectarian violence, particularly around Al Sweida and Damascus.

triggers.title: Fractured security landscape
triggers.description: The fractured security landscape, marked by divisions within the transitional Government’s forces and perceived bias toward Sunni factions, has eroded trust among Druze communities. Failed mediation efforts and the involvement of affiliated militias in the violence have further exposed the state's inability to ensure protection.

triggers.title: Israel likely to deepen its involvement
triggers.description: Israel is likely to escalate its involvement by moving from airstrikes to deploying troops or proxies near Druze-majority areas, citing protection as a pretext. This risks triggering clashes with the transitional Government and fueling wider sectarian conflict.

triggers.title: Growing division among the Druze
triggers.description: The Druze community is increasingly divided, with some leaders cooperating with the transitional Government and others rejecting its legitimacy and calling for international protection (especially from Israel) or self-governance. These internal fractures risk sparking local clashes and creating openings for external interference or renewed attacks by Sunni armed groups.

rationaleUpdates.text: This risk has largely materialised. Until 24 November 2025, about 187,000 people remained displaced owing to clashes and insecurity in Al Sweida governorate. Since the clashes broke out between Druze and Bedouin communities in July, government forces have been struggling to restore safety and security, indicating their weak control over armed groups. The people affected continue to face disruptions in services, such as shortages in health supplies, intermittent constraints in access, and deteriorating electricity and telecommunications services. High protection needs are also reported as a result of localised clashes, movement restrictions, and sporadic security incidents, including explosive ordnance-related casualties. Needs for food continue to be high, driven by shortages of bread given the limited supplies entering the governorate, resulting in the closure of bakeries. Humanitarian aid trucks can enter the governorate, but tensions and sporadic violence along key routes, such as the Damascus–Al Sweida route, often restrict access. These also limit civilian movement and access to essential services. ([OCHA 13/11/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/syrian-arab-republic/syrian-arab-republic-humanitarian-response-southern-syria-situation-report-no-3-11-november-2025), [IMC 19/11/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/syrian-arab-republic/sweida-emergency-response-situation-report-u6-november-19-2025))

Clashes escalated between Druze and Bedouin militias between 11–20 July, triggered by the reported robbery and assault of a Druze merchant by Bedouin gunmen on the Damascus-Al Sweida highway on 11 July. Israeli forces conducted airstrikes on Syrian security forces that attempted to enter Al Sweida, with the pretext to neutralize threats against the Druze community and keep southern Syria a demilitarised area. A ceasefire was reached on 20 July after violent clashes that led to the killing of at least 1,300 people, including civilians and armed men from both sides and Syrian security forces.  These clashes exacerbated sectarian tensions between the Druze and the transitional Government and among the Druze community itself, as Al Hijri seeks collaboration with Israeli forces. 
As of 21 July, the clashes displaced at least 93,000 people, mostly within Al Sweida, others went to Dar’a and Rural Damascus governorates. IDPs are staying with relatives or public building such as schools and mosques, and they need shelter, ready to eat meals, clean water, and medical care. Power outages, unstable internet and mobile connection, and severe shortage in water supply and medical services are reported in Al Sweida. ([UNHCR 21/07/2025](https://reliefweb.int/attachments/fba9ec77-7b57-4aa0-849e-4a43472838a4/EXTERNAL%20%233%20Flash%20update%20on%20the%20situation%20in%20Sweida%2021%20July%202025.pdf), [SARI Global 23/07/2025](https://reliefweb.int/attachments/f98c4560-6fe4-4bea-b6a1-508fa7c53803/SWEIDA%E2%80%99S%20CEASEFIRE%2C%20A%20TENUOUS%20CALM%20AMID%20TENSIONS.pdf))

title: Further Israeli expansion in southern Syria triggers armed group resistance, displacement, and heightened food insecurity
rationale: Israel is likely to expand deeper into southern Syria to prevent a potential return of Iran-backed militias, such as Hezbollah, and respond to escalating sectarian violence, particularly near Druze communities, under the pretext of security and humanitarian intervention. This expansion, driven by the transitional Government’s inability to maintain control and provide protection, could result in further displacement and local clashes. Immediately after the fall of Al Assad’s rule in December 2024, Israel expanded its presence in southern Syria, seizing the demilitarised buffer zone (around 400km²) beyond the Golan Heights and occupying strategic areas in Quneitra, including Tel Al Hara and several border villages. The Israeli Defense Forces (IDF) launched intensive air strikes targeting Syrian and Iranian military infrastructure, significantly weakening local resistance, which included remnants of Syrian army units and Iran-backed militias still active in the area at the time. These moves prompted clashes and displacement, notably from villages such as Al Hameidiyyeh, Rasem Al Rawadi,
expectedImpact: If Israel expands further into southern Syria, thousands more people are expected to displace internally or internationally. Although the military parties differ – Israel in 2025 versus Al Assad’s forces in 2018 – the pattern of displacement following large-scale offensives in southern Syria remains consistent. During the 2018 Dar’a offensive, intensive ground operations and air strikes by Al Assad’s forces internally displaced around 270,000 peo
materialised: The expected humanitarian impacts partially materialised. Continued Israeli incursions displaced additional households, damaged homes, roads, water infrastructure, and agricultural land, and restricted civilian access to farmland and essential services in affected communities, increasing humanitaria

triggers.title: Potential return of Iran-backed militias
triggers.description: Israel fears the potential return of Iran-backed militias, particularly Hezbollah, to areas near the Golan Heights, prompting it to maintain and expand its military presence in southern Syria. Despite the withdrawal of many such forces after Al Assad’s fall, Israel has declared their re-emergence a red line that would trigger immediate military action.

triggers.title: Attacks on minority groups
triggers.description: Israel is likely to expand its presence in Syria under the pretext of protecting minority groups, particularly the Druze, amid escalating sectarian violence. This includes conducting airstrikes on Sunni armed groups and evacuating Druze civilians, though many Druze leaders reject Israeli involvement and prefer local autonomy.

triggers.title: The transitional Government’s continued struggle with lack of security
triggers.description: The transitional Government’s ongoing inability to maintain security in southern Syria has created a power vacuum that Israel is increasingly filling. As armed groups remain active and state control weakens, Israel has issued ultimatums and taken military action to prevent perceived threats near its border.

triggers.title: Israeli actions in Southern Syria cause a legitimacy crisis for Al-Sharaa
triggers.description: Currently Al-Sharaa's takeover of SDF territories allows him to project a strong image at home to deal with insecurity, aloowing for diplomatic efforts to supercede military responses to Israel. However, Israeli forces in Al-Quneitra are increasing their activity, with arrests of farmers, spraying of crops and shootings at civilians. If local protest grows to this, as well as increased action by the Druze, Al-Sharaa

rationaleUpdates.text: The risk has further deteriorated as Israeli military expansion in southern Syria continues to drive local tensions, with protests against Israel’s advances and continued presence in Syrian territory reported in southern governorates in June 2026. The demonstrations in As Sweida and surrounding areas reflected the growing opposition of communities to Israeli military activity and concerns over sovereignty, despite Israel’s stated objective of preventing threats from armed groups and protecting Druze communities. The protests indicate that Israeli expansion risks increasing local resentment and could contribute to further instability, particularly in Druze-majority areas, where Israel has sought to position itself as a security party. ([SANA 19/06/2026](https://sana.sy/en/photos/2324228/), [Arab News 30/06/2026](https://www.arabnews.com/node/2649041/middle-east), [AJ 29/06/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/6/29/new-israeli-assault-in-southern-syria-forces-families-to-flee-their-homes))

The risk has deteriorated. Israeli incursions in April 2026 reflected a pattern of near-daily raids, arrests, and movement restrictions in southern Syria. On 11 April, Israeli forces conducted incursions into the towns of Kudna in Quneitra governorate and Wadi Al Raqad and Hamata in Daraa, by the Yarmouk Basin, arresting at least three civilians during house raids. The operations followed artillery shelling on 10 April targeting Jamlah town, damaging agricultural land. Around 12 military vehicles were involved in at least one incursion. Later in the month, protests erupted in southern Syria and Damascus, organised by families of Syrians detained by Israeli forces, indicating a deterioration in the risk given the increase in Israeli raids. ([AJ 11/04/2026](https://www.aljazeera.net/news/2026/4/11/%D9%82%D9%88%D8%A7%D8%AA-%D8%A5%D8%B3%D8%B1%D8%A7%D8%A6%D9%8A%D9%84%D9%8A%D8%A9-%D8%AA%D8%AA%D9%88%D8%BA%D9%84-%D9%81%D9%8A-%D8%AF%D8%B1%D8%B9%D8%A7), [EB 27/04/2026](https://english.enabbaladi.net/archives/2026/04/damascus-protesters-urge-action-on-syrians-held-by-israel/))

The risk continues to be valid but stable. On 28 March 2026, Israeli forces arrested a Syrian man and a child in southern Quneitra and conducted a ground incursion into Jbata Al Khashab town in the north, including house raids and searches. These incidents are part of a pattern of near-daily incursions in southern Syria involving the arrest of civilians, including herders and children. The continuation of these operations indicates a normalisation of Israeli ground activity inside Syrian territory, contributing to persistent insecurity in border communities. Recurrent raids, checkpoints, and arrests are likely to increase protection risks, restrict civilian movement and livelihoods, and further constrain the Syrian Government’s capacity to restore security, attract investment, and improve economic conditions in the south. ([AJ 01/03/2026](https://www.aljazeera.net/news/2026/3/1/%D8%A5%D8%B3%D8%B1%D8%A7%D8%A6%D9%8A%D9%84-%D8%AA%D8%AD%D8%B4%D8%AF-100-%D8%A3%D9%84%D9%81-%D9%85%D9%86-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A7%D8%AD%D8%AA%D9%8A%D8%A7%D8%B7-%D9%88%D8%AA%D8%B9%D9%84%D9%86))

Tensions in southern Syria have intensified since December 2025, driven by the Government's strategic shift towards consolidating control following its northeast offensive and Israel's continued military incursions.
A US-brokered agreement in January 2026 established joint Israeli–Syrian intelligence-sharing mechanisms on movements of the Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant, but negotiations stalled over future control of Mount Hermon, held by Israel since 2024. Israeli forces continued arrests and roadblocks in Quneitra governorate and launched strikes on Hezbollah targets on the Lebanese border post-agreement, demonstrating parallel diplomatic and military strategies. As Sweida Governor Mustafa Al Bakkour launched a ‘comprehensive settlement initiative’ to bring the governorate under state control, but Sheikh Hikmat Al Hijri, a prominent Druze spiritual leader, rejected this outright, demanding an independent Druze region with Israel as security guarantor. The Government has responded by providing services to undermine separatist narratives while strengthening its security posture. The collapse of the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) represents a setback to Israel's reported strategy of fragmenting Syria into smaller constituent regions, potentially increasing Israeli reliance on Druze militias.
Key escalation risks are apparent. The Government's offensive against the SDF in the northeast may embolden further pursuit of a unitary Syrian state. Syrian forces recognise that Israeli intervention on behalf of Druze communities is highly probable, unlike US restraint during the SDF offensive. While the likeliest scenario is the current status quo, any southern escalation raises the potential for a protracted, multiparty conflict with substantially higher civilian displacement, humanitarian needs, and potential for prolonged instability compared to the rapid northeast campaign. Despite its relatively swift conclusion, the northeast offensive displaced 190,000 people at peak displacement; a protracted southern campaign could have deeper ramifications for large populations, including in the governorates of Dar'a (1.3 million), As Sweida (480,000 people), Quneitra (111,000), sections of Hama, and southern Rural Damascus.
([CA-SYR 02/2026](https://ca-syr.org/periodical/january-2026-monthly-report), [The National 07/02/2026](https://www.thenationalnews.com/news/mena/2026/02/08/syrias-fragile-unity-faces-a-new-test-in-sweidas-druze-heartland/), [EUAA 02/12/2026](https://www.euaa.europa.eu/publications/country-guidance-syria-3), [The Syrian Observer 15/01/2026](https://syrianobserver.com/foreign-actors/israel-syria-security-agreement-stalls-over-mount-hermon-and-russian-presence.html), [IOM 31/01/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/syrian-arab-republic/syrian-arab-republic-emergency-mobility-tracking-situation-report-alepponorth-east-syria-nes-conflict-round-8-29-january-2026))

In November, Israeli forces continued their incursions in southern Syria, specifically in the northern Quneitra governorate countryside. The Israeli army has advanced in civilian farmlands, destroyed hundreds of acres of forests, and uprooted olive trees, further disrupting people’s livelihoods. They have also arrested residents and established military checkpoints. In October, Israeli forces established a barrier preventing farmers from reaching their land and restricting civilian movement. For example, checkpoints and barriers set up by the Israeli army have cut off all communication between Hamidiyeh, one of the largest farming towns in the region, and Khan Arnaba, the economic and administrative centre of Quneitra. This has forcibly displaced dozens of families in Hamidiyeh from their homes, while those who remain depend highly on humanitarian aid. That said, aid is not always available because of humanitarian access restrictions, mainly road closures. ([OCHA 13/11/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/syrian-arab-republic/syrian-arab-republic-humanitarian-response-southern-syria-situation-report-no-3-11-november-2025), [HRW 17/09/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/syrian-arab-republic/syria-israel-forcibly-displaces-villagers-occupied-south-enarhe), [Daily Sabah 22/11/2025](https://www.dailysabah.com/world/mid-east/israel-expands-military-raids-into-syrias-southern-countryside), [Le Monde 10/11/2025](https://www.lemonde.fr/en/international/article/2025/11/10/on-the-syrian-golan-heights-israel-uses-the-same-tools-of-repression-as-in-the-west-bank_6747318_4.html))

Clashes escalated between Druze and Bedouin militias between 11–20 July, triggered by the reported robbery and assault of a Druze merchant by Bedouin gunmen on the Damascus-Al Sweida highway on 11 July. Israeli forces conducted airstrikes on Syrian security forces that attempted to enter Al Sweida, with the pretext to neutralize threats against the Druze community and keep southern Syria a demilitarised area. Under the stated objective of protecting the Druze community, Israel carried out targeted airstrikes against Syrian military positions in Sweida and Damascus, including strategic sites like the Defence Ministry and areas near the presidential palace. These interventions, combined with Israel's reported coordination with the US to permit the deployment of Syrian Internal Security Forces, demonstrate its growing influence over the security dynamics in southern Syria. 
A ceasefire was reached on 20 July after violent clashes that led to the killing of at least 1,300 people, including civilians and armed men from both sides and Syrian security forces.  These clashes exacerbated sectarian tensions between the Druze and the transitional Government and among the Druze community itself, as Al Hijri seeks collaboration with Israeli forces. ([SARI Global 23/07/2025](https://reliefweb.int/attachments/f98c4560-6fe4-4bea-b6a1-508fa7c53803/SWEIDA%E2%80%99S%20CEASEFIRE%2C%20A%20TENUOUS%20CALM%20AMID%20TENSIONS.pdf))

title: A prolonged Syria–Lebanon border conflict results in displacement and increases shelter and livelihood needs
rationale: The Syria–Lebanon border remains a key smuggling corridor for fuel, drugs (especially Captagon), and weapons, primarily from Syria to Lebanon, often facilitated by networks linked to Hezbollah and Iran-backed militias. After Al Assad’s fall, Syria’s transitional Government’s forces launched an anti-smuggling campaign in early 2025, targeting routes used by Hezbollah-linked clans near Al Qasr village on the Lebanese side of the border. Armed networks, such as the Jaafar clan (of Lebanon), resisted violently, ambushing Syrian patrols and firing anti-tank rockets. These confrontations escalated into clashes in March near Al Qasr. Without clear coordination between Lebanese and Syrian authorities, both aiming to stop smuggling, efforts to dismantle these networks will likely trigger more cross-border skirmishes, especially in areas where smuggling remains a main source of income and power for local armed groups. On 16 March 2025, clashes broke out along the Syria–Lebanon border after transitional Government soldiers crossed into Lebanon and were shot by local Lebanese clans. Syria’s tran
expectedImpact: If clashes on the Syria–Lebanon border intensify, displacement from both sides is likely. The Syrian and Lebanese villages that will be affected are the ones situated along active smuggling corridors, such as Rural Damascus in Syria and Al Qaa plain in Lebanon, where smuggling persisted under Al Assad’s rule and caused limited displacement. Given the transitional Government’s recent crackdown on these networks, renewed displacement is likely as s

triggers.title: Increased crackdown on smuggling routes
triggers.description: The Syria–Lebanon border remains a major smuggling corridor for fuel, weapons, and drugs—particularly Captagon—facilitated by networks linked to Hezbollah and Iran-backed militias. Efforts by Syria’s transitional Government to crack down on these routes have triggered violent resistance from local armed clans, risking further cross-border clashes in areas where smuggling underpins local power and livelihoods.

triggers.title: Hezbollah presence near the Lebanon - Syria border
triggers.description: Hezbollah’s presence along Lebanon’s northeastern border, supported by allied Shia clans and control over key smuggling routes, is viewed by Syria’s transitional Government as a security threat. Although direct clashes have been avoided, rising tensions and recent incidents—including the shelling of Shia villages and weapons seizures—have strained relations between Hezbollah, Syria, and the Lebanese Government.

rationaleUpdates.text: The risk improved slightly in April 2026 after tensions rose in March with an escalation between Hezbollah and Israel. Because of insecurity at the border, the Syrian transitional Government increased its military presence at Al Masnaa crossing and deployed more forces, establishing at least three new checkpoints and intensifying searches of travellers and vehicles. Tensions in March increased because of artillery shells being fired from Lebanon and landing in western Damascus. On 4 April, the Israeli military announced its intention to strike Al Masnaa crossing, citing Hezbollah's use of it for military purposes and the smuggling of combat equipment and urging residents to evacuate. Lebanese security sources confirmed evacuating the crossing following the Israeli threat. ([TNA 09/03/2026](https://www.newarab.com/analysis/why-tensions-are-rising-syria-lebanon-border), [Al-Monitor 04/04/2026](https://www.al-monitor.com/originals/2026/04/israel-says-will-strike-lebanon-syria-border-crossing))

Border tensions between Syria and Lebanon have stabilized since late 2025, despite one minor clash near Hermel in December, with both governments pursuing cooperative measures amid underlying security concerns. On 5 February, Lebanon and Syria reached a deal to repatriate approximately 300 Syrian inmates from Lebanese prisons, a priority for Damascus since Al Assad's fall and a signal of improving bilateral relations. However, Damascus filed a separate extradition request for over 200 former regime officers allegedly in Lebanon accused of using Lebanese territory to finance Alawite insurgency operations, led by Brigadier General Suheil Al Hassan and billionaire Rami Makhlouf in Moscow. Syrian authorities continue intercepting weapons and drug smuggling attempts, seizing assault rifles, RPG launchers, Iranian Shahed drones, and ammunition in January heading to Hezbollah via border crossings near Tartous and Sarghaya, alongside ongoing Captagon interdiction efforts. Israeli airstrikes on four Syria–Lebanon border crossings used by Hezbollah for arms smuggling in January complicated dynamics. Turkey has facilitated limited communication between Damascus and Hezbollah to defuse tensions, though Hezbollah justifies retaining weapons citing potential Syrian threats.
([CA-SYR 02/2026](https://ca-syr.org/periodical/january-2026-monthly-report), [Al Jazeera 11/02/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/2/11/why-is-the-issue-of-syrian-prisoner-repatriation-from-lebanon-complicated), [Le Monde 01/02/2026](https://www.lemonde.fr/en/international/article/2026/02/01/between-lebanon-and-syria-the-search-for-a-fresh-start-since-assad-s-fall-and-hezbollah-s-collapse_6750025_4.html), [L'Orient Today 14/12/2025](https://today.lorientlejour.com/article/1488404/clashes-between-lebanese-army-and-syrian-general-security-agents-near-hermel.html), [Times of Israel 17/01/2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/liveblog_entry/syria-says-it-foiled-attempt-to-smuggle-rifles-drones-into-lebanon-via-illegal-border-crossing/), [Times of Israel 26/01/2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/syrias-new-regime-says-it-stopped-weapons-shipment-heading-to-hezbollah-in-lebanon/))

Tensions on the Syria–Lebanon borders continue to be reported, contributing to the increased likelihood of clashes. On 15 November, residents of Jrajir town in Qalamoun region (of Syria) protested at the informal Zamrani border crossing after the Lebanese army began establishing military points on their privately owned agricultural lands, which contain over 100,000 fruit trees (mainly cherries and apples). These lands have been inaccessible to farmers since 2017, when Syrian government forces and Hezbollah took control of the Qalamoun Mountains. On 13 November, foreign fighters from the Syrian army were redeployed from the Harem area in Idleb governorate to Al Qusayr, near the Syria–Lebanon border, alongside the movement of heavy military equipment and armoured units. At the same time, forces linked to the Ministry of Defense of the Syrian Transitional Government attempted to advance into Lebanese territory in Wadi Al Thalajat in Ras Al Ma‘ara, an area without Lebanese army presence. These deployments took place at the same time as clashes between Syrian army units and cells of the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria positioned opposite the Lebanese town of Arsal. ([The Cradle 13/11/2025](https://thecradle.co/articles/exclusive-syria-deploys-foreign-fighters-to-lebanon-border#google_vignette), [SOHR 15/11/2025](https://www.syriahr.com/%D8%A7%D8%AD%D8%AA%D8%AC%D8%A7%D8%AC-%D8%B4%D8%B9%D8%A8%D9%8A-%D9%81%D9%8A-%D8%AC%D8%B1%D9%8A%D8%AC%D9%8A%D8%B1-%D8%A8%D8%B1%D9%8A%D9%81-%D8%AF%D9%85%D8%B4%D9%82-%D8%B6%D8%AF-%D8%A5%D9%86%D8%B4%D8%A7/784475/))

In September, media reports indicated that Hezbollah was working to retrieve weapons stored in Syria, including former Syrian army stockpiles and arms held by Iranian-backed militias, to rebuild capabilities weakened by Israeli strikes. Between July–September, the Syrian Government foiled around 13 smuggling attempts from Syria into Lebanon, most involving weapon shipments. Although Syrian authorities say they control over 75% of the Syria–Lebanon border, security gaps remain, mainly along the rugged border areas near Homs governorate, the Syrian Coast, and Qalamoun region, allowing smuggling operations to continue. ([Majjala 04/09/2025](https://www.majalla.com/node/327209/%D8%B3%D9%8A%D8%A7%D8%B3%D8%A9/%D8%AD%D8%B2%D8%A8-%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%84%D9%87-%D9%8A%D8%B5%D8%B1-%D8%B9%D9%84%D9%89-%D8%AA%D9%87%D8%B1%D9%8A%D8%A8-%D8%A3%D8%B3%D9%84%D8%AD%D8%AA%D9%87-%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%85%D8%AE%D8%B2%D9%86%D8%A9-%D9%81%D9%8A-%D8%B3%D9%88%D8%B1%D9%8A%D8%A7))

The transitional Government continues with efforts to combat the smuggling of drugs and weapons. In July 2025, the Syrian Ministry of Interior confirmed being engaged in a non-publicised security cooperation with Saudi Arabia focused on combating the trafficking of drugs – especially Captagon – and remnants of the Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant. The collaboration includes intelligence sharing, joint operations, and planned Saudi-led training for Syrian personnel. Both sides have held multiple meetings to deepen cooperation across areas including border control, tackling organised crime, and institutional development, with Saudi officials expressing commitment to supporting Syria’s security and stability. ([Asharq Al-Awsat accessed 23/07/2025](https://aawsat.com/%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B9%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%85-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B9%D8%B1%D8%A8%D9%8A/%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%AE%D9%84%D9%8A%D8%AC/5185620-%D8%AA%D8%B1%D8%AD%D9%8A%D8%A8-%D8%B9%D8%B1%D8%A8%D9%8A-%D9%88%D8%A5%D8%B3%D9%84%D8%A7%D9%85%D9%8A-%D8%A8%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A7%D8%B9%D8%AA%D9%85%D8%A7%D8%AF-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A3%D9%85%D9%85%D9%8A-%D9%84%D9%80%D8%A5%D8%B9%D9%84%D8%A7%D9%86-%D9%86%D9%8A%D9%88%D9%8A%D9%88%D8%B1%D9%83))

title: Severe shortage of services triggers unrest and breakout attempts in Al Hol and Al Roj camps
rationale: If security in Al Hol and Al Roj camps collapses due to mass rioting or breakouts, ISIS-affiliated IDPs are likely to escape, regroup, and rejoin IS cells, potentially sparking renewed insurgencies in both Syria and Iraq. Unlike typical displacement sites, Al Hol and Al Roj function as detention facilities housing individuals with suspected IS ties, including non-Syrians and their families, making the risk of escape a security concern rather than a humanitarian one. As of April 2024, Al Hol hosts 42,000 people, and as of December 2024 Al Roj hosts over 2,600 people. As of early April, around 1,500 international troops remain in Syria, some of whom are tasked with preventing an IS resurgence; large-scale escapes could prompt renewed military operations in Syria. Iraqi officials have repeatedly warned that instability in Al Hol poses a direct threat to their internal security, as escaped IS members may attempt to cross into Iraq. Compounding this risk, a recent US funding freeze has weakened camp management, including WASH services, and could create further security vacuums that IS may
expectedImpact: A mass unrest at Al Hol and Al Roj camps is likely to result in casualties and displacement. Past disturbances in Al Hol have resulted in injuries and casualties, so riots or escape attempts are likely to lead to significant injuries or fatalities among residents and guards. This means that healthcare services, including emergency medical teams, trauma care, and ambulances, will likely be needed to treat the injured. However, existing shortages a

triggers.title: US funding freeze
triggers.description: The US funding freeze, ordered in January 2025, halted nearly all humanitarian aid to northeastern Syria, including critical support for Al Hol and Al Roj camps. This led to the suspension of essential services like water, sanitation, food distribution, and security, creating severe gaps in camp management and raising the risk of unrest, disease outbreaks, and mass escape attempts.

triggers.title: Severe lack of services
triggers.description: Overcrowding and poor sanitation in Al Hol and Al Roj camps have led to disease outbreaks, including cholera in late 2024. The deterioration of WASH infrastructure, worsened by the US funding freeze, is likely to trigger mass rioting and escape attempts, particularly as weekly escapes, mostly by women and children, continue.

rationaleUpdates.text: The risk of mass breakouts from Al Hol and Al Roj camps nearly materialized during the January 2026 control transfer from Kurdish-led forces to the transitional Government but has since substantially decreased. Riots erupted in Al Hol's Syrian and Iraqi sections, with residents burning a bakery and tents as NGOs and security personnel withdrew, creating temporary security vacuums. However, the International Coalition and CENTCOM have transferred over 4,500 detainees to Iraq, and Al Hol's foreign annex, which previously held 6,200 foreign nationals, is now almost empty. The transitional Government announced plans to permanently close both camps within a year. Foreign governments continue refusing to repatriate their nationals detained for IS links, leaving Iraq to absorb foreign fighters. Separately, 120 ISIS detainees escaped from Al Shaddadi prison in Hasakah governorate on 19 January, with 81 recaptured and 39 remaining at large who could rejoin active ISIS cells. ([Al Jazeera 19/01/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/1/19/isil-fighters-flee-jail-as-syrian-army-clashes-with-kurdish-led-sdf), [The Guardian 22/01/2026](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/jan/22/open-the-gates-riots-fires-and-escape-attempts-as-syrian-army-takes-over-is-camp), [Al-Monitor 11/02/2026](https://www.al-monitor.com/originals/2026/02/syrian-kurdish-officials-say-66-turkish-isis-fighters-transferred-relocation-iraq), [MEE 12/02/2026](https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/syrias-al-hol-camp-emptied-foreigners-sources-say), [Manassa 10/02/2026](https://manassa.news/en/news/30223))

As of November, the risk of unrest and breakout attempts in Al Hol and Al Roj camps continues to be reported. As US funding cuts of at least 117 million dollars have severely weakened security and services in al-Hol and Roj camps, more than 20 humanitarian projects including medical, mental health, and child-protection activities were affected. Children are now more vulnerable to radicalisation, while escape attempts have increased. There are reportedly audio messages from ISIS members circulating urging supporters to launch “individual jihad” operations to help the detainees in the camps, likely creating a major security crisis that could trigger a mass breakout. Since the May deal enabling departures from al-Hol to government-controlled areas, only around 360 Syrians have returned due to political delays, restrictive procedures, and limited aid capacity. ([Shia Waves 27/11/2025](https://shiawaves.com/english/news/islam/syria/137319-warning-over-security-crisis-in-northeast-syrias-isis-detention-camps/), [TNH 12/11/2025](https://www.thenewhumanitarian.org/news-feature/2025/11/12/despite-promises-returns-notorious-syrian-camp-remain-rare)).

title: Water scarcity, especially in northeast and northwest Syria result in livelihoods and services’ disruptions, reduced food production and protests
type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale: As of February 2025, about 13.6 million Syrians lack access to safe water and sanitation. Conflict since 2011 has damaged water infrastructure, resulting in a 40% reduction in the drinking water supply as of 2021. Almost half of the water systems no longer function reliably, forcing many to rely on tankers or unsafe wells. Ongoing electricity and fuel shortages have crippled water pumps and treatment plants, exacerbating water rationing and existing sanitation problems and driving disease outbreaks. Syria and the region experienced an exceptionally dry winter and spring in 2024/2025, with significantly below-average rainfall and higher temperatures. In April 2025, water levels in Lake Euphrates Dam dropped to about six meters, which is five meters below the normal level. Upstream water retention and weaponisation of water are also drivers of water scarcity in Syria. Türkiye has sharply reduced the Euphrates’ waters flow into Syria by restricting releases from upstream dams, such as the Atatürk Dam, often to around 200 cubic meters per second, well below the 500 cubic meters per secon
expectedImpact: Syria’s dry conditions and water scarcity are likely to worsen food and water insecurity. Agriculture and livelihoods are already strained as crops fail, contributing to increasing food insecurity. An estimates 14.5 million Syrians face food insecurity, with agriculture-dependent communities severely impacted by conflict and resource depletion. The expected failure of the 2024/2025 wheat production, a stable in Syria, will likely further reduce t

triggers.title: Dry winter and spring in 2024/2025
triggers.description: Syria experienced an unusually dry winter and spring in 2024/2025, with significantly below-average rainfall and higher temperatures. This contributed to declining water levels, including a major drop at the Euphrates Dam, worsening the country’s ongoing drought and water scarcity.

triggers.title: The weaponisation or politicisation of water
triggers.description: Water scarcity in Syria is worsened by its politicisation and weaponisation. Türkiye has restricted Euphrates River flow below treaty levels and targeted infrastructure like the Alouk station, while Israel’s control over the Yarmouk basin and Unity Dam has cut off southern water sources, leaving over a million people affected.

triggers.title: Upcoming lean season
triggers.description: The lean season in Syria, typically from June to September, is expected to be one of the driest since 1989 due to poor rainfall and low reservoir levels. Water scarcity is likely to intensify during this period, further straining resources and increasing humanitarian needs.

rationaleUpdates.text: The risk has slightly improved because above-average rainfall in February and March 2026 provided some short-term relief to water availability in parts of Syria. However, structural drivers of water scarcity remain in place, including damaged water infrastructure, limited pumping and treatment capacity, and the long-term effects of climate change. At the same time, several flooding events affected Al Hasakah, Ar Raqqa, and Deir ez Zor governorates, impacting an estimated 6,000 people in March. Additional heavy rainfall affected approximately 19,000 people in Aleppo and Idlib governorates. While the rainfall may temporarily improve water availability and soil moisture in some areas, flooding has also damaged crops, agricultural land, and infrastructure, potentially reducing food production and access to food for affected communities.

Water scarcity has intensified since December 2025, with catastrophic agricultural impacts. Wheat production has falled by over 50% compared to pre-war norms, while barley production has dropped by 65% below the five-year average as a result of drought, extreme heat, insecurity, and high input costs. Agricultural drought models indicate over 700,000 hectares in central and northern Syria will face drought between January–March 2026, with Aleppo, Al Hasakeh, Ar Raqqa, Hama, and Idleb governorates worst affected. In early February, flash floods in Idleb and Lattakia killed at least two children and inundated displacement camps. While rainfall is desperately needed, intense storms risk washing away fertile topsoil rather than replenishing reservoirs. During January clashes, residents in Aleppo and Al Hasakeh experienced days without water after authorities took control of Tishreen Dam. The transitional Government's northeast takeover has transferred water management from Kurdish-led authorities to Damascus. Damascus has reaffirmed commitments to share 58% of Euphrates flows with Iraq and announced multilevel water governance reforms, though implementation details remain pending.
([FEWS NET 31/12/2025](https://fews.net/middle-east-and-asia/syria/special-report/december-2025), [IOM 19/12/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/syrian-arab-republic/syrian-arab-republic-population-mobility-and-baseline-assessment-round-10-november-2025), [TNA 08/02/2026](https://www.newarab.com/news/two-killed-others-missing-flash-floods-hit-northwest-syria))

Some of the triggers suggested are materialising as rainfall dropped nationwide, with Damascus receiving only 29% of its annual average compared with 86% in 2024, and Al Sweida and Daraa falling to less than half of 2024 levels. Flooding from intense, uneven rain failed to replenish reservoirs. War damage has left irrigation systems over 500,000 hectares largely nonfunctional. Reduced surface-water flows and groundwater recharge have triggered a nationwide water crisis affecting more than 80% of the population. Over 75% of cultivated crops and grazing areas are impacted, with livestock numbers down by 40% and feed prices are up by 100–300%. Vegetable prices have risen by 20–40% amid reduced production and disrupted road access between areas controlled by different authorities. Across northeast Syria, prolonged drought and delayed rainfall have severely depleted rivers, wells, and soil moisture, threatening rain-fed agriculture in key areas such as Qamishli, Amuda, and Hasakeh. Although no protests or social unrest have been reported because of water scarcity, but some analysts consider climate-driven livelihood collapse as a contributing factor to the July clashes between Druze and Bedouin communities in Al Sweida, in addition to factors such as disputes over land and smuggling routes and state manipulation. Farmers in western rural Al Sweida have lost over 70% of their olive harvest this season because drought, insecurity, and displacement have prevented them from reaching their land, while armed groups have looted crops, dismantled the main Thaala olive press, and cut trees for firewood.([BBC 17/09/2025](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c70x500lkdno), [IFRC 30/08/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/syrian-arab-republic/syrian-arab-republic-drought-2025-dref-operation-mdrsy017), [Shafaq 23/08/2025](https://shafaq.com/en/Middle-East/Drought-and-war-leave-Syria-struggling-with-water-shortages), [Ultra Syria 17/11/2025](https://ultrasyria.ultrasawt.com/%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%AC%D9%81%D8%A7%D9%81-%D9%8A%D9%88%D8%A7%D8%B5%D9%84-%D8%AA%D9%87%D8%AF%D9%8A%D8%AF-%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%82%D9%85%D8%AD-%D9%81%D9%8A-%D8%B4%D9%85%D8%A7%D9%84-%D9%88%D8%B4%D8%B1%D9%82-%D8%B3%D9%88%D8%B1%D9%8A%D8%A7-%D9%88%D9%85%D8%B7%D8%B1-%D9%85%D8%AA%D8%A3%D8%AE%D8%B1-%D9%8A%D8%AB%D9%8A%D8%B1-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A3%D9%85%D9%84-%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%87%D8%B4/%D9%87%D9%8A%D9%84%D9%8A%D9%86-%D8%B9%D9%84%D9%8A/%D9%85%D8%AC%D8%AA%D9%85%D8%B9-%D9%88%D8%A7%D9%82%D8%AA%D8%B5%D8%A7%D8%AF), [Ultra Syria 18/11/2025](https://ultrasyria.ultrasawt.com/%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B2%D9%8A%D8%AA%D9%88%D9%86-%D9%81%D9%8A-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B3%D9%88%D9%8A%D8%AF%D8%A7%D8%A1-%D8%A8%D9%8A%D9%86-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%AC%D9%81%D8%A7%D9%81-%D9%88%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%86%D8%B2%D9%88%D8%AD-%D9%85%D9%88%D8%B3%D9%85-%D8%B6%D8%A7%D8%A6%D8%B9-%D9%88%D9%85%D8%AD%D8%A7%D8%B5%D9%8A%D9%84-%D9%85%D9%86%D9%87%D9%88%D8%A8%D8%A9/%D8%B9%D9%85%D8%B1%D9%88-%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%85%D8%AD%D9%8A%D8%AB%D8%A7%D9%88%D9%8A/%D9%85%D8%AC%D8%AA%D9%85%D8%B9-%D9%88%D8%A7%D9%82%D8%AA%D8%B5%D8%A7%D8%AF), [AJ 02/09/2025](https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2025/9/2/the-druze-bedouin-clashes-in-syria-were-not-a-sectarian-conflict)).

title: Renewed violence in As Sweida or settler outpost establishment drives Israeli expansion in southern Syria, displacing civilians and restricting access
type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale: Since the fall of Bashar Al Assad in December 2024, Israel’s military presence in southern Syria has evolved from incursions into sustained territorial control. By early 2026, Israeli forces have expanded beyond the UN-monitored 1974 separation line into parts of Quneitra and western Dar’a, establishing military posts, outposts, and checkpoints. By mid-2026, the presence had become increasingly entrenched, with regular patrols and ground activity beyond the former separation area. Further expansion of positions, checkpoints, or closed military zones would indicate movement towards a more permanent security zone. Sustained territorial control or restrictions on civilian access could increase local resistance and create conditions for further expansion towards areas linked to As Sweida. Two pathways could accelerate or formalise this existing trajectory in the next three to six months. One is the revival of a proposal for a humanitarian corridor, first suggested in 2025 by Israeli officials to provide aid for Druze in As Sweida, particularly if renewed violence in As Sweida gives Israe
expectedImpact: If the risk materialises, As Sweida, Dar’a, and Quneitra governorates are expected to face increased displacement, agricultural and livestock livelihood losses, deteriorating food access, and further disruption to water and essential services. Further Israeli restrictions on farmland and grazing areas would reduce household income and food production. Between 70–80% of communities in southern Syria are dependent on farming for food, but Quneitra

triggers.title: Expansion of Israeli military control
triggers.description: A further expansion of Israeli positions, checkpoints or closed military zones beyond the current areas of control in Quneitra and western Dar'a could indicate movement towards a more permanent security zone. If Israeli forces begin holding additional territory or restricting civilian access on a sustained basis, this could increase local resistance and create conditions for a broader Israeli-controlled zone extendin

triggers.title: Renewed large-scale violence in As-Sweida
triggers.description: An escalation of violence between Druze groups, Syrian Government forces or other armed actors in As-Sweida could prompt Israel to reframe military intervention as necessary to protect the Druze population. This could revive calls for a Golan–As-Sweida humanitarian corridor and provide a justification for expanding or formalising Israeli military access in southern Syria.

triggers.title: Establishment of a settler outpost
triggers.description: Pioneers of Bashan or other Israeli settler groups successfully establishing a sustained civilian outpost inside southern Syria, rather than being detained and removed, could create pressure for Israeli forces to protect the settlement. This could accelerate the conversion of the existing military presence into a more permanent security or territorial arrangement.

rationaleUpdates.text: The risk increased in September as Israeli ground activity in Quneitra and western Dar'a governorates intensified, while tensions in As Sweida persisted. During 1–7 September, 19 Israeli incursions were recorded in Quneitra (13) and Dar'a (6), including house searches, temporary checkpoints, and detentions. On 13 September, Israeli reservists called for deeper advances into southern Syria, while Israeli forces were already operating from 10 positions inside Syrian territory. On 22 September, Israeli forces shelled Jamlah and Abdeen villages in the Yarmouk Basin, followed by five incursions across Quneitra and western Dar'a within 24 hours on 29 September. In As Sweida, Sheikh Hikmat Al Hijri's factions continued calling for separation from Syria and blocked more than 13,000 students from reaching examination centres. Israel also called for the demilitarisation of Quneitra, Dar'a, and As Sweida, indicating continued efforts to shape the security environment in southern Syria. ([SOHR 07/09/2026](https://www.syriahr.com/%d9%81%d9%8a-%d8%a7%d9%84%d8%a3%d8%b3%d8%a8%d9%88%d8%b9-%d8%a7%d9%84%d8%a3%d9%88%d9%84-%d9%85%d9%86-%d8%a3%d9%8a%d9%84%d9%88%d9%84-%d8%aa%d8%b5%d8%b9%d9%8a%d8%af-%d8%a5%d8%b3%d8%b1%d8%a7%d8%a6%d9%8a/), [TNA 13/09/2026](https://www.newarab.com/news/israeli-troops-syria-call-conquest-damascus), [SOHR 22/09/2026 a](https://www.syriahr.com/%d8%aa%d8%b5%d8%b9%d9%8a%d8%af-%d9%85%d8%aa%d9%88%d8%a7%d8%b5%d9%84-%d9%81%d9%8a-%d8%ad%d9%88%d8%b6-%d8%a7%d9%84%d9%8a%d8%b1%d9%85%d9%88%d9%83-%d9%82%d8%b5%d9%81-%d9%85%d8%af%d9%81%d8%b9%d9%8a/), [SOHR 29/09/2026 b](https://www.syriahr.com/%d8%aa%d8%b5%d8%b9%d9%8a%d8%af-%d8%a5%d8%b3%d8%b1%d8%a7%d8%a6%d9%8a%d9%84%d9%8a-%d9%85%d8%aa%d8%b3%d8%a7%d8%b1%d8%b9-%d9%81%d9%8a-%d8%b1%d9%8a%d9%81%d9%8a-%d8%a7%d9%84%d9%82%d9%86%d9%8a%d8%b7%d8%b1/), [AJ 06/09/2026](https://www.aljazeera.net/opinions/2026/9/6/%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%87%D8%AC%D8%B1%D9%8A-%D9%8A%D9%86%D8%A7%D8%AC%D9%8A-%D8%A5%D8%B3%D8%B1%D8%A7%D8%A6%D9%8A%D9%84-%D9%88%D9%85%D8%B8%D9%84%D9%88%D9%85-%D9%8A%D9%86%D8%AF%D9%85%D8%AC), [AJ 02/09/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/9/2/syrias-restrained-approach-to-israel-carries-risks))

title: Spreading of the violent insurgency of Cabo Delgado into the Tanzanian territory.
rationale: There has been no violent attacks taking place in Tanzania since the entry of this risk in November. On 14 October, some 300 insurgents from Mozambique attacked Kitaya, a riverside border village in the Mtwara region. The Tanzanian authorities acknowledged for the first time an attack in Tanzania carried out by insurgents coming from the neighbouring country. In November 2020, Tanzania and Mozambique have signed a memorandum of understanding aimed to join forces against ISIL-linked fighters in Cabo Delgado. Recently raids have been carried out in Tanzanian villages near the border and many fighters are believed to come from Tanzania. The population of Mtwara region (which borders with Cabo Delgado) is over 1,270,000 people. Update (Sep 2021): Rwandan and Tanzanian police forces held a bilateral meeting to discuss their approach to counter the possible threat of insurgents from Cabo Delgado. Terrorists fleeing from their hideouts in Mozambique may infiltrate the borders and establish cells in Rwanda, Tanzania or other neighboring countries.

title: Flooding and landslides in Tanzania kill people, destroy infrastructure, damage crops, and increase waterborne diseases, aggravating socioeconomic and environmental vulnerabilities
rationale: Since 2010, the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events in Tanzania have increased, including heavy rainfall, flooding, and landslides. These events pose a significant threat to people’s lives, basic infrastructure, food security, and public health. According to Intergovernmental Authority on Development Climate Prediction and Applications Centre forecasts for February–April 2025, several regions will experience above-average rainfall, which could heighten existing vulnerabilities, such as weak infrastructure, poor waste management, and unsustainable land use. Past floods in Kilimanjaro, Kilombero, Manyara, Mbeya, Morogoro, and Rufiji regions have had significant humanitarian and socioeconomic impacts, including loss of life, property destruction, displacement, and economic decline. Crop damage poses a serious threat to livelihoods, and stagnant floodwaters increase the spread of waterborne diseases such as cholera and malaria. The lack of effective disaster preparedness and response mechanisms further aggravate the crisis, leaving affected populations with limited coping c
expectedImpact: Flooding in Tanzania is expected to cause loss of life, property destruction, and community displacement, leading to severe livelihood disruptions. Damage to critical infrastructure and agricultural losses would lead to an economic downturn, slowing growth and stability. Stagnant floodwaters could also create breeding grounds for vector-borne diseases and increase the spread of waterborne illnesses, such as cholera and malaria. This poses signifi
materialised: The direct consequences of the materialised hazard were significant and widespread across the affected regions. rationaleUpdates.text:
Four months following the capture of Nicolás Maduro and the transfer of government to Delcy Rodríguez, the overall risk environment in Venezuela remains stable with tentative signs of short-term improvement. No immediate risk of internal power struggles within Rodríguez's political circle has been identified, and no significant Chavista figures appear to be actively opposing the agreements reached between Rodríguez and US President Donald Trump, allowing the Venezuelan government to continue functioning with relative normalcy.
Economic conditions in Venezuela in 2026 also appear to be gradually improving, continuing the upward trajectory in household incomes that began in 2025. Additionally, the US Government's engagement in a conflict with Iran has necessitated a reallocation of military focus away from Venezuela, reducing the likelihood of naval blockades or further armed operations in the country in the near term — a development that further contributes to the current period of relative stability.
([BBC 01/04/2026](https://www.bbc.com/mundo/articles/c36r5l25429o); [HumVenezuela 31/03/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/venezuela-bolivarian-republic/2025-follow-report-complex-humanitarian-emergency-venezuela-january-2026?_gl=1*utepnc*_gcl_au*NDg0NTgzNTEuMTc3NjM2OTYxMg..*_ga*NDU4MTg0MzExLjE3Njg1NjMzNjI.*_ga_E60ZNX2F68*czE3NzcxNzY4NTQkbzkzJGcxJHQxNzc3MTc2ODY1JGo0OSRsMCRoMA))

Three months after Nicolás Maduro's capture and Delcy Rodríguez's elevation to Interim President of Venezuela, the overall risk trend has shown a slight improvement. No signs of power struggles within the Rodríguez government have emerged, and figures seen as misaligned with the Trump administration's agenda seem to have been gradually pushed out of influential positions. Most notably, Vladimir Padrino López — one of Maduro's closest allies and a key figure in maintaining territorial control and military loyalty to the Socialist Party — was removed as Defense Minister after 14 years in the role. This marks a significant shift away from a Maduro and Chávez loyalist leadership toward a more politically neutral and ideologically independent cabinet. So far, his removal has not caused visible fractures or internal conflict within the armed forces.
These developments have been accompanied by the US Government's decision to reopen its Embassy in Venezuela, which had been closed since 2019. Despite these small gains, sustained US political and military pressure on Venezuela continues, highlighting the fragility of the current situation. The relationship between the two governments could quickly deteriorate and become much more confrontational if the Trump administration perceives non-compliance from Rodríguez and her cabinet.

Two months after the capture of Nicolás Maduro by US forces and the installation of former Vice-President Delcy Rodríguez as Interim President, the overall risk trend in Venezuela has moved towards stabilisation. There are no immediate indications of power struggles within the Government's senior political leadership, nor a significant increase in non-state armed group (NSAG) activity, although the risk of rapid deterioration persists. The new authorities have implemented the economic agreements with the US, including the dispatch of at least 80 million barrels of oil — Venezuela's primary export — and high-level engagement with US political and economic figures to establish platforms for foreign direct investment. Also, Delcy's administratation have pushed for laws that dicriminilized political opposition and the release of more than 400 previously detained opposition leaders, as well as the reversal of key policies implemented under the Maduro administration. 
That said, the United States continues to maintain some naval forces off the Venezuelan coast and sustained political pressure through consistent public messaging from the Trump administration on the conduct expected of Rodríguez and her administration. This highlights the fragility of current political arrangements and the possibility of military tension escalating rapidly as it did in early 2026, increasing risks of limited access to food and health services, as well as displacement spikes and reduced access to humanitarian services in high-risk conflict areas.
([DW 08/02/2026](https://www.dw.com/es/oposici%C3%B3n-reporta-400-presos-pol%C3%ADticos-excarcelados-en-venezuela/a-75858342); [BBC 06/02/2026](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/crmlz7r0zrxo); [Aljazeera 26/02/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/2/25/trump-says-us-has-received-80m-barrels-of-venezuelan-oil-3rd-tanker-seized))

Since the capture of Nicolás Maduro by US forces and the installation of former vice-president Delcy Rodríguez as interim president, the overall risk environment has stabilised. There are no immediate indications of power struggles within Venezuela’s senior political leadership or a significant increase in non-state armed group activity. The new authorities have reached economic agreements with the US, including oil sales – Venezuela’s main export – and planned investments by US companies, alongside political measures such as the release of political prisoners and a partial normalisation of diplomatic relations.
That said, the US continues to maintain a military presence off the Venezuelan coast, sustaining pressure despite the current period of relative calm. At the same time, the interim government has publicly stated that US military intervention must end, highlighting the fragility of the current arrangements and the risk that tensions could escalate again with little warning, increasing the risk of limited access to food, health, and protection services, as well as displacement spikes and reduced access to humanitarian services in conflict areas. ([CNN 21/01/2026](https://cnnespanol.cnn.com/2026/01/21/venezuela/delcy-rodriguez-venezuela-eeuu-petroleo-300-millones-dolares-efe), [InSight Crime 22/01/2026](https://insightcrime.org/news/will-guerrillas-lose-haven-post-maduro-venezuela/), [El Tiempo 25/01/2026](https://www.eltiempo.com/mundo/venezuela/delcy-rodriguez-basta-de-las-ordenes-de-washington-sobre-politicos-en-venezuela-3527009), [CNN 22/01/2026](https://cnnespanol.cnn.com/2026/01/22/venezuela/trump-mira-petroleo-rodriguez-demandas-trax))

Since early January 2026, the risk trend has deteriorated sharply, shifting from potential destabilisation to an acute crisis. The US military's capture of Nicolás Maduro on 3 January, followed by Delcy Rodríguez's installation as interim president, has triggered immediate power struggles among Rodríguez, military leaders, and Interior Minister Diosdado Cabello, who controls the police and colectivo networks.
Rodríguez has invited Washington to cooperate, stating that post-Maduro, Venezuela seeks an "agenda of cooperation" with the US Government, including in the energy sector. On 7 January, the US Department of Energy eased sanctions to permit Venezuelan oil transport to the US, indicating negotiation advances. That said, Cabello's defiant rhetoric, despite US President Donald Trump's threats, signals ideological pushback and risks colectivo mobilisation into militia violence and instability.
Cúcuta border crossings in Colombia hold steady at around 60,000 daily pendular movements, unchanged since 3 January, with official data and reports showing no displacement surge amid the turmoil. The risk outlook stays precarious, balancing between consolidation and fracture, depending on compliance in oil negotiations and sustained military cohesion. Pragmatic signals (such as Rodríguez's oil overtures and US sanctions relief) clash with military fragility, yielding a bifurcated short-term risk path. Oil deal progress and stabilised regime revenue for military salaries could keep needs high but without a sudden surge. That said, Cabello's opposition to Rodríguez's approach, plus delayed pay from stalled oil income, might ignite colectivo mobilisation, military splits, and conflict, leading to displacement spikes and restricted humanitarian access in conflict zones.
([Defense One 05/01/2026](https://www.defenseone.com/threats/2026/01/the-d-brief-january-05-2026/410450/#:~:text=), [CBS accessed 07/05/2025](https://www.cbsnews.com/live-updates/venezuela-maduro-capture-president-trump-senate-oil/), [Latina Republic 05/01/2026](https://latinarepublic.com/2026/01/05/colombia-reports-normal-operations-at-border-crossings-with-venezuela/), [CNN 07/01/2025](https://edition.cnn.com/world/live-news/trump-venezuela-oil-greenland-07-01-26), [NYT 03/01/2025](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/01/03/world/americas/us-venezuela-tensions-timeline.html), [CFR accessed 07/01/2025](https://www.cfr.org/global-conflict-tracker/conflict/instability-venezuela), [UN 06/01/2026](https://news.un.org/en/story/2026/01/1166708))

The US Government has designated the so‑called Cartel de los Soles as an international terrorist entity, granting the Trump administration expanded economic and legal instruments to increase pressure on Venezuela and potentially pursue armed action against individuals associated with the group. Shortly thereafter, President Donald Trump signalled a shift in US operations from primarily maritime interdiction in the Caribbean Sea to possible on‑land actions inside Venezuela. This prompted the Maduro administration to place the armed forces on alert while simultaneously leaving open a diplomatic track, in which any easing of US pressure appears tied to Nicolás Maduro’s departure from power and the prospect of exile options, including in countries such as Türkiye.
Public statements from both Washington and Caracas, as well as third‑party actors such as Türkiye, suggest that channels for dialogue remain nominally open and that some parties are encouraging a negotiated de‑escalation between the US and Venezuela. That said, there is currently no clear evidence of formal negotiations aimed at reducing tensions or reaching a political settlement, and reports of talks or proposals largely stem from isolated offers, indirect contacts, or unconfirmed media leaks rather than an established negotiation process.
([The Conversation 24/11/2025](https://theconversation.com/por-que-la-presion-de-trump-sobre-venezuela-no-tiene-precedentes-y-podria-llevar-a-una-intervencion-militar-268954), [CNN 24/11/2025](https://cnnespanol.cnn.com/2025/11/24/eeuu/gobierno-trump-designa-maduro-venezuela-organizacion-terrorista-extranjera-trax), [CNN 27/11/2025](https://edition.cnn.com/2025/11/27/americas/maduro-venezuela-military-caribbean-trump-intl-latam-vis), [DW 28/11/2025](https://www.dw.com/es/maduro-ordena-a-la-fuerza-a%C3%A9rea-estar-lista-para-defender-venezuela/a-74933077), [TWP 27/11/2025](https://www.washingtonpost.com/national-security/2025/11/27/venezuela-turkey-maduro-erdogan-exile/))
